options.why: Divided the wrong way. Conditioning on survival divides 3.80% by the survival rate (92.6%), which is below 1, so the figure grows.

options.label: Equal
options.why: Treated $C_3 - C_2$ as if it were already conditional. It is the unconditional view from time zero.

scenarios.takeaway: Conditional PD = marginal PD / survival to the start of the year, so it always exceeds the unconditional figure once defaults have occurred.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe a rating migration matrix and calculate the probability of default, cumulative probability of default, and marginal probability of default.

scenarios.setup: One-year rating migration matrix, years independent. Row X: 92% stay in X, 6% move to Y, 2% default. Row Y: 8% move to X, 82% stay in Y, 10% default. An issuer is rated X today.
scenarios.ask: Its unconditional probability of default during year 2, compared with the 2% year-1 PD, is:

options.label: Lower
options.why: Scaled 2% by the 98% that survive year 1 (1.96%), as if survivors kept the same 2% default rate. That ignores the 6% that migrate to Y.

options.label: Equal to 2%
options.why: Assumed a constant default rate. The matrix moves some issuers into Y, where default risk is five times higher.

working.label: Defaults from X after staying in X

scenarios.takeaway: For good grades the marginal PD rises with time because migration feeds the riskier grades. Cumulative two-year PD is 4.44%.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe a rating migration matrix and calculate the probability of default, cumulative probability of default, and marginal probability of default.

scenarios.setup: Merton model over a 3-year horizon, with the risk-free rate as asset drift: $d_2 = 1.60$, so the risk-neutral PD by year 3 is $N(-1.60) = 5.48\%$. The firm's expected asset return is 9%. A CVA system needs one constant average hazard rate.
scenarios.ask: The hazard rate to enter, per year, is closest to:

options.why: Scale slip: 1/30 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Scale slip: 1/10 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Divided $-\ln(1-0.0548) = 0.0564$ by $T^2 = 9$ instead of by $T = 3$.

scenarios.takeaway: Average hazard = $-\ln(1-Q(T))/T$. The 9% expected return would give a real-world PD, not the risk-neutral one a CVA system needs.
scenarios.lo_text: Define the hazard rate and use it to define probability functions for default time as well as to calculate conditional and unconditional default probabilities.

scenarios.setup: A five-year CDS on a mining company trades at 180 bp, with expected recovery of 35%. The average hazard rate follows from $s = \bar\lambda\,(1-R)$.
scenarios.ask: The implied average hazard rate, compared with the 1.80% spread, is:

options.label: Lower than 1.80%
options.why: Multiplied the spread by $(1-R)$ instead of dividing: $1.80\% \times 0.65 = 1.17\%$.

options.label: Equal to 1.80%
options.why: Ignored recovery, which is only valid when the loss given default is 100%.

scenarios.takeaway: The spread pays for expected loss, $\lambda \times LGD$, so the hazard rate is always above the spread when recovery is positive.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe CDS spreads and explain how CDS spreads can be used to estimate hazard rates.

scenarios.setup: CDS spreads on one name, recovery 40%: 3-year 400 bp, 5-year 350 bp. The average hazard rate to each maturity is $s/(1-R)$, giving 6.67% to year 3 and 5.83% to year 5.
scenarios.ask: The average hazard rate between year 3 and year 5 must be:

options.label: Between 5.83% and 6.67%
options.why: Averaged the two figures (6.25%). The 5-year number already contains the 3-year hazard, so the forward rate must lie on the far side of it.

options.label: Above 6.67%
options.why: Swapped the averages in the bootstrap, $(5 \times 6.67 - 3 \times 5.83)/2 = 7.9\%$.

scenarios.takeaway: An average that falls as the horizon lengthens means the forward hazard is below the longer average. An inverted CDS curve signals near-term distress.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe CDS spreads and explain how CDS spreads can be used to estimate hazard rates.

scenarios.setup: Merton model, one year: asset value JPY 800bn, debt due 600bn, asset volatility 20%, risk-free rate 4%, expected asset return 10% (continuous). With the risk-free drift the distance to default is 1.54, a risk-neutral PD of 6.2%. A stress scenario needs the real-world PD.
scenarios.ask: The real-world PD, compared with 6.2%, is:

options.label: Higher
options.why: Read the higher expected return as extra risk. A higher drift pushes assets further above the debt, so distance to default widens and PD shrinks.

options.label: Equal
options.why: Only the drift changes between the two cases, but the drift enters the numerator of the distance to default.

scenarios.takeaway: Real-world PD uses the expected return $\mu$ as drift; risk-neutral uses $r$. When $\mu > r$ the real-world PD is the smaller one.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe the difference between real-world and risk-neutral default probabilities and determine which one to use in the analysis of credit risk.

scenarios.setup: Merton distance to default $d_2$, computed with the risk-free rate over the whole life of the debt. Borrower (KRW bn): assets 500, zero-coupon debt 300 due in 2 years, asset volatility 22%, risk-free rate 4%. Bands: DD 3.0 or more A; 2.0 to below 3.0 BBB; 1.0 to below 2.0 BB; below 1.0 B.
scenarios.ask: The borrower's band is:

options.label: BBB
options.why: Used a one-year horizon (DD about 2.39). The debt runs for two years, so the numerator picks up two years of drift and the s.d. is $0.22\sqrt{2}$.

options.label: B
options.why: Kept only the drift term and dropped $\ln(A/D)$, which gives DD about 0.10.

scenarios.takeaway: Use the debt's own maturity in both the drift term and $\sigma\sqrt{T}$. The one-year short form would flatter the borrower by a full band.
scenarios.lo_text: Calculate distance to default and default probability using the Merton model.

scenarios.setup: Basel II IRB on a residential mortgage book: EAD GBP 400m, PD 1.50%, LGD 25%, average remaining maturity 18 years, 99.9% confidence. Retail correlation is fixed at 0.15, which gives a worst-case default rate (WCDR) of 14.56%. Capital is $K = EAD \times LGD \times (WCDR - PD)$.
scenarios.ask: The risk-weighted assets are closest to:

options.label: ≈ GBP 1.6m
options.why: Scale slip: 1/100 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ GBP 13m
options.why: Stopped at the capital charge $K$ and never multiplied by 12.5 to convert it into RWA.

options.label: ≈ GBP 54m
options.why: Scale slip: 1/3 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: RWA = 12.5 × K. The 18-year maturity is a distractor for retail; the risk weight here is about 41% of EAD.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe the application of the Vasicek’s model to estimate capital requirements under the Basel II internal-ratingsbased (IRB) approach.

scenarios.setup: Basel II advanced IRB, corporate loan of EUR 250m, $PD = 0.80\%$, $LGD = 40\%$, maturity $M = 4$ years. The maturity slope is $b = [0.11852 - 0.05478\ln(PD)]^2 = 0.1467$, and the maturity adjustment is $MA = \dfrac{1 + (M - 2.5)\,b}{1 - 1.5\,b}$.
scenarios.ask: The multiplier $MA$ applied to capital is closest to:

options.why: Computed the numerator $1 + 1.5 \times 0.1467$ and forgot to divide by $1 - 1.5b = 0.78$.
Applied no maturity adjustment, as is correct for retail. A 4-year corporate loan can be downgraded, so capital is scaled up.

scenarios.takeaway: For a 4-year corporate loan, capital is about 56% higher than the one-year figure because of the maturity adjustment.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe the application of the Vasicek’s model to estimate capital requirements under the Basel II internal-ratingsbased (IRB) approach.

scenarios.setup: Two-way CSA. The portfolio is worth +USD 58.6m to the bank. The counterparty has just been downgraded from AA (threshold USD 50m) to AA- (threshold USD 25m). The bank's own threshold term is zero because the portfolio is in its favour. The bank already holds USD 8.0m of cash collateral.
scenarios.ask: The credit support amount, before the minimum transfer amount and rounding, is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.6m
options.why: Still used the old AA threshold of USD 50m: $58.6 - 50 - 8.0 = 0.6$.

options.label: ≈ USD 33.6m
options.why: Subtracted the new threshold but forgot the USD 8.0m already held.

scenarios.takeaway: Thresholds are rating-linked: a downgrade lowers the threshold and the call jumps. Always net off collateral already held.
scenarios.lo_text: Differentiate between a two-way and one-way CSA agreement and describe how collateral parameters can be linked to credit quality.

scenarios.setup: Unilateral CVA on an uncollateralised 5-year swap, notional USD 200m, counterparty recovery 40%, no wrong-way risk. Discounted EPE (% of notional), years 1 to 5: 2.0, 3.2, 3.6, 3.0, 1.6. Counterparty cumulative PD (%): 1.5, 3.2, 5.0, 6.9, 8.9. The dealer's own spread is 90 bp.
scenarios.ask: The size of the UCVA charge is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.0014m
options.why: Left out the USD 200m notional, so the answer stays a fraction of notional (0.143%).

options.label: ≈ USD 0.097m
options.why: Scale slip: 1/3 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 0.79m
options.why: Weighted EPE by CUMULATIVE PDs instead of the marginal PD of each year.

scenarios.takeaway: UCVA = −LGD × Σ EPE × marginal PD × notional. The dealer's own spread belongs to DVA, not UCVA.
scenarios.lo_text: Calculate CVA and CVA as a spread with no wrong-way risk, netting, or collateralization.

scenarios.setup: Uncollateralised 5-year swap, notional EUR 150m, both LGDs 60%, survival adjustments ignored. $\sum EPE \times PD_C = 23.82 \times 10^{-4}$ and $\sum ENE \times PD_P = -7.66 \times 10^{-4}$ (ENE is negative). Convention: CVA negative, DVA positive, $BCVA = CVA + DVA$.
scenarios.ask: Compared with the CVA leg alone, the BCVA is:

options.label: Negative, and larger in size
options.why: Subtracted the DVA from the CVA ($-0.214 - 0.069 = -0.283$). DVA is a gain, so it is added with a positive sign.

options.label: Positive
options.why: The DVA leg (0.069) is only about a third of the CVA leg (0.214), so the net cannot turn positive.

scenarios.takeaway: DVA offsets part of CVA but rarely all of it. Check the sign of ENE before multiplying: a negative ENE turns the DVA into a positive number.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe debt value adjustment (DVA) and bilateral CVA (BCVA).

scenarios.setup: Gregory's average-exposure approximation: $UCVA \approx -\overline{EPE} \times s_C$, as a running spread. Undiscounted EPE (% of notional), years 1 to 5: 1.8, 2.6, 3.0, 2.8, 1.8. Counterparty 5-year spread 180 bp. LGD is 60%, but it is already inside the quoted spread.
scenarios.ask: The UCVA as a running spread is closest to:

options.label: ≈ -2.6 bp p.a.
options.why: Applied the 60% LGD on top of a spread that already embeds it.

options.label: ≈ -430 bp p.a.
options.why: Entered the average EPE as 2.4 instead of 0.024, a percent-as-decimal slip.

scenarios.takeaway: Average EPE × credit spread gives CVA as a running spread. No LGD input is needed because the spread already prices it.
scenarios.lo_text: Calculate DVA, BCVA, and BCVA as a spread.

scenarios.setup: A new 5-year swap, notional EUR 150m, is added to an existing netting set with the same counterparty. CVA figures (EUR m, negative convention): existing netting set $-1.84$; netting set including the new swap $-2.27$; new swap on its own $-0.96$.
scenarios.ask: The upfront CVA to charge for the new swap is:

options.label: -EUR 0.96m
options.why: Used the standalone CVA and ignored that the swap partly offsets the existing trades.

options.label: -EUR 2.27m
options.why: Charged the whole netting set's CVA to the new trade, including the part already booked.

scenarios.takeaway: Price a new trade at its incremental CVA: the netting set with it, minus the netting set without it.
scenarios.lo_text: Define and calculate incremental CVA and marginal CVA and explain how to convert CVA into a running spread.

scenarios.setup: A two-way, zero-threshold CSA with daily margin on an 8-year netting set (uncollateralised CVA $-$EUR 4.2m, 250 business days a year). Best-case collateralised CVA is the uncollateralised CVA divided by $\sqrt{\text{maturity}/\text{MPoR}}$. With over 5,000 trades the MPoR is 20 business days, not the usual 10.
scenarios.ask: The divisor $\sqrt{\text{maturity}/\text{MPoR}}$ is closest to:

options.why: Used the standard 10-day MPoR, $\sqrt{2000/10} = 14.1$. This netting set has 20 days.
Forgot the square root: $2000/20 = 100$.

scenarios.takeaway: A longer MPoR weakens the benefit of margining: the best case leaves about 10% of the CVA here, and reality is worse.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain the impact of incorporating collateralization into the CVA calculation, including the impact of margin period of risk, thresholds, and initial margins.

scenarios.setup: Final year of a 5-year CLO of 100 loans of USD 1m at Libor + 350 bp, Libor flat at 5%. Senior USD 85m at Libor + 50 bp, mezzanine USD 10m at Libor + 500 bp. By year 4, 24 loans have defaulted; 6 more default in year 5 (40% recovery, paid at once). The 70 survivors pay final interest and repay at par. A recovery account (5% interest) holds USD 16.385m after year 4 and is released at maturity.
scenarios.ask: After the senior notes are paid in full (principal and final interest, USD 89.675m), the cash left for the mezzanine is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 3.5m
options.why: Left out the USD 2.4m of year-5 recoveries on the 6 new defaults.

options.label: ≈ USD 10.0m
options.why: Counted 76 survivors, ignoring the 6 year-5 defaults. That overstates both interest and principal.

scenarios.takeaway: Waterfalls are paid top-down: with USD 5.9m left against USD 11.0m owed, the mezzanine loses about USD 5.1m.
scenarios.lo_text: Calculate and evaluate one or two iterations of interim cashflows in a three-tiered securitization structure.

scenarios.setup: Credit card master trust, month-end receivables INR 48.0bn. Past due: 30-59 days 2.4bn; 60-89 days 1.5bn; 90-119 days 1.2bn; 120+ days 0.6bn. Receivables written off during the month: 0.36bn. For credit card ABS, a delinquent receivable is one more than 90 days past due.
scenarios.ask: The delinquency ratio is closest to:

options.why: Divided 1.8 by 48.0 (0.0375) and wrote it as a percentage without multiplying by 100.
Scale slip: 1/30 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Used the month's write-offs, $0.36/48.0$. Write-offs are the default ratio, not delinquency.

scenarios.takeaway: Delinquency ratio = 90+ day receivables / pool balance. It leads the default ratio, so a rise is an early warning for amortisation triggers.
scenarios.lo_text: Define and calculate the delinquency ratio, default ratio, monthly payment rate (MPR), debt service coverage ratio (DSCR), the weighted average coupon (WAC), the weighted average maturity (WAM), and the weighted average life (WAL) for relevant securitized structures.

scenarios.setup: A credit card ABS has an early-amortisation trigger if the monthly payment rate (MPR) falls below 15.0%. MPR is the share of the pool repaid in the month, principal and interest together. This month: pool balance AUD 1,500m; principal collections 210m; finance-charge collections 27m; write-offs 6m; new receivables bought 180m.
scenarios.ask: The trigger is:

options.label: Hit: MPR is below 15%
options.why: Used principal collections only ($210/1500 = 14.0\%$). MPR counts interest collections as well.

options.label: Not hit: MPR is just above 15%

scenarios.takeaway: MPR = (principal + finance-charge collections) / pool balance. Write-offs and new purchases do not enter it.
scenarios.lo_text: Define and calculate the delinquency ratio, default ratio, monthly payment rate (MPR), debt service coverage ratio (DSCR), the weighted average coupon (WAC), the weighted average maturity (WAM), and the weighted average life (WAL) for relevant securitized structures.

scenarios.setup: An RMBS collateral pool has three loan groups: CAD 60m at 4.0% (300 months left), CAD 90m at 5.2% (240 months left) and CAD 150m at 6.0% (120 months left). The simple average of the three mortgage rates is 5.07%.
scenarios.ask: The pool's weighted average coupon (WAC), compared with 5.07%, is:

options.label: Below
options.why: The largest group (CAD 150m, half the pool) carries the highest rate, so the balance weights pull the average up, not down.

options.label: Equal
options.why: Treated the three groups as equal in size. WAC weights each rate by its balance.

scenarios.takeaway: WAC weights by balance, not by group count. The remaining terms are irrelevant to WAC (they feed WAM).
scenarios.lo_text: Define and calculate the delinquency ratio, default ratio, monthly payment rate (MPR), debt service coverage ratio (DSCR), the weighted average coupon (WAC), the weighted average maturity (WAM), and the weighted average life (WAL) for relevant securitized structures.

scenarios.setup: An RMBS pool, 18 months after origination. Start-of-month balance USD 820.0m, scheduled principal 1.4m, prepayments 5.2m, so $SMM = 5.2/818.6 = 0.635\%$ and $CPR = 7.36\%$. To state the speed against PSA, you need the 100% PSA benchmark CPR for this month.
scenarios.ask: The 100% PSA CPR at month 18 is:

options.why: Used the 6% plateau, which applies only from month 30. At month 18 the pool is still on the seasoning ramp.
Used the ramp step of 0.2% per month without multiplying by the 18 months of seasoning.

scenarios.takeaway: 100% PSA ramps 0.2% a month to 6% at month 30. Early in a pool's life that ramp, not 6%, is the denominator.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain the prepayment forecasting methodologies and calculate the constant prepayment rate (CPR) and the Public Securities Association (PSA) rate.

scenarios.setup: A portfolio of two bonds: A is GBP 1.0m (PD 4%, recovery 70%), B is GBP 0.8m (PD 6%, recovery 60%). Their default correlation is 25%, with joint default probability 1.45%. Correlation then rises to 50%.
scenarios.ask: The portfolio's expected credit loss:

options.label: Rises
options.why: Mixed up expected loss with unexpected loss. Correlation fattens the loss tail (VaR, UL) but expected loss is a sum of means.

options.label: Falls
options.why: Same mix-up in the other direction: more correlation never lowers the sum of the individual expected losses.

scenarios.takeaway: Expected loss is additive and does not depend on default correlation. Correlation drives the spread of losses, not their mean.
scenarios.lo_text: Define and calculate expected loss (EL).

scenarios.setup: A USD 200m bond portfolio: AA bonds USD 120m (1-year PD 4%, recovery 65%) and BB bonds USD 80m (PD 6%, recovery 40%). Defaults are independent.
scenarios.ask: Which bucket contributes more to the one-year expected loss?

options.label: AA, because it is the larger holding
options.why: Looked at exposure alone. BB has 1.5× the PD and 1.7× the loss rate (60% against 35%), which outweighs AA's 1.5× larger balance.

options.label: They contribute equally
options.why: Neither bucket's EL matches: 1.68m for AA against 2.88m for BB.

options.label: BB, despite being the smaller holding

scenarios.takeaway: Loss rate is 1 minus recovery, and EL = EAD × PD × loss rate for each bucket. A smaller, riskier bucket can dominate.
scenarios.lo_text: Define and calculate expected loss (EL).

scenarios.setup: A USD 50m bond book holds USD 30m of AA paper (1-year PD 1%, recovery 80%) and USD 20m of BB paper (1-year PD 2.5%, recovery 60%). You are building the 1-year expected credit loss bucket by bucket.
scenarios.ask: Which bucket contributes more to the expected loss?

options.label: BB, roughly three times as much as AA
AA, because it is the larger holding
options.why: Looked at exposure alone. BB has 2.5 times the default probability and twice the loss rate (40% against 20%), which more than offsets its smaller size.

options.label: About the same
options.why: Assumed the smaller BB position offsets its higher PD. Done properly it is USD 60,000 for AA against USD 200,000 for BB.

scenarios.takeaway: Expected loss is exposure x PD x loss rate. A riskier name can dominate the total even when it is the smaller position.
scenarios.lo_text: Define and calculate expected loss (EL).

scenarios.setup: One-year bond portfolio: USD 7m of Taylor (PD 6%, recovery 80%) and USD 9m of Simon (PD 5%, recovery 90%).
scenarios.ask: Portfolio expected loss from default is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 870,000
options.why: Used exposure x PD and never applied the loss rate (1 - recovery): 420,000 + 450,000.

options.label: ≈ USD 2,300,000
options.why: Used exposure x loss rate and never applied the default probability: 1.4m + 0.9m.

options.label: ≈ USD 13,000,000
options.why: Scale slip: 100× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: EL needs all three ingredients (exposure, PD, 1 - recovery) and is additive across positions.
scenarios.lo_text: Define and calculate expected loss (EL).

scenarios.setup: Two one-year bonds. Bond 1: USD 500,000, PD 5%, recovery 50%. Bond 2: USD 300,000, PD 3%, recovery 30%. The two default together with probability 2%, and their default correlation is 25%.
scenarios.ask: How does the portfolio expected loss compare with the sum of the two stand-alone expected losses?

options.label: Higher than the sum, because the defaults are positively correlated
options.why: Mixed up expected loss with unexpected loss. Correlation fattens the tail of the loss distribution; it does not move the mean.

options.label: Lower than the sum, because joint defaults overlap
options.why: Treated the 2% joint default as double counting. Expectations add whatever the dependence, so nothing is netted off.

scenarios.takeaway: Expectation is linear: portfolio EL is the sum of the parts. Correlation matters for unexpected loss, not EL.
scenarios.lo_text: Define and calculate expected loss (EL).

scenarios.setup: A firm's only debt is a 5-year zero-coupon bond with face value USD 100m, trading at USD 88m. The risk-free rate is 1%, continuously compounded. You are partway through finding the credit spread.
scenarios.ask: The bond's continuously compounded yield, before the risk-free rate is taken off, is closest to:

options.label: ≈ 12.8% a year
options.why: Used $-\ln(0.88)$ as it stands and forgot to divide by the 5 years, so the figure is a total over five years, not a yearly rate.

options.label: ≈ 1.6% a year
options.why: That is the spread, not the yield. The risk-free 1% has already been subtracted, which is the last step.

scenarios.takeaway: A zero-coupon yield is $-\ln(P/F)/T$. Divide by T first, then subtract the risk-free rate.
scenarios.lo_text: Compare default probabilities calculated from historical data with those calculated from credit yield spreads.

scenarios.setup: A firm's only debt is a 6-year zero-coupon bond with face value USD 200m, now worth USD 110m. The risk-free rate is 5%, continuously compounded.
scenarios.ask: The credit spread on the bond (continuous compounding) is closest to:

options.label: ≈ 0.17% a year
options.why: Scale slip: 1/30 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ 0.50% a year
options.why: Scale slip: 1/10 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ 1.7% a year
options.why: Divided by the 6 years twice: the 9.96% yield became 1.66%, and the risk-free rate was then ignored.

scenarios.takeaway: Spread = $-\ln(P/F)/T - r_f$. Both the 1/T and the subtraction are needed; a spread of tens of percent is a missing 1/T.
scenarios.lo_text: Compare default probabilities calculated from historical data with those calculated from credit yield spreads.

scenarios.setup: Debt with 5 years to maturity has face value USD 1,000 and trades at USD 834. The risk-free rate is 2%, continuously compounded.
scenarios.ask: The credit spread on this debt is:

options.label: Zero
options.why: Spread is zero only if the price equals the riskless value, $1000e^{-0.02 \times 5} = 904.84$. The market price is well below that.

options.label: Negative
options.why: Read the price discount to face (834 against 1,000) as a sign of a low yield. A lower price than the riskless value means a higher yield, so a positive spread.

scenarios.takeaway: Price below the riskless value of the same cash flow means yield above the risk-free rate, so the spread is positive.
scenarios.lo_text: Compare default probabilities calculated from historical data with those calculated from credit yield spreads.

scenarios.setup: A 5-year zero-coupon bond with face value USD 100m was issued two years ago and now trades at USD 80m. Its credit spread is 2%, continuously compounded. You want the risk-free rate implied by these data.
scenarios.ask: Which maturity goes into $y = -\ln(P/F)/T$?

options.label: 5 years, the original maturity
options.why: Used the original term. The price is today's, so T is what remains to maturity. This gives y = 4.46% and a risk-free rate of 2.46%.

options.label: 2 years, the time elapsed since issue
options.why: Used the age of the bond. Age plays no part in discounting the remaining payment.

scenarios.takeaway: Discount over the time remaining, not the original term. The yield is 7.44% and the risk-free rate 5.44%.
scenarios.lo_text: Compare default probabilities calculated from historical data with those calculated from credit yield spreads.

scenarios.setup: A firm's only debt is a 1-year zero-coupon bond with face value USD 800m. A Merton-type model gives an expected loss of USD 8.4m and a 0.1% quantile of the bond's future value of USD 503m. Credit VaR is defined as the 99.9th percentile loss in excess of the expected loss.
scenarios.ask: Compared with the 99.9th percentile loss of USD 297m (800 - 503), the credit VaR is:

options.label: Equal, since both measure the worst case
options.why: Ignored the "in excess of the expected loss" part of the definition. Credit VaR here is a deviation from the mean, not the raw tail loss.

options.label: Smaller, by the USD 8.4m expected loss
Larger, by the USD 8.4m expected loss
options.why: Added EL instead of subtracting it: 297 + 8.4 = 305.4.

scenarios.takeaway: When credit VaR is defined as the tail loss in excess of EL, always take EL off the percentile loss.
scenarios.lo_text: Define and calculate Credit VaR.

scenarios.setup: A USD 1m credit book is cut into ten equal USD 100,000 positions, all of them claims on the same obligor. The obligor has a 1-year default probability of 5% and recovery is zero. Credit VaR is the 99th percentile loss minus the expected loss.
scenarios.ask: The 99th percentile loss is closest to:

options.label: USD 100,000
options.why: Assumed one position defaults at a time, as if diversified. All ten sit on one obligor and default together.

options.label: USD 50,000
options.why: That is the expected loss (5% x 1m), not a percentile.

options.label: USD 0
options.why: No loss occurs 95% of the time, but a 99th percentile needs 99% coverage. The loss only takes the values 0 and 1m, so the percentile is 1m.

working.label: Loss distribution
working.display: Loss = 0 with probability 95%, USD 1m with probability 5%

scenarios.takeaway: One obligor means one perfectly correlated bet: the loss is all or nothing, and a 5% default chance puts the whole exposure at the 99th percentile.
scenarios.lo_text: Define and calculate Credit VaR.

scenarios.setup: A portfolio holds one 1-year zero-coupon bond with face value USD 6.5m. Its 1-year default probability is 7% and recovery is 88%. Credit VaR (99%) is the 99th percentile loss minus the expected loss.
scenarios.ask: The 99% credit VaR is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 7,300
options.why: Scale slip (1/100): a percent-versus-decimal mix-up.

options.label: ≈ USD 55,000
options.why: Reported the expected loss (7% x 780,000) instead of the percentile loss less EL.

options.label: ≈ USD 241,667
options.why: Scale slip: 1/3 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: With a single bond whose PD exceeds the tail probability, the percentile loss is the full loss given default; credit VaR is that minus EL.
scenarios.lo_text: Define and calculate Credit VaR.

scenarios.setup: A homogeneous loan book has EAD USD 350m, an expected default rate of 2.5% and recovery of 60%. The 99.9% worst-case default rate (WCDR) is 10.25%. Here credit VaR is defined as the loss not exceeded at 99.9%, namely WCDR x EAD x LGD.
scenarios.ask: Compared with the unexpected loss (worst-case loss minus expected loss), this credit VaR is:

options.label: The same
options.why: Assumed credit VaR always nets off EL. Under this definition it is the whole worst-case loss, so EL stays inside it.

options.label: Smaller, by the expected loss
options.why: Reversed the comparison: the unexpected loss is the one with EL removed, so it is the smaller figure.

scenarios.takeaway: Check which definition the question states: WCDR x EAD x LGD includes EL; the unexpected-loss version takes it off.
scenarios.lo_text: Define and calculate Credit VaR.

scenarios.setup: Two loans. Loan 1: EAD USD 200m, LGD 45%, PD 2%, 99.9% WCDR 8%. Loan 2: EAD USD 100m, LGD 60%, PD 3%, 99.9% WCDR 12%. Credit VaR is the sum of the loans' worst-case losses, WCDR x EAD x LGD.
scenarios.ask: The 1-year 99.9% credit VaR is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 3.6 million
options.why: Used the average PDs (2% and 3%) in place of the worst-case rates, which gives the expected loss.

options.label: ≈ USD 36 million
options.why: Applied the 12% WCDR to the whole USD 300m and skipped LGD.

options.label: ≈ USD 140 million
options.why: Scale slip: 10× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: Worst-case loss per loan is WCDR x EAD x LGD. Swap in PD and you get the expected loss, far below the tail figure.
scenarios.lo_text: Define and calculate Credit VaR.

scenarios.setup: Two borrowers, A and B, each have a 9.0% probability of default. Their default correlation is 0.28.
scenarios.ask: The joint probability that both default is closest to:

options.why: Scale slip: 1/10 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Assumed independence: $0.09 \times 0.09$. The positive correlation was ignored.
Used the perfect-correlation limit, where B defaults whenever A does.

scenarios.takeaway: Joint PD = $\pi_1\pi_2 + \rho\sigma_1\sigma_2$. At correlation 0.28 the covariance term is almost three times the independent one.
scenarios.lo_text: Define and calculate default correlation for credit portfolios.

scenarios.setup: Companies A and B have default probabilities of 5% and 10%. Their default correlation is 0.6, a high value.
scenarios.ask: The joint probability of default lies:

options.label: Below 0.5%
options.why: Took 0.5% (the independent product 5% x 10%) as the ceiling. A positive correlation pushes the joint PD above it.

options.label: Above 5%
options.why: Added the PDs or let the correlation inflate it past A's own PD. Both must default, so it cannot exceed the smaller PD of 5%.

scenarios.takeaway: Joint PD is bounded: at least the independent product (for positive correlation) and at most the smaller of the two PDs.
scenarios.lo_text: Define and calculate default correlation for credit portfolios.

scenarios.setup: Two credits have default probabilities of 0.4% and 1.0%, with default correlation 10%. You build the joint PD from two terms: the independent product $\pi_1\pi_2$ and the correlation term $\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2$.
scenarios.ask: Which term is larger?

options.label: The independent product, because the PDs are small
options.why: Compared the PDs as small numbers. The standard deviations $\sqrt{\pi(1-\pi)}$ are about 6% and 10%, far larger than the PDs, so the correlation term wins.

options.label: They are about equal
options.why: Neither term is close: 0.0628% against 0.004%.

options.label: The correlation term, by roughly 15 times

scenarios.takeaway: For rare defaults the standard deviations are roughly the square roots of the PDs, so the correlation term dwarfs $\pi_1\pi_2$ even at modest correlation.
scenarios.lo_text: Define and calculate default correlation for credit portfolios.

scenarios.setup: Loans to X and Y have default probabilities of 10% and 4%. The probability that both default is 3.93%. Independence would give 0.4%, and the largest possible joint probability is 4%.
scenarios.ask: The implied default correlation is:

options.label: Close to zero
options.why: Looked at the small joint probability in absolute terms. It must be compared with the 0.4% independence benchmark, and it is almost ten times that.

options.label: Moderate, around 0.3
options.why: Took the midpoint of the range. The joint PD is 3.93% against a ceiling of 4%, which sits at the very top of the range.

scenarios.takeaway: Judge a joint PD against its two benchmarks: the independent product (rho = 0) and the smaller PD (rho near 1).
scenarios.lo_text: Define and calculate default correlation for credit portfolios.

scenarios.setup: Two credits have default probabilities of 0.3% and 0.4% and a joint default probability of 0.2%. Default correlation is covariance divided by $\sigma_1\sigma_2$, where $\sigma = \sqrt{\pi(1-\pi)}$.
scenarios.ask: The denominator $\sigma_1\sigma_2$ is closest to:

options.why: Multiplied the two variances $\pi(1-\pi)$ and skipped the square roots.
Added the two standard deviations (0.055 + 0.063) instead of multiplying them.

scenarios.takeaway: The denominator is a product of standard deviations, each about the square root of a small PD, so it is a few thousandths here.
scenarios.lo_text: Define and calculate default correlation for credit portfolios.

scenarios.setup: 1,000 equal loans to borrowers all rated BB at the start of year 1. Cumulative default rates for BB: 0.63% after year 1, 1.93% after year 2, 3.46% after year 3. Ratings changes are ignored. You want the defaults that occur during year 3 only.
scenarios.ask: The year-3-only default rate is closest to:

options.why: Used the cumulative three-year figure, which includes defaults from years 1 and 2.
Picked the year-2 cumulative figure instead of the year-3 increment.
Used the year-1 figure, which is the first-year default rate, not year 3.

scenarios.takeaway: Cumulative default rates need differencing: the default rate in a single year is the increase in the cumulative curve.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe the relationship between borrower rating and probability of default.

scenarios.setup: A firm has USD 2.0m of senior debt and USD 0.5m of subordinated debt. In liquidation its assets realise USD 2.25m, distributed strictly by seniority.
scenarios.ask: The subordinated debt recovers:

options.label: Nothing
options.why: Assumed juniors are wiped out whenever assets fall short of total debt (2.5m). Assets still exceed the senior claim by 0.25m, which goes to the juniors.

options.label: All of its face value
options.why: Ignored that total debt (2.5m) exceeds the assets (2.25m), so someone takes a loss, and it is the junior class.

scenarios.takeaway: Pay senior first, then see what is left: junior debt takes the shortfall, here a 50% recovery.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe recovery rates and their dependencies on default rates.

scenarios.setup: Expected loss rate = PD x (1 - recovery). In normal times PD is 2% and recovery 40%. In a recession stress PD rises to 5%, and historically recovery rates fall when default rates rise, to 30% here. Holding recovery at 40% would give a loss rate of 3.0%.
scenarios.ask: The stressed expected loss rate with 30% recovery is:

options.label: Equal to 3.0%
options.why: Kept recovery at its normal level. Defaults and recoveries move against each other, so the stress must lower recovery.

options.label: Lower than 3.0%
options.why: Read a lower recovery rate as a smaller loss. Lower recovery means a larger loss given default.

scenarios.takeaway: Recovery is negatively correlated with default. In a stress, raise PD and cut recovery together.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe recovery rates and their dependencies on default rates.

scenarios.setup: Two credits (A- and BBB+) have 1-year default probabilities of 2.5% and 3.3%, and the probability that both default is 0.8%. Default correlation is the covariance $\pi_{12} - \pi_1\pi_2$ divided by the product of the two Bernoulli standard deviations $\sqrt{\pi(1-\pi)}$.
scenarios.ask: The implied default correlation is closest to:

options.why: Divided by the sum of the two standard deviations instead of their product.
Scale slip: 3× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Divided by the product of the variances $\pi(1-\pi)$ instead of the standard deviations; a correlation can never exceed 100%.

scenarios.takeaway: Default correlation divides by the standard deviations, not the variances: with small $\pi$, $\sigma \approx \sqrt{\pi}$ is far bigger than $\pi$.
scenarios.lo_text: Define and calculate default correlation for credit portfolios.

scenarios.setup: A BBB credit (default probability 0.3%) and a CCC credit (0.5%) have a joint default probability of 0.02% over the horizon. You have the covariance, $0.0002 - 0.003 \times 0.005 = 0.000185$, and still need the divisor of the default-correlation formula, $\sigma_1\sigma_2 = \sqrt{\pi_1(1-\pi_1)\pi_2(1-\pi_2)}$.
scenarios.ask: The divisor $\sigma_1\sigma_2$ is closest to:

options.why: Multiplied the two variances $\pi(1-\pi)$ and forgot the final square root (this is about $\pi_1\pi_2$).
Added the two standard deviations (0.0547 + 0.0705) instead of multiplying them.

scenarios.takeaway: The divisor is a product of standard deviations, a few thousandths here; the answer is a correlation near 0.05, not 0.5 or 5.
scenarios.lo_text: Define and calculate default correlation for credit portfolios.

scenarios.setup: Two prime counterparties each have a 1-year default probability of 5.0%, modelled as Bernoulli events with default correlation 0.5. The joint default probability is the sum of a correlation term $\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2$ and an independence term $\pi_1\pi_2$.
scenarios.ask: Which term dominates the joint default probability?

options.label: The independence term $\pi_1\pi_2$
options.why: $\pi_1\pi_2 = 0.0025$ is the product of two small numbers; the correlation term is $0.5 \times 0.0475 = 0.02375$, about ten times larger.

options.label: The correlation term, by a wide margin
They are about equal
options.why: Roughly equal would need $\rho$ near 0.05 (the correlation term would then be about 0.0024).

scenarios.takeaway: At moderate correlation the covariance term swamps $\pi_1\pi_2$: a 5% name pair with $\rho = 0.5$ defaults jointly about 2.6% of the time, not 0.25%.
scenarios.lo_text: Define and calculate default correlation for credit portfolios.

scenarios.setup: Two credits each have a 1-year default probability of 2.0%. In a single-factor model with asset correlation 0.25, their joint default probability is 0.136%. Default correlation is $(\pi_{12} - \pi^2) / (\pi(1-\pi))$.
scenarios.ask: Compared with the asset correlation of 0.25, the implied default correlation is:

options.label: About the same
options.why: Treated asset correlation and default correlation as one quantity. They differ: default correlation sits well below asset correlation.

options.label: Higher
options.why: Saw the joint probability (0.136%) is over three times the independent 0.04% and read that as a bigger correlation; the ratio is not the correlation.

scenarios.takeaway: Default correlation is much smaller than the asset correlation that produces it: here 0.25 of asset correlation gives only about 0.05 of default correlation.
scenarios.lo_text: Estimate the probability of a joint default of any pair of credits and the default correlation between any pair of credits using the single factor model.

scenarios.setup: A USD 1 million portfolio holds 100 equal credits, each with a 3% default probability and zero recovery. Defaults are independent, so the number of defaults is binomial with $n = 100$, $\pi = 0.03$ (mean 3). The 95th percentile of the number of defaults is 6.
scenarios.ask: The 95th-percentile portfolio loss is:

options.label: USD 30,000
options.why: Used the expected number of defaults (3) instead of the 95th percentile (6); that is the expected loss, not the loss quantile.

options.label: USD 600,000
options.why: Sized each credit at USD 100,000 (divided by 10 instead of 100) before multiplying by 6 defaults.

scenarios.takeaway: Credit VaR is the loss quantile minus expected loss. Here 6 defaults against a mean of 3 gives a VaR equal to the expected loss.
scenarios.lo_text: Assess the impact of correlation on a credit portfolio and its Credit VaR.

scenarios.setup: A USD 1,000,000 portfolio has 20 positions, each with a 2% default probability and zero recovery. All 20 are obligations of the same obligor, so default correlation is 1 and the portfolio behaves like one credit: a 2% chance of losing everything, 98% of losing nothing.
scenarios.ask: The 99th-percentile portfolio loss is:

options.label: USD 0
options.why: Read the 98% chance of no loss as covering the 99% level; but the worst 1% of outcomes lies inside the 2% default scenario.

options.label: USD 20,000
options.why: Quoted the expected loss ($0.02 \times$ 1,000,000), which is the mean, not a quantile.

working.label: Compare with default probability
working.display: $2\% > 1\%$, so the 1% tail sits inside the default outcome

scenarios.takeaway: At correlation 1, if the default probability exceeds the tail (1 minus the confidence level), the loss quantile is the whole portfolio.
scenarios.lo_text: Assess the impact of correlation on a credit portfolio and its Credit VaR.

scenarios.setup: A USD 100 million portfolio of credits that all behave identically (default correlation 1). Each has a 2% default probability and zero recovery. Credit VaR is the loss quantile at the confidence level minus the expected loss.
scenarios.ask: At 95% confidence the credit VaR is:

options.label: Positive
options.why: Took the 95th-percentile loss as the full USD 100 million. But default has only a 2% chance, below the 5% tail, so the quantile is not the full loss.

options.label: Exactly zero
options.why: Stopped at the zero loss quantile and did not subtract the USD 2 million expected loss.

working.label: 95th percentile loss
working.display: 0, because 98% of outcomes have no loss

scenarios.takeaway: Credit VaR is a quantile minus the mean, so it can be negative when the default probability is below the tail probability.
scenarios.lo_text: Assess the impact of correlation on a credit portfolio and its Credit VaR.

scenarios.setup: A USD 1,000,000 portfolio holds 50 equal credits, each with a 2% default probability and zero recovery. With default correlation 0 the 99th percentile is 4 defaults. With correlation 1 the portfolio acts as one credit that defaults entirely with probability 2%.
scenarios.ask: Moving correlation from 0 to 1 raises the 99% credit VaR by about:

options.label: ≈ USD 2,760,000
options.why: Scale slip: 3× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 9,200,000
options.why: Scale slip (10×): the change cannot exceed the USD 1,000,000 portfolio.

options.label: ≈ USD 27,600,000
options.why: Scale slip: 30× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: Expected loss is unchanged by correlation; only the tail moves. Going from 0 to 1 takes VaR from about 6% to about 98% of the portfolio.
scenarios.lo_text: Assess the impact of correlation on a credit portfolio and its Credit VaR.

scenarios.setup: A USD 600 million portfolio holds 40 equal credits, each with a 3.0% default probability and loss given default 80%. Default correlation is 0. The 99th percentile of the number of defaults is 4. You are building credit VaR as the 99th-percentile loss minus expected loss.
scenarios.ask: The expected loss is closest to:

options.label: USD 18m
options.why: Left out the 80% loss given default: $600 \times 0.03 = 18$.

options.label: USD 12m
options.why: Took the loss on a single default ($15 \times 0.8$) instead of scaling by the number of expected defaults.

options.label: USD 48m
options.why: That is the 99th-percentile loss (4 defaults), not the expected loss.

scenarios.takeaway: Expected loss uses PD $\times$ LGD $\times$ exposure; the quantile loss uses the defaults count $\times$ LGD $\times$ exposure. VaR is the gap.
scenarios.lo_text: Assess the impact of correlation on a credit portfolio and its Credit VaR.

scenarios.setup: Single-factor credit model. A position has $\beta = 0.8$ and default probability 1%, so $k = N^{-1}(0.01) = -2.33$. For a loss level $x = 0.01$, also $N^{-1}(x) = -2.33$. The market value that produces that loss level is $m = [k - \sqrt{1-\beta^2}\,N^{-1}(x)]/\beta$.
scenarios.ask: The market-factor value $m$ is:

options.label: Below -2.33
options.why: Added the second term instead of subtracting it: $(-2.33 - 1.398)/0.8 = -4.66$.

options.label: Positive
options.why: Flipped the sign of $k$ (used +2.33), which gives $m = +4.66$; a bad market outcome must be negative.

scenarios.takeaway: Subtracting a negative term pulls the numerator toward zero, so $m$ is a milder bad draw than $k$ itself.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe the use of a single factor model to measure portfolio credit risk, including the impact of correlation.

scenarios.setup: Single-factor model: conditional default probability $p(m) = N[(k - \beta m)/\sqrt{1-\beta^2}]$. A firm has $\beta = 0.60$ and $k = -1.645$ (unconditional PD 5.0%). In a downturn the market factor is $m = -1.41$.
scenarios.ask: The argument of $N(\cdot)$ is closest to:

options.why: Left out the division by $\sqrt{1-\beta^2} = 0.8$: the numerator alone is $-0.799$.
Ignored the downturn: $-1.645 / 0.8 = -2.06$ is just the unconditional threshold rescaled.

scenarios.takeaway: A bad factor draw ($m < 0$) shifts the numerator toward zero; the rescaled argument near $-1$ means roughly a 16% default probability, triple the 5% baseline.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe the use of a single factor model to measure portfolio credit risk, including the impact of correlation.

scenarios.setup: Single-factor model: asset return $a = \beta m + \sqrt{1-\beta^2}\,\epsilon$, with $m$ (market) and $\epsilon$ (idiosyncratic) independent standard normals. A firm's systematic risk is 70% of its return variance and idiosyncratic risk the other 30%.
scenarios.ask: The loading $\beta$ is closest to:

options.why: Used the idiosyncratic share (30%) instead of the systematic share.
Took the square root of the idiosyncratic share, $\sqrt{0.30} = 0.55$.
Treated the variance share as the loading itself; $\beta^2$ is the share, so $\beta$ needs a square root.

scenarios.takeaway: The loading $\beta$ is the square root of the systematic variance share; $\beta^2$ is the share itself.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe the use of a single factor model to measure portfolio credit risk, including the impact of correlation.

scenarios.setup: One-factor Gaussian copula with common copula correlation 0.25, so each loading is $a = \sqrt{0.25} = 0.5$. Each company has a 10% 5-year default probability ($N^{-1}(0.10) = -1.2816$). The common factor is at its 1st percentile, $F = -2.326$. Conditional PD is $N[(N^{-1}(Q) - aF)/\sqrt{1-a^2}]$.
scenarios.ask: The conditional 5-year default probability is closest to:

options.why: Scale slip: 3× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Scale slip: 10× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Scale slip: 30× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: A 1st-percentile factor almost cancels the firm's default threshold, so the conditional PD lands just under 50% even though the unconditional PD is 10%.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe the Gaussian copula model for time to default and calculate the probability of default using the one-factor Gaussian copula model.

scenarios.setup: A Gaussian-copula simulation tracks default over 5 years. A company's cumulative default probabilities at years 1 to 5 are 1%, 3%, 6%, 10% and 15%. Its simulated standard normal draw is $x = -1.60$, and $N(-1.60) = 5.5\%$. The company defaults in the first year whose cumulative probability exceeds that figure.
scenarios.ask: In which year does it default?

options.label: Year 2
options.why: Picked the last year whose cumulative probability (3%) is still below 5.5%, which is the year it survives, not the year it defaults.

options.label: No default within 5 years
options.why: Thought $x$ must fall below the 1% threshold ($-2.33$); the draw only has to fall below the year-3 threshold.

scenarios.takeaway: Compare the draw with the cumulative thresholds: default happens in the first year whose cumulative probability exceeds $N(x)$.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe the Gaussian copula model for time to default and calculate the probability of default using the one-factor Gaussian copula model.

scenarios.setup: Four CDS trades on the same reference credit and maturity, all compressed into one contract. The bank is long protection (it bought) on notionals of USD 300,000 and USD 900,000, and short protection (it sold) on USD 800,000 and USD 250,000.
scenarios.ask: The single compressed contract is:

options.label: Short protection
options.why: Swapped the labels: long protection is the bought side, and the bought trades (USD 1,200,000) outweigh the sold ones (USD 1,050,000).

options.label: Flat: the trades cancel completely
options.why: Compression offsets only the overlapping notional. The legs are USD 1,200,000 and USD 1,050,000, so USD 150,000 survives.

scenarios.takeaway: Compression nets same-credit, same-maturity trades into one position on the bigger side: here USD 150,000 of long protection replaces four trades.
scenarios.lo_text: Provide examples of trade compression of derivative positions, calculate net notional exposure amount, and identify the party holding the net contract position in a trade compression.

scenarios.setup: Three single-name CDS trades, same maturity, different counterparties and coupons. The bank is long protection EUR 9m on NUMU, long protection EUR 6m on WKL, and short protection EUR 7m on NUMU. Trades are compressed by reference credit only.
scenarios.ask: Total notional across the contracts left after compression is closest to:

options.label: ≈ EUR 0.8m
options.why: Scale slip (1/10). The total cannot fall below the untouched WKL position of 6.

options.label: ≈ EUR 2m
options.why: Netted NUMU ($9 - 7 = 2$) but dropped the WKL EUR 6m, which has nothing to offset against and stays on the books.

options.label: ≈ EUR 22m
options.why: No compression: just the gross sum $9 + 6 + 7$. The NUMU long and short legs must be offset.

scenarios.takeaway: Compress by reference credit and maturity; counterparty and coupon do not matter. Positions on a credit with nothing to offset stay in the total.
scenarios.lo_text: Provide examples of trade compression of derivative positions, calculate net notional exposure amount, and identify the party holding the net contract position in a trade compression.

scenarios.setup: A firm writes a European call: spot EUR 67, strike EUR 45, 9 months. The option is deep in the money and worth roughly EUR 23. The buyer paid the full premium at inception and owes nothing further.
scenarios.ask: The firm's counterparty credit exposure on this trade is:

options.label: About EUR 23, the option's value
options.why: That is the exposure of the option buyer. For the writer the option is a liability, $V = -c$, and exposure is $\max(V, 0)$.

options.label: Negative, about −EUR 23
options.why: Exposure is floored at zero. A negative mark-to-market is what the firm owes, not something a counterparty's default can take from it.

scenarios.takeaway: Only the holder of a long option faces counterparty exposure once the premium is paid; the writer's exposure is zero however deep in the money the option is.
scenarios.lo_text: Identify typical credit exposure profiles for various derivative contracts and combination profiles.

scenarios.setup: 21 exposures sit in one netting set. They are jointly normal with equal volatility and an average pairwise correlation of 0.3. The netting factor (net over gross exposure) is $\sqrt{n + n(n-1)\bar\rho}\,/\,n$.
scenarios.ask: The netting factor is closest to:

options.why: Scale slip: 3× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Left out the square root: $147/21 = 7.0$. A netting factor cannot exceed 1.
Scale slip: 100× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: The factor runs from $1/\sqrt{n}$ (independent) up to 1 (perfectly correlated). With $\bar\rho = 0.3$ it sits well above the independent case.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain the general impact of aggregation on exposure, and the impact of aggregation on exposure when there is correlation between transaction values.

scenarios.setup: Eight independent exposures with equal volatility sit in one netting set. The netting factor is net exposure divided by gross exposure, so 100% means no netting benefit.
scenarios.ask: The netting factor is:

options.label: Between 50% and 100%
options.why: Took $1 - 1/n = 87.5\%$, as if each extra exposure removed only a sliver. Independent standard deviations add in quadrature: $\sqrt{n}\sigma$ against $n\sigma$.
Added the volatilities in a straight line, which is the perfectly correlated case. Independence gives a large benefit.

scenarios.takeaway: For independent equal-volatility exposures the netting factor is $1/\sqrt{n}$: already about 35% at $n = 8$.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain the general impact of aggregation on exposure, and the impact of aggregation on exposure when there is correlation between transaction values.

scenarios.setup: Two trades under five equally likely scenarios. Trade 1: 20, 14, 3, −5, −15. Trade 2: −15, −5, 3, −10, −30. Exposure is the positive part of value. With netting, the two values are added first and then floored at zero.
scenarios.ask: Netting removes the most exposure in:

options.label: Scenario 3 (3 and 3)
options.why: Both trades are positive, so the sum equals the gross exposure: nothing offsets. Netting helps only when values have opposite signs.

options.label: Scenario 5 (−15 and −30)
options.why: Both trades are negative: gross and netted exposure are already zero, so there is nothing left to remove.

scenarios.takeaway: Add the trade values first, then take the positive part. Netting reduces exposure only where one trade is in the money and the other out of it.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain the general impact of aggregation on exposure, and the impact of aggregation on exposure when there is correlation between transaction values.

scenarios.setup: A bank holds a swap with a client under an enforceable netting agreement; the CVA charge on it is EUR 410,000. A second trade with the same client would carry a standalone charge of EUR 360,000. With both trades in the netting set the CVA charge is EUR 280,000.
scenarios.ask: The second trade's incremental CVA charge is:

options.label: Positive, equal to its standalone EUR 360,000
options.why: Used the standalone charge, which ignores netting with the swap already held. Incremental CVA is the netting-set charge after minus before.

options.label: Positive, equal to EUR 280,000
options.why: Took the new netting-set charge as the increment without subtracting the EUR 410,000 already being carried.

options.label: Negative: it lowers the total charge

scenarios.takeaway: Incremental CVA is after minus before. A trade that offsets existing exposure can lower the charge even though its standalone CVA is positive.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain how netting can be incorporated into the CVA calculation.

scenarios.setup: Stress loss is stressed EL minus current EL, with EL = value × PD × (1 − recovery). Taylor bond: USD 7m, PD 6% rising to 12%, recovery 80%. Simon bond: USD 9m, PD 5% rising to 18%, recovery 90%.
scenarios.ask: Which bond adds more to the portfolio's stress loss?

options.label: Taylor
options.why: Went by the bigger loss given default (20% against 10%) and the higher starting PD. The stress loss is the rise in EL: Simon's PD jumps 13 points against Taylor's 6, on a larger bond.

options.label: They are about equal
options.why: Compared the stressed ELs (USD 168,000 against USD 162,000), which are close. The stress loss uses the increase over each current EL: USD 84,000 against USD 117,000.

scenarios.takeaway: Stress loss is the change in EL, so compare the increases, not the stressed levels: the larger PD jump outweighs the smaller LGD.
scenarios.lo_text: Differentiate between stressed expected loss and stress loss of a credit portfolio, and calculate the stress loss on a loan portfolio and the stress loss on a derivative portfolio.

scenarios.setup: Expected loss is EPE × LGD × PD for each counterparty. A: PD 3% to 4%, LGD 5% to 10%, EPE USD 4.37m to USD 5.46m. B: PD 18% to 23%, LGD 20% to 40%, EPE USD 3.99m to USD 4.99m. Suppose only one of the three inputs is stressed.
scenarios.ask: Which single stressed input would add the most to the portfolio's expected loss?

options.label: PD
options.why: PD is the headline input, but it rises only about a third at A and a quarter at B. Adds roughly USD 42,000.

options.label: EPE
options.why: EPE rises about 25% at both counterparties, less than a doubling. Adds roughly USD 38,000.

working.label: LGD only
working.display: LGD doubles at both, so EL doubles: $+0.150\text{m}$

scenarios.takeaway: Compare proportional moves: LGD doubles for both counterparties, while PD and EPE rise by only a quarter to a third. The biggest multiplier dominates.
scenarios.lo_text: Differentiate between stressed expected loss and stress loss of a credit portfolio, and calculate the stress loss on a loan portfolio and the stress loss on a derivative portfolio.

scenarios.setup: Counterparty DD: EPE USD 300m, LGD 65%, default probability 1.00% now and 1.60% under stress. Expected loss is PD × EPE × LGD, and the stress loss is stressed EL minus current EL.
scenarios.ask: DD's stress loss is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.117m
options.why: Scale slip (1/10). A PD rise of 0.6% on EPE × LGD of 195 is already over 1.

options.label: ≈ USD 3.12m
options.why: Reported the stressed EL itself ($0.016 \times 300 \times 0.65$) without subtracting the current EL.

options.label: ≈ USD 117m
options.why: Used the PD change as 0.6 instead of 0.006 (percent entered as a whole number).

scenarios.takeaway: Stress loss is the increase in EL, not the stressed EL: here 1.17 against 3.12.
scenarios.lo_text: Differentiate between stressed expected loss and stress loss of a credit portfolio, and calculate the stress loss on a loan portfolio and the stress loss on a derivative portfolio.

scenarios.setup: A loan book of USD 250m has recovery 60%. PD is 2.5% in normal conditions and 7.0% under stress, and the asset correlation is 0.25. The stress loss is defined as stressed expected loss minus current expected loss.
scenarios.ask: If the correlation were raised to 0.60, with PDs unchanged, the stress loss would:

options.label: Rise
options.why: Treated correlation as a driver of expected loss. It shapes the tail of the loss distribution, but $\text{EL} = \text{EAD} \times \text{PD} \times \text{LGD}$ has no correlation term.

options.label: Fall
options.why: Read higher correlation as a diversification effect on the expected loss. Either way, correlation does not enter EL.

scenarios.takeaway: Stress loss on an expected-loss basis is $\text{EL}^S - \text{EL}$. Correlation matters for unexpected loss, not here.
scenarios.lo_text: Differentiate between stressed expected loss and stress loss of a credit portfolio, and calculate the stress loss on a loan portfolio and the stress loss on a derivative portfolio.

scenarios.setup: CVA = LGD × EE × $q^*$. Exposure is USD 5m with LGD 60%. After a shock the marginal default probability $q^*$ doubles from 1.5% to 3.0%; exposure is unchanged.
scenarios.ask: The stress loss on the CVA, as a percentage of the initial CVA, is:

options.why: Divided the increase by the stressed CVA ($45{,}000 / 90{,}000$) instead of the initial CVA.
Gave the ratio stressed CVA over initial CVA. The stress loss is the excess, which is one times the initial.

scenarios.takeaway: CVA is linear in $q^*$ at fixed exposure, so doubling $q^*$ doubles CVA: the stress loss equals the initial charge.
scenarios.lo_text: Calculate the stressed CVA and the stress loss on CVA.

scenarios.setup: $\text{BCVA} = \text{LGD}_n \cdot EE \cdot q_n S_I - \text{LGD}_I \cdot NEE \cdot q_I S_n$. Counterparty: LGD 60%, EE USD 150m, $q_n = 2\%$, $S_n = 0.97$. Bank: LGD 50%, NEE USD 100m. Under stress the bank's own $q_I$ rises 1% to 5% and $S_I$ falls 0.98 to 0.94. Counterparty inputs are unchanged.
scenarios.ask: For the bank, the stress is a:

options.label: Loss: the net BCVA charge rises
options.why: Assumed wider spreads are bad news. The bank's own widening enlarges the second (own-default) term, which reduces the net charge.

options.label: No effect: counterparty inputs are unchanged
options.why: The bank's own $q_I$ and $S_I$ enter the formula: they drive the second term and scale the first.

options.label: Gain: the net BCVA charge falls by about USD 2m

working.label: Change
working.display: $-0.733 - 1.279 = -2.01$: the charge falls by about USD 2.01m

scenarios.takeaway: The own-default (DVA) leg grows with the bank's own spread, so widening can turn a charge into a gain. A negative 'stress loss' means a gain.
scenarios.lo_text: Calculate the DVA and explain how stressing DVA enters into aggregating stress tests of CCR.

scenarios.setup: B-rated issuers: 7-year cumulative default probability 20.99%, average 7-year credit spread 481 bp, recovery 40%. The spread-implied average hazard rate $s/(1-R)$ is 8.02% a year.
scenarios.ask: The historical average hazard rate, $-\ln(1 - 0.2099)/7$, compared with 8.02% is:

options.label: About the same
options.why: Took $20.99\%/7 = 3.0\%$ and the spread as the same thing; either way the historical figure is far below 8.02%.

options.label: Higher
options.why: Assumed real-world defaults must exceed what the market prices. The spread includes a risk premium, so the spread-implied rate is the larger one.

scenarios.takeaway: Spread-implied (risk-neutral) default intensities exceed historical (real-world) ones: here the historical rate is about 42% of the spread-implied one.
scenarios.lo_text: Compare default probabilities calculated from historical data with those calculated from credit yield spreads.

scenarios.setup: A BBB-type issuer class has a 7-year average credit spread of 150 bp and an expected recovery rate of 40%. The 7-year cumulative historical default probability is 2.80%.
scenarios.ask: The spread-implied (risk-neutral) average hazard rate $s/(1-R)$ is:

options.label: 0.90% a year
options.why: Multiplied the spread by $1 - R$ instead of dividing: $1.5\% \times 0.6$.

options.label: 1.50% a year
options.why: Used the spread as the hazard rate, forgetting that the spread compensates for loss given default, not for default alone.

scenarios.takeaway: Spread $\approx$ hazard $\times$ LGD, so hazard $\approx s/(1-R)$: always above the spread itself when recovery is positive.
scenarios.lo_text: Compare default probabilities calculated from historical data with those calculated from credit yield spreads.

scenarios.setup: One-year zero-coupon bonds, risk-free rate 3.0%, one possible default date at maturity. Issuer P yields 6.0% with recovery 60%. Issuer Q yields 7.0% with recovery 20%. Issuer R yields 6.5% with recovery 40%.
scenarios.ask: Which issuer has the highest implied one-year default probability?

options.label: Q
options.why: Ranked by yield. The spread prices PD × LGD, and Q's 3.74% loss rate divides by a large LGD of 80%, leaving only 4.67%.

options.label: R
options.why: Picked the middle yield. R's loss rate of 3.29% over LGD 60% gives 5.48%, below P's 7.08%.

scenarios.takeaway: A spread prices expected loss, PD × LGD. Strip out LGD before ranking default probabilities: the widest spread need not be the riskiest PD.
scenarios.lo_text: Compare default probabilities calculated from historical data with those calculated from credit yield spreads.

scenarios.setup: A book of 40 loans of CAD 10m each, independent, PD 3%, recovery 40%. Cumulative probability of the number of defaults: $P(\le 2) = 0.8822$, $P(\le 3) = 0.9686$, $P(\le 4) = 0.9933$, $P(\le 5) = 0.9988$.
scenarios.ask: The 99% quantile of the number of defaults is:

options.label: 3 defaults
options.why: Took the last count with cumulative probability below 99% (0.9686). The quantile is the smallest count whose cumulative probability reaches 99%.

options.label: 5 defaults
options.why: Went one step past the first count at or above 99%: $P(\le 4) = 0.9933$ already clears 0.99.

scenarios.takeaway: Quantile = first count whose cumulative probability reaches the confidence level. Credit VaR is that loss minus expected loss (4 defaults gives 16.8).
scenarios.lo_text: Define and calculate Credit VaR.

scenarios.setup: Two borrowers have one-year default probabilities of 6% and 10%. The probability that neither defaults during the year is 86.5%.
scenarios.ask: The probability that both default is:

options.why: Assumed independence ($0.06 \times 0.10$). The stated 86.5% implies the defaults cluster.
Took $1 - 0.865$, the probability that at least one defaults, not both.
Added the two PDs, counting the joint-default case twice.

scenarios.takeaway: $P(\text{neither}) = 1 - \pi_1 - \pi_2 + \pi_{12}$, so the joint probability is the overlap of the two PDs beyond what 'at least one' accounts for.
scenarios.lo_text: Define and calculate default correlation for credit portfolios.

scenarios.setup: Single-factor model: conditional PD $= \Phi\big((k - \beta m)/\sqrt{1-\beta^2}\big)$ with $k = \Phi^{-1}(p)$. A borrower has $p = 2\%$, so $k = -2.054$, and $\beta = 0.60$. A mild slowdown sets the market factor at $m = -0.5$.
scenarios.ask: The conditional default probability is:

options.label: Above 2%
options.why: Assumed any slowdown raises PD. The argument $(k - \beta m)/0.8 = -2.19$ lies further in the tail than $k = -2.054$, so the probability is smaller.

options.label: Exactly 2%
options.why: Assumed a mild shock leaves PD unchanged. The factor shifts the argument and also narrows the conditional spread by $\sqrt{1-\beta^2}$.

scenarios.takeaway: Conditioning narrows the distribution by $\sqrt{1-\beta^2}$: a mild negative factor can still leave the conditional PD below the unconditional one.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe the use of a single factor model to measure portfolio credit risk, including the impact of correlation.

scenarios.setup: One-factor Gaussian copula: conditional PD $= N\big((N^{-1}(p) - aF)/\sqrt{1-a^2}\big)$. Two borrowers each have $p = 2\%$ ($N^{-1}(p) = -2.054$). K is a copper miner with loading $a = 0.6$; L is a water utility with $a = 0.2$. In the recession scenario $F = -1.5$.
scenarios.ask: In the recession, which borrower has the higher conditional PD?

options.label: L
options.why: Read the loading as firm-specific risk, so the low-$a$ utility looked more exposed. A high loading means more sensitivity to the common factor.

options.label: Equal
options.why: The unconditional PDs are equal (2%), but the loadings differ, so the conditional PDs do too.

scenarios.takeaway: In a recession the high-loading name takes the larger jump: the argument is shifted up by $|aF|$ and a larger share of its risk is systematic.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe the Gaussian copula model for time to default and calculate the probability of default using the one-factor Gaussian copula model.

scenarios.setup: Gregory's approximation: running unilateral CVA $\approx -\text{average EPE} \times \text{CDS spread}$. Average EPE is 3.5% of notional in both months. The client's 5-year CDS spread widens from 140 bp to 220 bp, and the assumed recovery is cut from 40% to 20%.
scenarios.ask: Within the approximation, the recovery cut on its own changes today's running CVA by:

options.label: About +33% in size
options.why: Scaled by LGD (60% to 80%). The spread already embeds LGD, and the formula takes the spread directly with no LGD input.

options.label: About −50% in size
options.why: Scaled by the recovery ratio (40% to 20%). Recovery does not appear in the formula.

scenarios.takeaway: The approximation has no recovery input, so the whole change in running CVA (−2.80 bp) comes from the spread.
scenarios.lo_text: Evaluate the impact of changes in the credit spread and recovery rate assumptions on CVA.

scenarios.setup: Unilateral CVA on a 5-year EUR 400m swap. The CDS curve is flat at 300 bp and does not move. Hazard rate $\lambda = s/\text{LGD}$, and the same LGD measures the loss. The recovery estimate is revised from 40% to 25%, so LGD rises from 60% to 75%. Discounted EPE (% of notional), years 1–5: 1.5, 2.4, 2.8, 2.4, 1.4.
scenarios.ask: After the revision the CVA charge is:

options.label: About 25% larger
options.why: Raised the loss by 75/60 but kept the old default probabilities. The hazard rate $s/\text{LGD}$ falls when LGD rises.

options.label: About 20% smaller
options.why: Cut the hazard rate to 4% but kept the loss at 60%. The loss given default is now 75%.

scenarios.takeaway: LGD enters twice: it lowers the implied PD and raises the loss, and the two nearly cancel. The CVA moves by only about 2%.
scenarios.lo_text: Evaluate the impact of changes in the credit spread and recovery rate assumptions on CVA.

scenarios.setup: A 4-year swap with a project vehicle that has no CDS. The bank uses a proxy curve flat at 240 bp, calibrated at the market 40% recovery. The swap ranks as senior secured, so the credit team expects 75% recovery on it. Default probabilities come from the proxy curve with a constant hazard rate; the swap's own recovery sets the loss.
scenarios.ask: The constant hazard rate to use for the default probabilities is:

options.why: Used the spread as the hazard rate, ignoring that it compensates for default times the market LGD.
Divided the spread by the swap's own LGD of 25%. The proxy curve's market LGD of 60% is what links its spread to default probability.

scenarios.takeaway: PD comes from the market curve with the market LGD; the swap's own LGD is applied only to the loss.
scenarios.lo_text: Evaluate the impact of changes in the credit spread and recovery rate assumptions on CVA.

scenarios.setup: Derivative exposure enters the credit stress as $\alpha \times \text{EPE}$ with $\alpha = 1.2$ and LGD 60% unchanged. Under the stress, counterparty Y's EPE falls from CAD 40m to CAD 35m while its PD rises from 2.0% to 2.5%.
scenarios.ask: Y's expected loss under stress, compared with now, is:

options.label: Lower
options.why: Counted only the 12.5% fall in EPE. The PD rises by 25%, a bigger proportional move, so the product increases.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: Assumed the opposing moves cancel. $0.875 \times 1.25 = 1.09$, not 1.

scenarios.takeaway: EL is a product, so compare proportional moves: EPE $\times 0.875$ and PD $\times 1.25$ give EL up about 9%.
scenarios.lo_text: Differentiate between stressed expected loss and stress loss of a credit portfolio, and calculate the stress loss on a loan portfolio and the stress loss on a derivative portfolio.

scenarios.setup: A 2-year swap's counterparty has a flat CDS spread that doubles from 180 bp to 360 bp; recovery is 40%, so the hazard rate $\lambda = s/(1-R)$ goes from 3% to 6%. Discounted exposures are USD 12m (year 1) and USD 15m (year 2), unchanged. CVA $= 0.60 \times \sum EE \times (\text{marginal PD})$.
scenarios.ask: The stressed CVA is:

options.label: Exactly double
options.why: Assumed CVA is proportional to the spread. Marginal PDs are $e^{-\lambda(t-1)} - e^{-\lambda t}$: a higher hazard rate shrinks later years' PDs through lower survival.

options.label: More than double
options.why: Expected compounding in the tail. Here the opposite happens: survival falls, so later marginal PDs rise by less than 2×.

options.label: Less than double the base CVA

scenarios.takeaway: Doubling the spread slightly less than doubles CVA: the extra default probability in year 1 reduces the survival-weighted default probability later.
scenarios.lo_text: Calculate the stressed CVA and the stress loss on CVA.

scenarios.setup: CVA $= \text{LGD} \times \sum EE \times q^*$ with both EE and $q^*$ stressed. P (LGD 60%): year 1 EE 20 to 26, $q^*$ 1.0% to 2.0%; year 2 EE 25 to 30, $q^*$ 1.1% to 2.2%. Q (LGD 75%): year 1 EE 10 to 9, $q^*$ 2.5% to 3.5%; year 2 EE 8 to 6, $q^*$ 2.4% to 3.4%. USD m.
scenarios.ask: Which counterparty accounts for most of the portfolio's stress loss on CVA?

options.label: Q
options.why: Looked at Q's higher LGD and higher $q^*$ levels. The stress loss is the change, and Q's falling exposure offsets part of its spread rise.

options.label: About equal
options.why: Compared how much both $q^*$ rise (one point each). P's exposures rise too, so its terms multiply up, while Q's partly offset.

scenarios.takeaway: Both inputs rising multiply up (P); one rising and one falling partly cancel (Q). Compare changes, not levels.
scenarios.lo_text: Calculate the stressed CVA and the stress loss on CVA.

scenarios.setup: IFRS 9 lifetime ECL on a \$50m two-year loan book. Expected loss (PD × EAD × LR) is \$2.10m in year 1 and \$1.33m in year 2. The effective interest rate is 7.9%. Defaults are assumed to occur in the middle of each year, so the losses are discounted for 0.5 and 1.5 years.
scenarios.ask: Compared with discounting the two losses for a full 1 and 2 years, the mid-year convention gives a present value that is:

options.label: Lower
options.why: Read mid-year as a longer wait. Half a year of discounting is less than a full year, so each loss is discounted less and the PV is higher.

options.label: The same
options.why: The rate and the cash flows are unchanged, but the discount periods are not: 0.5 and 1.5 years instead of 1 and 2, so the PV differs.

scenarios.takeaway: Mid-year default means shorter discount periods, so a higher PV of expected loss than the end-of-year convention.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain the requirements for estimating expected loss under IFRS 9.

scenarios.setup: Standardised approach. Bank M holds Tier 1 capital of \$60m and Tier 2 capital of \$20m. Its assets are \$400m of corporate loans (risk weight 100%), \$300m of residential mortgages (50%) and \$200m of loans to highly rated banks (20%), \$900m in total. The unweighted ratio of capital to total assets is 8.9%.
scenarios.ask: Bank M's capital adequacy ratio (capital / RWA) is:

options.label: Below 8.9%
options.why: Assumed risk weighting inflates the denominator. Weights of 100% or less can only shrink RWA below total assets, so the ratio rises.

options.label: Equal to 8.9%
options.why: That needs every asset at a 100% weight. Here half the book is weighted at 50% or 20%.

scenarios.takeaway: Risk weights below 100% shrink the denominator, so CAR sits above the simple capital-to-assets ratio.
scenarios.lo_text: Estimate risk-weighted assets and capital adequacy ratio of a financial institution.

scenarios.setup: A bank has \$120m of total capital and \$1,000m of RWA (CAR 12%). \$200m of its exposures carry a 100% risk weight. The regulator raises that weight to 150%; capital and exposures are unchanged.
scenarios.ask: Total RWA after the change is closest to:

options.label: \$1,200m
options.why: Added the whole \$200m exposure again instead of only the extra 50% of it.

options.label: \$1,300m
options.why: Added the new \$300m of weighted exposure without removing the old \$200m.

options.label: \$1,500m
options.why: Multiplied all RWA by 1.5, although only the \$200m class is re-weighted.

scenarios.takeaway: Swap the old weighted amount for the new one; do not stack one on top of the other. CAR falls to about 10.9%.
scenarios.lo_text: Estimate risk-weighted assets and capital adequacy ratio of a financial institution.

scenarios.setup: Basel II IRB retail book. $EAD = \$400$m, $LGD = 35\%$, worst-case default rate $WCDR = 10\%$, $PD = 2\%$, maturity adjustment $MA = 1$. $RWA = 12.5 \times EAD \times LGD \times (WCDR - PD) \times MA$.
scenarios.ask: RWA is closest to:

options.label: ≈ \$400m
options.why: Left out LGD: $12.5 \times 400 \times 0.08$.

options.label: ≈ \$1,750m
options.why: Left out the $(WCDR - PD)$ term altogether: $12.5 \times 400 \times 0.35$.

options.label: ≈ \$14,000m
options.why: Scale slip: 100× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: Check the order of magnitude: capital charge of about 3% of EAD, times 12.5, gives RWA of about 35% of EAD.
scenarios.lo_text: Estimate risk-weighted assets and capital adequacy ratio of a financial institution.

scenarios.setup: CAP accuracy ratio: $AR = \dfrac{\text{area between model curve and random line}}{\text{area between perfect and random line}}$. The area between the perfect line and the random line is 0.40. Provider A's curve encloses 0.34 above the random line.
scenarios.ask: Provider A's accuracy ratio is closest to:

options.why: Multiplied the two areas ($0.34 \times 0.40$) instead of dividing.
Reported the raw area and never divided by the perfect-model area.
Inverted the ratio ($0.40/0.34$). A model cannot do better than perfect, so AR cannot exceed 1.

scenarios.takeaway: AR is the share of the perfect model's lift that the model captures, so it lies between 0 and 1.
scenarios.lo_text: Discuss the measurement and monitoring of a scorecard performance including the use of cumulative accuracy profile (CAP) and the accuracy ratio (AR) techniques.

scenarios.setup: A bank has 10,000 loans of \$10,000 each, all priced at a flat 10%, LGD 50%. Prime: 6,000 loans, PD 1%. Subprime: 4,000 loans, PD 6%. A competitor offers prime borrowers 8%, so half the prime customers leave under flat pricing; subprime customers stay.
scenarios.ask: Under flat pricing, annual risk-adjusted income (interest less expected loss) from the prime customers who remain is closest to:

options.label: \$5.70m
options.why: Counted all 6,000 prime loans, although half have left.

options.label: \$3.00m
options.why: Took interest only on the 3,000 remaining loans and left out expected loss.

options.label: \$0.15m
options.why: Took only the expected loss on the 3,000 remaining loans instead of interest minus expected loss.

scenarios.takeaway: Reprice only after you count who is left: lost customers take their income with them.
scenarios.lo_text: Discuss the benefits of risk-based pricing of financial services.

scenarios.setup: A protection buyer pays a CDS spread of 90 bp a year on a \$100m, 5-year CDS, in quarterly instalments in arrears. A credit event occurs exactly one month after the most recent payment date.
