scenarios.ask: The accrued premium the buyer must still pay at the credit event is closest to:

options.why: Used the full annual premium.
Paid a full quarter, ignoring that only one month has accrued.
Counted the two months left in the quarter instead of the one month already elapsed.

scenarios.takeaway: On a credit event the buyer pays only the premium accrued since the last payment date, then payments stop.
scenarios.lo_text: Define a credit default swap (CDS) and explain its mechanics including the obligations of both the default protection buyer and the default protection seller.

scenarios.setup: You sell \$1m of protection on each of the 125 names in a 5-year CDX NA IG index quoted 141 / 143 bp. At the start of year 3, before the annual premium is paid, one name defaults. You pay the full \$1m notional on it (ignore the bond you receive). The year-3 premium is paid on the other 124 names.
scenarios.ask: Your net cash flow for year 3 is:

options.label: A net outflow
options.why: Counted the \$1m payout and forgot that the premium on the 124 survivors is about \$1.75m.

scenarios.takeaway: A protection seller collects the bid spread on the survivors; one default of 125 costs less than the year's premium.
scenarios.lo_text: Define a credit default swap (CDS) and explain its mechanics including the obligations of both the default protection buyer and the default protection seller.

scenarios.setup: A Ba-rated bond has an unconditional probability of default in year 3 of 1.914%. The probability of surviving through the end of year 2 is 97.413%.
scenarios.ask: The probability of default in year 3, conditional on no earlier default, compared with 1.914% is:

options.label: Lower
options.why: Multiplied by survival ($1.914\% \times 0.974 = 1.865\%$). Conditioning on survival divides by it.

options.label: Equal
options.why: Treated conditional and unconditional probabilities as the same thing. They differ whenever survival to the start of the period is below 100%.

scenarios.takeaway: Conditional PD = unconditional PD ÷ survival to the start of the period, so it is always the larger of the two.
scenarios.lo_text: Calculate the probability of default using credit spreads.

scenarios.setup: A 2-year corporate bond yields 190 bp over the risk-free rate. The recovery rate is 35%. Use the approximation: average hazard rate $\approx$ spread / (1 − recovery).
scenarios.ask: The average hazard rate is closest to:

options.label: ≈ 0.95% a year
options.why: Divided the spread by the 2-year maturity and never applied LGD.

options.label: ≈ 8.7% a year
options.why: Scale slip: 3× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ 29% a year
options.why: Read 190 bp as 19% instead of 1.90%, then divided by LGD.

scenarios.takeaway: Hazard rate is spread divided by LGD, so it is a bit above the spread. A hazard rate below the spread means a slip.
scenarios.lo_text: Calculate the probability of default using credit spreads.

scenarios.setup: Single-period bond. Risk-free rate $r = 2.0\%$, default probability 3.0%, loss given default 60% (recovery $R = 40\%$). The minimum spread $z$ solves $(1-PD)(1+r+z) + PD \times R = 1 + r$.
scenarios.ask: The minimum spread $z$ compared with the rule of thumb $PD \times LGD = 1.80\%$ is:

options.label: Below 1.80%
options.why: Assumed the rule of thumb is an upper bound. The exact $z$ is larger: $z = PD(1+r-R)/(1-PD)$ divides by survival and includes the time value on the lost principal.

options.label: Equal to 1.80%
options.why: Used $z = PD \times LGD$ as exact. It drops the factor $1/(1-PD)$ and the $r$ in $(1 + r - R)$.

scenarios.takeaway: z is slightly above PD × LGD, because the survivors must also cover the time value of the money lost.
scenarios.lo_text: Calculate the probability of default using credit spreads.

scenarios.setup: A GBP 85m retail exposure. One-year average PD 2.50%, recovery rate 72%. A one-factor Gaussian copula gives a 99.9% worst-case default rate of 10.73% (1-year). Credit VaR $= L \times (1 - RR) \times V$.
scenarios.ask: The 99.9% credit VaR is closest to:

options.label: ≈ GBP 0.026m
options.why: Scale slip: 1/100 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ GBP 0.087m
options.why: Scale slip: 1/30 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ GBP 0.6m
options.why: Used the average PD of 2.5% instead of the 99.9% worst-case default rate.

scenarios.takeaway: Credit VaR = exposure × LGD × worst-case default rate. Three factors, each well below 1.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe how to estimate credit VaR using the Gaussian copula and the CreditMetrics approach.

scenarios.setup: Modus Corp has a 7-year, 5% coupon bond rated AA. The 7-year CDS spread is 3%. Swap fixed rates are 3% for 5 years and 4% for 7 years. To rule out arbitrage the bond's yield spread over the matching swap rate must equal the CDS spread.
scenarios.ask: Which swap rate is the benchmark for Modus's bond yield?

options.label: 3% (5-year swap rate)
options.why: Matched the wrong maturity. The bond is a 7-year bond, so the 7-year swap rate applies.

options.label: 5% (the bond coupon)
options.why: Confused the coupon with a market benchmark. The coupon says nothing about the swap curve.

scenarios.takeaway: Match the benchmark swap rate to the bond's maturity; then yield = swap rate + CDS spread.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe a credit derivative, credit default swap (CDS), total return swap, and collateralized debt obligation (CDO).

scenarios.setup: A 5-year CDS reference entity has a constant hazard rate of 1.5% a year (continuous), so survival to the end of year $t$ is $e^{-0.015t}$. Notional \$10m, recovery 40%.
scenarios.ask: The unconditional probability that default happens during year 3 is closest to:

options.why: Took the cumulative default probability to the end of year 3, $1 - e^{-0.045}$, which includes years 1 and 2.
Used the hazard rate itself. That is the default probability conditional on surviving to the start of the year; the unconditional figure is smaller.
Reported the survival probability to the end of year 3 instead of a default probability.

scenarios.takeaway: Unconditional year-3 PD is the drop in survival over that year: below the hazard rate, because some names have already gone.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain how to account for credit risk exposure in valuing a CDS.

scenarios.setup: Your firm sells a European call on Electric Inc. (stock \$47, strike \$25, 3 months, implied volatility 23%) and receives the premium in full upfront. The risk-free rate is 1.5%.
scenarios.ask: Your counterparty credit exposure to the buyer is:

options.label: About \$22, the option's intrinsic value
options.why: Treated the option's value as money the buyer owes. The buyer owes nothing more; you are the one who may owe a payoff.

options.label: About \$47, the stock price
options.why: Used the underlying's price. Exposure is a claim on the counterparty, and a written option gives you no claim.

working.label: Premium
working.display: Received in full at inception, so the buyer owes nothing further

working.label: Value to you
working.display: A written option can never be worth more than nothing to you, so exposure $= \max(V, \text{nothing})$ is nil

scenarios.takeaway: Credit exposure is a claim on the counterparty. An option seller who has been paid upfront has none.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe transactions that carry counterparty risk and explain how counterparty risk can arise in each transaction.

scenarios.setup: An investor has agreed to pay \$2.6m and receive €2m at a future date (rate 1.30 USD/EUR). Before settlement the euro rises to 1.35 USD/EUR, and the counterparty defaults before settlement. Ignore collateral and recovery.
scenarios.ask: At the default, the investor's contract is:

options.label: In the money, so the investor loses the replacement cost
Out of the money, so there is no loss
options.why: Wrong direction. The investor receives euros, and euros are now worth more than the \$2.6m owed.

options.label: Worth zero, so the investor loses the full \$2.6m
options.why: That is settlement risk, which needs the dollars to be paid and the euros not delivered. Before settlement the loss is only the replacement cost.

scenarios.takeaway: Pre-settlement loss is the positive replacement cost, not the notional. Receiving the currency that has risen means the position is in the money.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe transactions that carry counterparty risk and explain how counterparty risk can arise in each transaction.

scenarios.setup: Prime Bank receives 8% fixed on a GBP 200m, 5-year annual-pay swap. After one year, four payments remain and the market swap rate has fallen 150 bp to 6.5%. The mark-to-market is the 1.5% annual advantage on GBP 200m times the annuity factor for the remaining payments, discounted at 6.5%.
scenarios.ask: The annuity factor for four annual payments at 6.5% is closest to:

options.why: Counted the original five payments instead of the four that remain.
Added up four payments with no discounting.

scenarios.takeaway: An annuity factor is below the number of payments, here 3.4 against 4. The swap is in the money to Prime Bank, so exposure is positive.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe credit exposure, credit migration, recovery, mark-to-market, replacement cost, default probability, loss given default, and the recovery rate.

scenarios.setup: A market maker holds a fixed-for-floating swap with \$80.0m notional. Its replacement cost is 3.0% of notional, \$2.4m. The counterparty's one-year default probability is 1.0% and recovery is 40% of the claim.
scenarios.ask: The expected one-year credit loss on the current exposure is closest to:

options.label: ≈ \$1.4m
options.why: Left out the default probability: exposure × LGD.

options.label: ≈ \$48m
options.why: Left out both the default probability and the replacement-cost step: notional × LGD.

options.label: ≈ \$480k
options.why: Applied PD and LGD to the \$80m notional instead of the \$2.4m replacement cost.

scenarios.takeaway: Expected loss = exposure × PD × LGD. The exposure is the replacement cost, not the notional.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe credit exposure, credit migration, recovery, mark-to-market, replacement cost, default probability, loss given default, and the recovery rate.

scenarios.setup: A hedge fund's positions with AB&B, all under an enforceable netting agreement (positive means AB&B owes the fund), in USD m: A +44.0, B +88.0, C −35.2, D −3.3, E +20.0. AB&B defaults with zero recovery.
scenarios.ask: The fund's exposure after netting compared with the largest single contract, B at +88.0, is:

options.label: Below 88.0
options.why: Assumed netting always cuts exposure below the biggest claim. The other positives (A and E, 64.0) outweigh the negatives (38.5), so the net is more than B alone.

scenarios.takeaway: Netting sums the whole book first, then floors at zero. The negatives only offset 38.5 of the 152.0 owed.
scenarios.lo_text: Identify and describe the different ways institutions can quantify, manage, and mitigate counterparty risk.

scenarios.setup: An uncollateralised derivative has a base value of +\$50.0m. xVA terms (each stated positive): CVA \$5.0m cost, DVA \$2.0m benefit, FVA \$1.0m cost, ColVA 0, KVA \$4.0m cost, MVA \$3.0m cost.
scenarios.ask: The net xVA adjustment to the \$50.0m is closest to:

options.label: −\$15.0m
options.why: Treated DVA as a cost as well: $5 + 1 + 4 + 3 + 2 = 15$. Own default risk is a benefit to the firm.

options.label: −\$13.0m
options.why: Ignored DVA, counting costs only.

options.label: −\$3.0m
options.why: Counted only CVA and DVA ($-5 + 2$) and left out FVA, KVA and MVA.

scenarios.takeaway: Costs (CVA, FVA, KVA, MVA) reduce value; DVA is the one benefit. Sign each term before adding.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain the components of the X-Value Adjustment (xVA) term.

scenarios.setup: A CCP's loss waterfall, in order: defaulter's margin \$80m, defaulter's default-fund contribution \$30m, CCP's own capital \$25m, surviving members' default-fund contributions \$200m, then assessment calls up to \$700m. A clearing member defaults and the loss is \$275m.
scenarios.ask: Will the CCP have to make assessment calls?

options.label: Yes, the default fund is exhausted first
options.why: Left out the surviving members' \$200m, so only \$135m seemed available. The \$275m loss reaches into the default fund but does not exhaust it.

scenarios.takeaway: Walk the waterfall in order: defaulter pays first, CCP capital next, survivors' fund after that. Assessment is the last resort.
scenarios.lo_text: Provide examples of a loss waterfall.

scenarios.setup: A CCP's waterfall: defaulter's margin \$80m, defaulter's default-fund contribution \$30m, CCP's own capital \$25m, surviving members' default fund \$200m, then assessment calls. A member defaults with a total loss of \$420m.
scenarios.ask: After the defaulter's margin and contribution and the CCP's own capital are used, but before the surviving members' fund, the unmet loss is closest to:

options.label: \$340m
options.why: Applied only the defaulter's margin ($420 - 80$).

options.label: \$310m
options.why: Applied the defaulter's margin and contribution but skipped the CCP's own capital.

options.label: \$85m
options.why: Went one layer too far: that is the loss left after the surviving members' \$200m as well.

scenarios.takeaway: Each layer is applied in order. Here \$285m still needs the survivors' fund, which then leaves \$85m for assessment calls.
scenarios.lo_text: Provide examples of a loss waterfall.

scenarios.setup: Freecone pays 3.0% fixed and receives six-month SOFR on USD 50.0m, semi-annually, with 1.25 years left (payments in 0.25, 0.75 and 1.25 years). The next floating rate was set at 2.40%. The SOFR curve is flat at 2.60% continuously compounded, and SOFR is also the discount rate.
scenarios.ask: Freecone's current exposure on the swap (the positive part of its mark-to-market) is:

options.label: About +USD 0.34m: the swap is an asset to Freecone
options.why: Flipped the sign of the mark-to-market. Freecone receives floating (2.4%, then about 2.6%) and pays 3.0%, so every net payment is a small outflow.

options.label: Zero: the mark-to-market is negative, so exposure floors at 0
About USD 0.34m: the size of the mark-to-market, whatever its sign
options.why: Used the absolute value. Exposure is $\max(V, 0)$: a negative mark-to-market is what the bank owes, not what it stands to lose.

scenarios.takeaway: Paying 3.0% against floating rates of 2.4% to 2.6% means the swap is out of the money, so current exposure is zero however large the negative value.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe and calculate the following metrics for credit exposure: expected mark-to-market, expected exposure, potential future exposure, expected positive exposure and negative exposure, effective expected positive exposure, and maximum exposure.

scenarios.setup: A portfolio's future value is normally distributed with mean USD 0 and standard deviation USD 10m. The 95% one-sided normal quantile is 1.645.
scenarios.ask: 95% potential future exposure (PFE) is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.53m
options.why: Scale slip: 1/30 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 1.6m
options.why: Left out $\sigma$: used the 1.645 z-score as if it were already in dollars.

options.label: ≈ USD 4.0m
options.why: Gave the expected exposure $\sigma\phi(0) = 0.399 \times 10$ instead of the 95th percentile.

scenarios.takeaway: PFE is a high percentile of the future value (about 1.6 standard deviations here); expected exposure is only about 0.4 standard deviations.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe and calculate the following metrics for credit exposure: expected mark-to-market, expected exposure, potential future exposure, expected positive exposure and negative exposure, effective expected positive exposure, and maximum exposure.

scenarios.setup: A one-year trade has expected exposure (USD m) of 0.20, 0.35, 0.30, 0.40 and 0.25 at t = 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 and 1.0 years. Effective EE is the non-decreasing version of EE: at each date it is the larger of that date's EE and the previous effective EE.
scenarios.ask: Effective EE at t = 1.0 year is:

options.label: USD 0.25m
options.why: Read off the raw EE at t = 1.0. Effective EE never falls below an earlier value, and EE already reached 0.40 at t = 0.8.

options.label: USD 0.34m
options.why: Averaged the effective EE path (that is the effective EPE, one number for the whole profile), not the value at one date.

options.label: USD 0.35m
options.why: Stopped the running maximum at the 0.4-year peak and missed the new high of 0.40 at t = 0.8.

scenarios.takeaway: Effective EE is a running maximum: once exposure has peaked, the effective figure holds that level for the rest of the profile.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe and calculate the following metrics for credit exposure: expected mark-to-market, expected exposure, potential future exposure, expected positive exposure and negative exposure, effective expected positive exposure, and maximum exposure.

scenarios.setup: For a zero-mean normal mark-to-market, expected exposure is approximately $EE(t) \approx 0.4\,\sigma\sqrt{t}$. The exposure has volatility $\sigma = 9.0\%$ per annum, with 250 trading days per year.
scenarios.ask: Expected exposure after 10 trading days is closest to:

options.why: Used $t = 0.04$ without the square root: $0.4 \times 9.0\% \times 0.04$.
Left out the time factor altogether: $0.4 \times 9.0\%$ is the one-year figure.
Put 10 (days) in as if it were years: $\sqrt{10} = 3.16$ instead of $\sqrt{0.04} = 0.2$.

scenarios.takeaway: Exposure grows with the square root of time, and the clock must be in years: 10 days is a fifth of a one-year EE, not 4% of it.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe and calculate the following metrics for credit exposure: expected mark-to-market, expected exposure, potential future exposure, expected positive exposure and negative exposure, effective expected positive exposure, and maximum exposure.

scenarios.setup: A derivative's future value (USD m) is +10, +6, +3, +1, −1, −3, −6 or −10 with probabilities 5%, 10%, 15%, 20%, 20%, 15%, 10% and 5%. The distribution is symmetric, so its mean is zero.
scenarios.ask: The expected exposure (EE) of the position is:

options.label: Zero: gains and losses cancel in a symmetric distribution
options.why: Averaged the future value instead of the exposure. The expected value is zero, but exposure is $\max(V, 0)$, and the losses are floored at 0 rather than netted.

options.label: Positive: only the gains count, so the average cannot be zero

scenarios.takeaway: Expected exposure is the mean of the positive part, so it is positive whenever any outcome is positive, even when the expected value is zero.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe and calculate the following metrics for credit exposure: expected mark-to-market, expected exposure, potential future exposure, expected positive exposure and negative exposure, effective expected positive exposure, and maximum exposure.

scenarios.setup: An exposure profile has EE (USD m) of 3, 5, 8, 6 and 2, each held constant over the interval ending at dates 0.5, 1, 2, 3 and 5 years (interval lengths 0.5, 0.5, 1, 1 and 2 years). The plain average of the five EE figures is 4.8.
scenarios.ask: The time-weighted EPE over the five years is:

options.label: Above 4.8
options.why: Assumed the peak of 8 pulls the average up. But the low EE of 2 sits in the longest interval (2 years), while the 3 and 5 last only half a year each.

options.label: Equal to 4.8
options.why: Used the plain average of the five numbers, which treats a 6-month interval and a 2-year interval as equal weights.

scenarios.takeaway: EPE averages over time, not over observation dates: the longer an exposure level lasts, the more it counts.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe and calculate the following metrics for credit exposure: expected mark-to-market, expected exposure, potential future exposure, expected positive exposure and negative exposure, effective expected positive exposure, and maximum exposure.

scenarios.setup: At one future date a netting set has five equally likely mark-to-market outcomes to the bank (USD m): +40, +20, 0, −20, −30.
scenarios.ask: Expected exposure (EE) at that date is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 30m
options.why: Averaged only the positive outcomes, $(40 + 20)/2$. The three scenarios with zero exposure still carry weight in the average.

options.label: ≈ USD 110m
options.why: Added up the sizes of all five outcomes, positive and negative, and never divided by 5.

options.label: ≈ USD 360m
options.why: Scale slip: 30× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: EE is the probability-weighted average of the positive part over all outcomes: losses count as zero exposure but keep their probability weight.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe and calculate the following metrics for credit exposure: expected mark-to-market, expected exposure, potential future exposure, expected positive exposure and negative exposure, effective expected positive exposure, and maximum exposure.

scenarios.setup: A CLO waterfall is run on 1,000 simulated default threads. For the mezzanine bond the mean loss is USD 0.62m, the 10th-highest loss is USD 3.40m and the 50th-highest is USD 1.90m. Credit VaR is measured as the loss quantile minus the expected loss.
scenarios.ask: The 99% credit VaR, compared with USD 3.40m, is:

options.label: Equal to USD 3.40m: the quantile is the VaR
options.why: Reported the 99% loss quantile (10th of 1,000 is the top 1%) without netting off the 0.62 expected loss, as this definition requires.

options.label: Above USD 3.40m: the expected loss is added on
options.why: Added the expected loss instead of subtracting it. VaR here is the unexpected part of the loss.

options.label: Below USD 3.40m: the expected loss comes off the quantile

scenarios.takeaway: Credit VaR on this definition is the quantile loss less the expected loss, so it sits below the raw tail loss.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe a simulation approach to calculating credit losses for different tranches in a securitization.

scenarios.setup: A CVA analyst has counterparty credit spreads of 90, 110 and 130bp at 1, 2 and 3 years, with 40% recovery. The average hazard rate to maturity $T$ is spread/(1 − R) and survival is $e^{-\bar\lambda T}$. The 3-year average hazard is $\bar\lambda(3) = 2.17\%$ and $V(2) = 0.964$. The probability of default in year 3 is $q_3 = V(2) - V(3)$.
scenarios.ask: $q_3$ compared with the 3-year average hazard of 2.17% is:

options.label: Below 2.17%
options.why: Took the 2.17% average and shrank it for survival to year 2 (2.17% × 0.964 ≈ 2.09%). But the year-3 hazard is not the average: on a rising curve it is about 2.83%.

options.label: Equal to 2.17%
options.why: Used the average hazard to year 3 as if it were the default rate inside year 3. With spreads still widening, year 3's own hazard is higher.

scenarios.takeaway: A rising spread curve means the forward hazard in a later year (here about 2.8%) is above the average hazard to that date; the interval default probability follows the forward rate.
scenarios.lo_text: Calculate the probability of default using credit spreads.

scenarios.setup: An issuer has one zero-coupon bond: face JPY 50.0bn, 4 years to maturity. A calibrated Merton model gives firm assets of JPY 68.0bn and equity of JPY 24.5bn. The risk-free rate is 1.5% continuously compounded. The credit spread is the debt's continuously compounded yield $y$ (from $D = Fe^{-yT}$) minus the risk-free rate.
scenarios.ask: The credit spread on the debt is closest to:

options.label: ≈ 20 bps
options.why: Scale slip (1/10): treated 1.98% as 0.198%.

options.label: ≈ 66 bps
options.why: Scale slip: 1/3 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ 498 bps
options.why: Added the risk-free rate to the 3.48% yield instead of subtracting it.

scenarios.takeaway: Debt = assets minus equity; the spread is the extra yield over risk-free, and the log of the debt-to-face ratio must be annualised by $T$.
scenarios.lo_text: Calculate the probability of default using credit spreads.

scenarios.setup: Two one-year zero-coupon bonds of the same issuer, with the same default probability and risk-neutral pricing. Risk-free rate 3.0%. The senior bond yields 5.5% with a 45% recovery rate; the subordinated bond recovers only 15%.
scenarios.ask: The subordinated bond's yield spread over the risk-free rate is closest to:

options.label: 2.5%, the same as the senior bond
options.why: Same default probability does not mean same spread. The spread prices expected loss, PD × LGD, and the subordinated bond's LGD is higher.
Scaled the senior 2.5% by 85/45. The senior LGD is 1 − 45% = 55%, so the ratio is 85/55 = 1.55.
Scaled by the ratio of recovery rates (45/15 = 3). Spreads follow loss given default (55% vs 85%), not recovery.

scenarios.takeaway: With one default probability, spreads scale with LGD: here 85/55 ≈ 1.55 times the senior spread.
scenarios.lo_text: Calculate the probability of default using credit spreads.

scenarios.setup: One-factor Gaussian copula for a granular loan book: average one-year PD 1.5%, correlation $\rho = 0.12$, 99.9% confidence. Worst-case default rate $= N\!\left(\frac{N^{-1}(PD) + \sqrt{\rho}\,N^{-1}(0.999)}{\sqrt{1-\rho}}\right)$, with $N^{-1}(0.015) = -2.170$ and $N^{-1}(0.999) = 3.090$.
scenarios.ask: The 99.9% worst-case default rate is about how many times the 1.5% average?

options.label: About 1×: the same as the average
options.why: Dropped the correlation term. With $\rho = 0$ the argument is just $N^{-1}(PD)$ and the worst case equals the average PD.

options.label: About 2×
options.why: Used $\rho = 0.12$ in place of $\sqrt{\rho} = 0.346$, so the stress term was far too small: the argument is −1.92, giving about 2.8%.

scenarios.takeaway: Correlation makes the 1-in-1,000 default rate a multiple of the average, here about 8 times. Note the factor loading is $\sqrt{\rho}$, not $\rho$.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe how to estimate credit VaR using the Gaussian copula and the CreditMetrics approach.

scenarios.setup: Firm A has assets of USD 1,000m funded by USD 600m of debt at 4% and USD 400m of equity. EBIT is USD 90m before credit losses of USD 50m. Tax is 25% of positive pre-tax income.
scenarios.ask: Firm A's ROE after credit losses is closest to:

options.why: Ignored the credit losses: $(90 - 24) \times 0.75 / 400$.
Forgot the interest on the debt: $(90 - 50) \times 0.75 / 400$.
Skipped the tax: pre-tax income of 16 over equity of 400.

scenarios.takeaway: Leverage amplifies ROE only if the asset return exceeds the cost of debt; credit losses and tax come off before dividing by equity.
scenarios.lo_text: Discuss the motivations for managing or taking on credit risk.

scenarios.setup: A revolving facility has a USD 5.0m limit, of which USD 2.5m is drawn today. For the next 12 months the analyst sets PD at 2%, expects the drawn balance at default to be USD 3.2m, and expects to recover 55% of a defaulted balance.
scenarios.ask: Which amount belongs in $EL = PD \times EAD \times LGD$ as EAD?

options.label: USD 2.5m, today's drawn balance
options.why: Used the current balance. Borrowers tend to draw more as they approach default, so EAD is the expected drawn amount at default; this would give EL = USD 22,500.

options.label: USD 5.0m, the full limit
options.why: Assumed the line is fully drawn at default. That ignores the analyst's estimate of USD 3.2m and would overstate EL at USD 45,000.

options.label: USD 3.2m, the balance expected at default

scenarios.takeaway: EAD is the exposure expected at default, not today's drawn amount and not the limit.
scenarios.lo_text: Identify and explain the components of expected loss and differentiate between expected loss and unexpected loss.

scenarios.setup: A mortgage score band has a historical annual loss rate of 2.4%, where loss rate = PD × LGD, and an LGD of 60%.
scenarios.ask: The implied PD of the band is:

options.label: Below 2.4% (about 1.4%)
options.why: Multiplied the loss rate by LGD: $2.4\% \times 0.6 = 1.44\%$. That is applying LGD twice, since the loss rate already includes it.

options.label: Equal to 2.4%
options.why: Treated the loss rate as if it were the default rate, which holds only if LGD were 100%.

scenarios.takeaway: Loss rate is PD scaled down by LGD, so going back to PD must scale up: any LGD below 100% puts PD above the loss rate.
scenarios.lo_text: Discuss the key variables in a mortgage credit assessment and describe the use of cutoff scores, default rates, and loss rates in a credit scoring model.

scenarios.setup: One-year transitions: a B-rated credit goes to A with 10%, stays B with 70% and defaults with 20%; an A-rated credit stays A with 80% and falls to B with 20% (A cannot default directly); default is absorbing. Years are independent. A USD 15.0m loan to a B-rated borrower runs for three years.
scenarios.ask: The three-year cumulative probability of default for the B-rated borrower is closest to:

options.why: Used the one-year default probability and ignored that the borrower can default in year 2 or 3.
Added three years of 20%. Only the borrowers who have not yet defaulted can default later, and some of the 20% each year is already gone.

scenarios.takeaway: Cumulative PD sums default paths over the years, each weighted by survival; it is well below the sum of the annual rates. EL on the loan is $15.0 \times 44.2\% \times 60\% = $ USD 3.98m.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe the use of rating transition matrices for calculating credit VaR.

scenarios.setup: A BBB-rated company has a 91.93% chance of keeping its rating over one year, and rating changes in different years are independent. Taking off 8.07 points for each of four years would give 67.7%.
scenarios.ask: The true four-year probability of still being BBB is:

options.label: Below 67.7%
options.why: Thought risks pile up faster than a straight line. But each year's 8.07% loss applies only to the shrinking share still BBB, so the later losses are smaller than 8.07 points.

scenarios.takeaway: Independent annual retention compounds multiplicatively: $p^n$, which stays above the straight-line $1 - n(1-p)$.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe the use of rating transition matrices for calculating credit VaR.

scenarios.setup: In a default-correlation framework each of eight firms either defaults or survives over the horizon. A joint outcome says which of the eight firms defaulted.
scenarios.ask: The number of distinct joint default/survival outcomes is closest to:

options.why: Added instead of multiplied: $2 \times 8$.
Squared the number of firms: $8^2$.
Counted orderings of the firms, $8! = 40{,}320$, rather than default/survive states.

scenarios.takeaway: Binary outcomes multiply: $n$ firms give $2^n$ joint outcomes, which is why default-correlation frameworks explode in size.
scenarios.lo_text: Identify drawbacks in using the correlation-based credit portfolio framework.

scenarios.setup: In a single-factor model each firm's asset return is $a_i = \beta_i m + \sqrt{1-\beta_i^2}\,\epsilon_i$, with $m$ and every $\epsilon_i$ independent standard normals. Firm X has $\beta = 0.8$ and Firm Y has $\beta = 0.9$.
scenarios.ask: The correlation between the asset returns of X and Y is:

options.label: Between 0.80 and 0.90
options.why: Averaged the two betas (0.85). The only link between the firms is the common factor, so the correlation is the product, not a mean.

options.label: Above 0.90
options.why: Added the betas (1.7) or took the larger one. A correlation cannot exceed 1, and betas below 1 multiply to something smaller than either.

scenarios.takeaway: In the single-factor model, correlation is the product of the two betas, so it is below both of them.
scenarios.lo_text: Define beta and calculate the asset return correlation of any pair of firms using the single factor model.

scenarios.setup: In the single-factor model two firms in the same industry share the same beta to the market factor, and the correlation between their asset returns is estimated at 0.36.
scenarios.ask: The beta of each firm is closest to:

options.why: Squared the correlation instead of taking its root.
Split the correlation between the two firms, $0.36/2$. Betas multiply, they do not add.
Set beta equal to the correlation. That would give $\rho = 0.36^2 = 0.13$.

scenarios.takeaway: With equal betas, asset correlation is $\beta^2$, so each beta is the square root of the correlation, and larger than it.
scenarios.lo_text: Define beta and calculate the asset return correlation of any pair of firms using the single factor model.

scenarios.setup: A copula simulation of two USD 1.0m loans gives 1,000 one-year scenarios. Portfolio loss is USD 1.0m in 8 scenarios, USD 0.6m in 22, USD 0.4m in 40 and zero in the other 930.
scenarios.ask: Counting from the worst scenario, the loss of the 10th-worst scenario (the 99% level) is:

options.label: USD 1.0m
options.why: Took the maximum loss. Only the 8 worst scenarios (0.8%) lose 1.0m; the 10th worst is already past them.

options.label: USD 0.4m
options.why: Went too far into the tail: the 10th worst is within the 22 scenarios at 0.6m (ranks 9 to 30). Losses of 0.4m start at rank 31.

working.label: Ranks by loss
working.display: ranks 1–8 lose 1.0m; ranks 9–30 lose 0.6m; ranks 31–70 lose 0.4m

working.label: 99% credit VaR
working.display: rank 10 is in the 0.6m group $\Rightarrow$ USD 0.6m

scenarios.takeaway: Quantile from a simulation: rank the losses from the worst and read the entry at the tail-probability mark.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe how Credit VaR can be calculated using a simulation of joint defaults.

scenarios.setup: Bank A and Bank B have a zero-threshold, two-way collateral agreement with a 10-day margin period of risk. B stopped posting 10 days before it defaulted, so A holds collateral equal to the swap value of that earlier date: USD 40m. At default the swap is worth USD 50m to A.
scenarios.ask: A's credit exposure at default is:

options.label: Zero: A is fully collateralised
options.why: Assumed the collateral tracks the current value. It only covers the value as of 10 days earlier, so the 10m of value gained since then is unsecured.

options.label: Equal to the full USD 50m swap value
options.why: Ignored the collateral A holds: max(50 - 0, 0) = 50.

options.label: Positive, but smaller than the USD 50m swap value

scenarios.takeaway: The collateral lags by the margin period of risk, so a swap that gained value during the cure period leaves an unsecured gap.
scenarios.lo_text: Assess the credit risks of derivatives.

scenarios.setup: Four uncollateralised derivatives with one counterparty sit under a master netting agreement. Their values to the bank are +18, -7, +12 and -20 (USD m).
scenarios.ask: The bank's exposure to the counterparty with netting is closest to:

options.label: USD 0
options.why: Assumed the largest loss (-20) outweighs everything. The four values sum to +3, which is still owed to the bank.

options.label: USD 30m
options.why: That is the exposure with no netting: only the positive trades, 18 + 12.

options.label: USD 57m
options.why: Added the absolute values of all four trades, treating every trade as an exposure.

scenarios.takeaway: Netting sums the values first and floors the total at zero. Here that cuts the exposure from 30 to 3, a reduction of 27.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe, compare, and contrast various credit risk mitigants and their role in credit analysis.

scenarios.setup: A firm's hazard rate is a constant 2% a year over the next five years. Survival to time $t$ is $e^{-0.02t}$.
scenarios.ask: The probability that the firm defaults during year 2 (as seen today) is:

options.label: Exactly 2%
options.why: Treated the hazard rate as the unconditional yearly default probability. Year-2 default needs survival through year 1 first (about 98%).

options.label: Well above 2%
options.why: Looked at default by the end of year 2, about 3.9%, instead of default during year 2 alone.

scenarios.takeaway: The hazard rate is conditional on survival, so the unconditional default probability falls a little each year: about 0.98 x 2% = 1.94%.
scenarios.lo_text: Identify the default probabilities used to value a CDS.

scenarios.setup: Banko bought 5-year CDS protection on USD 5m two years ago at a spread of 1.85%. The 3-year spread for the same name is now 2.30%, and the PV of the expected payoff is USD 0.0312 per USD 1 of notional.
scenarios.ask: The CDS is now worth, to Banko:

options.label: A negative amount
options.why: Thought a contract struck at a lower spread than today's market is a loss. For the protection buyer it is a gain: protection now costs more than Banko pays.

options.label: About zero
options.why: Assumed the contract is marked to par. The 45 bp gap, paid over a risky annuity of about 1.36, is worth about USD 30,500.

scenarios.takeaway: A protection buyer who locked in a spread below today's market holds an asset: value = spread difference x risky annuity x notional.
scenarios.lo_text: Identify the default probabilities used to value a CDS.

scenarios.setup: A fund buys protection on the whole 5-year iTraxx Europe index: 125 equally weighted names with EUR 1m notional on each. The dealer quotes the index spread at 75 bp bid, 76 bp offer.
scenarios.ask: The annual premium the fund pays is closest to:

options.label: ≈ EUR 95m
options.why: Read 76 bp as 76 percent of 1 (0.76) instead of 0.0076, a hundred times too large.

options.label: ≈ EUR 7,600
options.why: Charged the spread on a single name's EUR 1m instead of on all 125 names.

options.label: ≈ EUR 95,000
options.why: Decimal slip: read 76 bp as 0.076% instead of 0.76%, ten times too small.

working.label: Rate paid
working.display: Protection buyer deals at the offer: $76\text{ bp} = 0.76\%$

scenarios.takeaway: A protection buyer pays the offer; premium = spread x notional on every name. 76 bp on EUR 125m is EUR 0.95m.
scenarios.lo_text: Evaluate the use of credit indices and fixed coupons in pricing CDS transactions.

scenarios.setup: A 5-year iTraxx Europe index trades at 45 bp. The standard fixed coupon is 50 bp and the contract's risky duration is 4.6 years. Alex buys protection on EUR 50m.
scenarios.ask: At trade date the up-front settlement is:

options.label: Alex pays a payment
options.why: Assumed the buyer always pays up front. Alex will pay a 50 bp coupon for protection worth only 45 bp, so the seller compensates him at the start.

options.label: Nothing: a 5 bp gap is too small to settle
options.why: On EUR 50m over 4.6 years of duration, 5 bp is worth EUR 115,000, which is not negligible.

working.label: Coupon above fair spread
working.display: $50\text{ bp} - 45\text{ bp} = 5\text{ bp}$ paid in excess by the buyer

scenarios.takeaway: Fixed coupon above the market spread: the buyer overpays every period, so he receives the difference up front. Below the market spread, he pays.
scenarios.lo_text: Evaluate the use of credit indices and fixed coupons in pricing CDS transactions.

scenarios.setup: Two trades with one counterparty, five equally likely scenarios. Exposure with no netting by scenario: 40, 25, 5, 0, 0. With netting: 40, 25, 0, 0, 0.
scenarios.ask: The netting benefit in expected exposure (EE without netting minus EE with netting) is closest to:

options.why: Divided by the five scenarios twice: 1/5.
Summed the difference across scenarios (70 - 65) without averaging.
That is EE without netting; never subtracted EE with netting.

scenarios.takeaway: Only scenario 3 gains anything from netting (5 down to 0), and it is one of five equally likely cases: 5/5 = 1.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe the effectiveness of netting in reducing credit exposure under various scenarios.

scenarios.setup: Two trades with one counterparty under four scenarios, MtM (trade 1, trade 2): (18, 4), (12, -3), (8, -5), (-4, 7). Gross exposure is the sum of positive MtMs; netted exposure is $\max(\text{sum}, 0)$. Netting benefit = 1 - (average netted / average gross).
scenarios.ask: The ratio of average netted exposure to average gross exposure is closest to:

options.why: Reported the benefit (1 - ratio, about 24.5%) instead of the ratio itself.
Assumed netting roughly halves exposure. In scenario 1, which makes up 22 of the 49 gross total, netting does nothing.

scenarios.takeaway: Take the max scenario by scenario before averaging. The ratio is 75.5%, so the netting benefit is only 24.5%.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe the effectiveness of netting in reducing credit exposure under various scenarios.

scenarios.setup: A valuation agent for a bilateral OTC portfolio sees net exposure of USD 18m after netting. Collateral already posted has market value USD 8m and carries a 10% haircut. Threshold USD 5m, no initial margin, minimum transfer amount USD 0.5m.
scenarios.ask: Before the threshold is applied, the exposure not covered by the posted collateral (after the haircut) is:

options.label: Exactly USD 10m
options.why: Ignored the haircut and counted the collateral at its full USD 8m market value.

options.label: Below USD 10m
options.why: Applied the haircut in the wrong direction (collateral worth 8.8m), giving 18 - 8.8 = 9.2.

working.label: After threshold
working.display: $10.8 - 5 = 5.8$, above the 0.5 minimum transfer amount, so call USD 5.8m

scenarios.takeaway: A haircut shrinks what posted collateral is worth, so uncovered exposure goes up. The 5m threshold is deducted afterwards, leaving a call of 5.8m.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe the role of a valuation agent.

scenarios.setup: A CCP loses USD 90m closing out defaulter X. It uses, in order: X's initial margin (30), X's default fund contribution (15) and its own skin in the game (10). The rest is met by variation margin gains haircutting (VMGH), pro rata to unrealised gains of surviving members: W has 80 and Y has 20 (USD m).
scenarios.ask: W's haircut is closest to (USD m):

options.why: Scale slip: 1/30 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Read W's 80% share as 8%.
Charged Y's 20% share of the loss to W instead of W's 80%.

scenarios.takeaway: VMGH is the last line of the waterfall: first strip out the defaulter's margin, fund contribution and CCP capital, then share the remainder pro rata to gains.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain the different methods of absorbing losses and managing the default of one or more members of a CCP.

scenarios.setup: A securitisation has tranches defined by attachment and detachment points: equity 0% to 6%, mezzanine 6% to 14%, senior 14% to 100% of the pool.
scenarios.ask: The width (thickness) of the senior tranche is:

options.why: Read the attachment point as the width. The senior tranche starts at 14% but extends to 100%.
Read the detachment point as the width, forgetting that the tranche starts at 14%, not at zero.

scenarios.takeaway: Width = detachment minus attachment. The senior tranche is by far the widest at 86%, even though it is the safest.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe tranching and the distribution of credit losses in a securitization.

scenarios.setup: A CLO holds 100 loans of USD 1m at par, paying reference rate 5% + 400 bp. Senior (85% of the pool) pays ref + 200 bp; junior (10%) pays ref + 500 bp; equity (5%) gets residuals. In year 1, 5 loans default and pay no interest. Excess spread goes to an overcollateralisation account up to USD 2m a year.
scenarios.ask: Loan interest received minus the senior and junior coupons is closest to:

options.label: USD 2.05m
options.why: Counted interest on all 100 loans, 9.0m, instead of the 95 that survive.

options.label: USD 2.6m
options.why: Left the junior coupon (USD 1.0m) out of the coupons due.

scenarios.takeaway: 1.6m is under the 2m cap, so all of it goes to the overcollateralisation account and equity receives nothing in year 1.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain the tests on the excess spread that a custodian must go through at the end of each year to determine the cash flow to the overcollateralization account and to the equity noteholders.

scenarios.setup: In a securitisation, loan interest for the year is USD 7.0m but coupons due to senior and mezzanine bondholders are USD 7.2m. The overcollateralisation account held USD 0.3m at last year-end and receives USD 0.7m of recoveries this year. Bondholders are paid in full from the account if it can cover the shortfall.
scenarios.ask: After the year-end test, the account balance is:

options.label: USD 1.0m
options.why: Forgot to draw the shortfall: 0.3 + 0.7 with nothing paid out.

options.label: USD 0.1m
options.why: Left out the year's recoveries: 0.3 - 0.2.

options.label: USD 0.2m
options.why: Reported the shortfall itself as the balance.

scenarios.takeaway: When interest falls short, the account pays the gap: the balance is prior balance plus recoveries, minus the shortfall.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain the tests on the excess spread that a custodian must go through at the end of each year to determine the cash flow to the overcollateralization account and to the equity noteholders.

scenarios.setup: ABS notes: subordinated tranche 1 USD 50m, subordinated tranche 2 USD 50m, senior USD 100m. The collateral pool is USD 220m. Losses are absorbed first by the overcollateralisation, then by the subordinated tranches, and only then by the senior tranche.
scenarios.ask: A USD 120m loss on the collateral reaches the senior tranche for:

options.label: USD 20m
options.why: Ignored the overcollateralisation (220 - 200 = 20): 120 - 100 = 20.

options.label: USD 50m
options.why: Counted only one subordinated tranche: 120 - 20 - 50 = 50.

scenarios.takeaway: The loss exactly exhausts the overcollateralisation and both subordinated tranches; the senior tranche's attachment point is 120m.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain the terms over-collateralization, first-loss piece, equity piece, and cash waterfall within the securitization process.

scenarios.setup: A pension fund has USD 20m in three sleeves: 30% US stocks ($\sigma = 12\%$), 40% US bonds ($\sigma = 5\%$), 30% non-US stocks ($\sigma = 18\%$). Portfolio volatility is 10%. One-year horizon, 99% ($z = 2.33$).
scenarios.ask: Roughly how big is the fund's **undiversified** VaR?

options.label: ≈ USD 0.47m
options.why: That is the diversification benefit (undiversified minus diversified VaR), not the undiversified VaR itself.

options.label: ≈ USD 1.7m
options.why: Stopped after one sleeve. That is the US-stock individual VaR alone, not the sum across all three.

options.label: ≈ USD 16m
options.why: Applied each sleeve's volatility to the full USD 20m. The weights were dropped, so every sleeve was counted at 100% of the fund.

scenarios.takeaway: Undiversified VaR is the plain sum of individual VaRs (the ρ = +1 case), so in a long-only book it always sits above diversified VaR.
scenarios.lo_text: Define, calculate, and compare the following portfolio VaR measures: diversified and undiversified portfolio VaR, individual VaR, incremental VaR, marginal VaR, and component VaR.

scenarios.setup: Same USD 20m fund (99%, $z = 2.33$). Diversified VaR $= 2.33 \times 10\% \times 20 =$ USD 4.66m. Two of three individual VaRs are done: US stocks 1.68 + US bonds 0.93 = USD 2.61m. Still to add: non-US stocks, USD 6m at $\sigma = 18\%$.
scenarios.ask: The diversification benefit (undiversified minus diversified VaR): positive, negative, or too close to call?

options.label: Negative
options.why: That would need the sum of individual VaRs to fall below diversified VaR. With every position long, the sum is the ρ = +1 upper bound, so it can't.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: The non-US sleeve adds about 2.52, so the sum is 5.13. That is USD 0.47m (about 10%) above 4.66, which is a clear gap.

scenarios.takeaway: Sum of individual VaRs ≥ diversified VaR for a long-only book, so the diversification benefit is never negative.
scenarios.lo_text: Define, calculate, and compare the following portfolio VaR measures: diversified and undiversified portfolio VaR, individual VaR, incremental VaR, marginal VaR, and component VaR.

scenarios.setup: A USD 1m portfolio holds 60% in Asset A (beta to the portfolio 0.80) and 40% in Asset B (beta 1.30). Diversified 95% VaR $= 1.645 \times 0.060606 \times 1{,}000{,}000 \approx$ USD 99,700. Component VaR of A $= 99{,}700 \times 0.80 \times 0.60 \approx$ USD 47,850.
scenarios.ask: Is B's component VaR bigger than A's, smaller, or too close to call?

options.label: A's is bigger
options.why: A has more capital, but component VaR scales with weight × beta: 0.40 × 1.30 = 0.52 for B against 0.60 × 0.80 = 0.48 for A.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: The weight × beta shares must sum to 1. A takes 0.48, so B takes 0.52, which puts B about USD 4,000 ahead.

scenarios.takeaway: Component VaR share = weight × beta. The smaller position can carry more risk if its beta is high enough.
scenarios.lo_text: Define, calculate, and compare the following portfolio VaR measures: diversified and undiversified portfolio VaR, individual VaR, incremental VaR, marginal VaR, and component VaR.

scenarios.setup: A USD 950m equity portfolio ($\sigma_p = 19\%$) holds USD 98m of one stock with $\sigma = 24\%$ and correlation 0.60 with the portfolio. One-year 95% VaR, $z = 1.65$.
scenarios.ask: The stock's **component** VaR is closest to…

options.label: ≈ USD 7m
options.why: Scale slip: about 0.3× the true figure.

options.label: ≈ USD 62m
options.why: Scaled the individual VaR by (1 + ρ) instead of ρ.

options.label: ≈ USD 230m
options.why: Stopped at $VaR_p \times \beta$ and forgot to multiply by the position's weight, 98/950.

scenarios.takeaway: Component VaR = individual VaR × ρ. The portfolio σ and NAV cancel out.
scenarios.lo_text: Define, calculate, and compare the following portfolio VaR measures: diversified and undiversified portfolio VaR, individual VaR, incremental VaR, marginal VaR, and component VaR.

scenarios.setup: Same position: USD 98m of a stock with $\sigma = 24\%$ and correlation 0.60 with the USD 950m portfolio. You've found its standalone (individual) 95% VaR: $1.65 \times 0.24 \times 98 =$ USD 38.8m.
scenarios.ask: Will its component VaR come out above, below, or equal to USD 38.8m?

options.label: Above
options.why: Component VaR = individual VaR × ρ. With ρ = 0.60 < 1 the figure shrinks, to 23.3.

options.label: Equal
options.why: They are equal only when ρ = +1, where there is no diversification credit. Here ρ = 0.60.

scenarios.takeaway: Individual VaR is the ceiling for component VaR. The discount is the position's correlation with the portfolio.
scenarios.lo_text: Define, calculate, and compare the following portfolio VaR measures: diversified and undiversified portfolio VaR, individual VaR, incremental VaR, marginal VaR, and component VaR.

scenarios.setup: USD 2m portfolio: USD 1m Technology and USD 1m Real Estate. Marginal VaRs are 0.3153 (Tech) and 0.5300 (Real Estate). Diversified 95% VaR is USD 845,301.
scenarios.ask: Tech holds half the capital. Is its share of diversified VaR more than half, less than half, or about half?

options.label: More than half
options.why: On equal dollars, Tech's marginal VaR (0.315) is well below Real Estate's (0.530). Component VaRs are 315,300 against 530,000.

options.label: About half
options.why: It's about 37% against 63%, which is not close.

scenarios.takeaway: Component VaR = marginal VaR × that position's dollars. On equal dollars, the lower marginal VaR is the smaller risk share.
scenarios.lo_text: Define, calculate, and compare the following portfolio VaR measures: diversified and undiversified portfolio VaR, individual VaR, incremental VaR, marginal VaR, and component VaR.

scenarios.setup: USD 1.3m portfolio: Financial fund USD 500k (individual VaR 329,000; marginal VaR 0.5897) and Energy fund USD 800k (individual VaR 263,200). Diversified 95% VaR is USD 513,900. Component VaR of Financial $= 0.5897 \times 500{,}000 \approx$ USD 294,850.
scenarios.ask: Is Financial's **incremental** VaR larger than its component VaR, smaller, or the same?

options.label: Larger
options.why: Removing Financial leaves Energy alone at 263,200. Incremental VaR = 513,900 − 263,200 = 250,700, which is below 294,850.

options.label: The same
options.why: The two only coincide for a tiny position. For a whole block, portfolio VaR is convex in the position, so the full-removal figure comes in lower.

scenarios.takeaway: Individual > component > incremental VaR for a large long position. Incremental VaR subtracts the *other* leg's standalone VaR.
scenarios.lo_text: Define, calculate, and compare the following portfolio VaR measures: diversified and undiversified portfolio VaR, individual VaR, incremental VaR, marginal VaR, and component VaR.

scenarios.setup: A two-currency portfolio: USD 2m CAD exposure (beta to the portfolio 0.615) and USD 1m EUR exposure (beta 1.770).
scenarios.ask: EUR holds a third of the capital. Is its share of portfolio VaR more than a third, less than a third, or exactly a third?

options.label: Less than a third
options.why: Share of VaR = weight × beta. A beta above 1 means more risk than capital: (1/3) × 1.77 = 59%.

options.label: Exactly a third
options.why: That would need beta = 1. EUR's beta is 1.77.

scenarios.takeaway: Percentage contribution to VaR = w × β. Beta above 1 means the position's risk share exceeds its capital share.
scenarios.lo_text: Define, calculate, and compare the following portfolio VaR measures: diversified and undiversified portfolio VaR, individual VaR, incremental VaR, marginal VaR, and component VaR.

scenarios.setup: A USD 20m portfolio is split between a Tech ETF and a REIT ETF. At a 50/50 mix, marginal VaR is 0.118 for Tech and 0.386 for the REIT.
scenarios.ask: To lower diversified VaR, should the manager shift money toward Tech, toward the REIT, or stay put?

options.label: Toward the REIT
options.why: Each dollar in the REIT adds 0.386 of VaR against Tech's 0.118. Move money from the high-marginal-VaR leg to the low one.

options.label: Stay put
options.why: VaR is at its minimum only when the marginal VaRs are equal. A 0.268 gap means the mix isn't there yet.

scenarios.takeaway: Minimum VaR means equal marginal VaRs. Shift dollars from the higher marginal VaR to the lower.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain and calculate the risk-minimizing position and position that maximizes the ratio of expected return to risk.

scenarios.setup: A USD 10m portfolio is split between an Energy ETF (expected excess return 6%) and a Healthcare ETF (12%). At 60% Energy, marginal VaR is 0.085 for Energy and 0.353 for Healthcare.
scenarios.ask: To raise the portfolio's excess-return-to-VaR ratio, shift toward Energy, toward Healthcare, or stay put?

options.label: Toward Healthcare
options.why: Healthcare has the higher raw return, but it earns only 12/0.353 = 34 per unit of marginal VaR. Energy earns 6/0.085 = 71.

options.label: Stay put
options.why: The ratio is at its best only when return / marginal VaR is equal across positions. 71 against 34 is far from equal.

working.label: Result
working.display: Tilt to Energy: at 75% Energy the ratios are 47.6 vs 45.6 and return/VaR rises from 0.437 to 0.468

scenarios.takeaway: Best return-to-VaR comes where E/ΔVaR is equal across positions. Add to the position with the higher ratio.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain and calculate the risk-minimizing position and position that maximizes the ratio of expected return to risk.

scenarios.setup: Two managers share a benchmark. Manager 1: alpha 2.35%, tracking error 25%. Manager 2: alpha 3.00%, tracking error 34%.
scenarios.ask: Which manager has the higher information ratio, or is it too close to call?

options.label: Manager 2
options.why: Manager 2 has the higher alpha, but 3.00/34 = 0.088 < 2.35/25 = 0.094. The extra active risk more than uses up the extra alpha.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: Cross-multiply: 2.35 × 34 = 79.9 against 3.00 × 25 = 75.0. That's a clear 6% edge to Manager 1.

scenarios.takeaway: IR = alpha / tracking error. The higher-alpha manager can still have the lower IR if the extra alpha came with proportionally more active risk.
scenarios.lo_text: Define and calculate alpha, tracking error, the information ratio, and the Sharpe ratio.

scenarios.setup: A manager has an information coefficient of 0.15 and makes 36 independent bets a year (breadth 36).
scenarios.ask: By the fundamental law of active management, her information ratio is closest to…

options.why: Dropped the square root: IC × BR instead of IC × √BR.
Scale slip: 30× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Scale slip: 100× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: IR = IC × √BR. Breadth pays off only as a square root.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe Grinold’s fundamental law of active management, including its assumptions and limitations, and calculate the maximum attainable information ratio using this law.

scenarios.setup: Today: $IC = 0.15$ with breadth 12, so $IR = 0.15\sqrt{12} \approx 0.52$. The manager proposes tripling breadth to 36 bets a year, but expects her IC to drop to 0.10 because the extra bets are lower-conviction.
scenarios.ask: Her information ratio: rises, falls, or roughly unchanged?

options.label: Falls
options.why: IC falls by a third (×0.67), but tripling breadth multiplies IR by √3 = 1.73. The net factor is 0.67 × 1.73 = 1.15, which is up.

options.label: Roughly unchanged
options.why: The net multiplier is 1.15, taking IR from 0.52 to 0.60, a 15% rise.

scenarios.takeaway: IR scales linearly with IC but only with √breadth. Tripling breadth offsets an IC cut of up to 42% (1/√3).
scenarios.lo_text: Describe Grinold’s fundamental law of active management, including its assumptions and limitations, and calculate the maximum attainable information ratio using this law.

scenarios.setup: A great manager (information coefficient 0.12) has a score of +1.5, a standardised view, on a stock with 30% residual volatility.
scenarios.ask: The implied alpha of this view is closest to…

options.why: Scale slip: 1/10 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Used the residual variance, 0.09, where the volatility, 0.30, belongs.
Scale slip: about 3× the true figure.

scenarios.takeaway: Alpha = IC × σ × score. The small IC shrinks even a strong view to a few percent.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe Grinold’s fundamental law of active management, including its assumptions and limitations, and calculate the maximum attainable information ratio using this law.

scenarios.setup: Single-factor pricing kernel: $E(m) = 1/1.03 = 0.9709$, $\text{var}(m) = 0.090$ (σ of $m$ = 30%), and $\text{cov}(r_i, m) = -0.1068$.
scenarios.ask: The asset's risk premium $E(r_i) - R_f$ is closest to…

options.why: Scale slip: 1/30 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Scale slip: 1/10 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Used σ(m) = 0.30 in place of var(m) in the beta denominator: β = −0.1068/0.30.

scenarios.takeaway: In the kernel model β and λ are both negative. Their product is the positive premium.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe factors that impact asset prices and explain the theory of factor risk premiums.

scenarios.ask: Next intermediate: the price of bad-times risk $\lambda(m)$. Is it positive, negative, or zero?

options.label: Positive
options.why: λ(m) = −var(m)/E(m). Both var(m) and E(m) are positive, so the leading minus makes it −0.0927. The premium is positive only because negative β × negative λ is positive.

scenarios.takeaway: λ(m) = −var(m)/E(m) is always negative. Paired with a negative β(i,m), it gives a positive premium.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe factors that impact asset prices and explain the theory of factor risk premiums.

scenarios.setup: A manager's alpha is 1.90% per month, and the monthly standard deviation of the alpha estimate is 4.0%. To reject 'it's luck' you need $t = \bar\alpha\sqrt{N}/\sigma(\alpha) \ge 1.645$, where $N$ is the number of months (two-sided 10%).
scenarios.ask: How long a track record is needed?

options.label: ≈ 0.29 years
options.why: Stopped at √N ≈ 3.46 and treated it as the number of months.

options.label: ≈ 3.5 years
options.why: Stopped at √N ≈ 3.46 and read it as years.

options.label: ≈ 12 years
options.why: N ≈ 12 is in months. Reading it as years is the unit slip.

scenarios.takeaway: N = (z·σ/α)² comes out in the data's own time unit. Convert months to years at the end.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain the difficulties in measuring the performance of actively managed portfolios.

scenarios.setup: A more ordinary manager: alpha 0.25% per month, and the monthly standard deviation of the alpha estimate is 4.0%. Reject 'luck' when $\bar\alpha\sqrt{N}/\sigma(\alpha) \ge 1.645$, where $N$ is the number of months.
scenarios.ask: How long a track record is needed?

options.label: ≈ 2.2 years
options.why: Stopped at √N ≈ 26.3 and treated it as months.

options.label: ≈ 19 years
options.why: Scale slip: about 0.3× the true figure.

options.label: ≈ 690 years
options.why: N ≈ 693 is in months. Reading it as years is the unit slip.

scenarios.takeaway: The required track record grows with 1/α². A modest alpha takes decades to prove.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain the difficulties in measuring the performance of actively managed portfolios.

scenarios.setup: A pension fund has USD 4,550m of assets with annual volatility 7%. You want one-year VaR at 95% ($z = 1.65$).
scenarios.ask: VaR is closest to…

options.label: ≈ USD 5.3m
options.why: Scale slip: 1/100 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 33m
options.why: Scaled the annual σ down to one day (÷√252), but the horizon is one year.

options.label: ≈ USD 160m
options.why: Scale slip: about 0.3× the true figure.

scenarios.takeaway: VaR = z × σ × W, with σ as a decimal and matched to the horizon.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain the use of VaR to monitor risk.

scenarios.setup: Two equally sized active managers, USD 360m each, both with $\sigma = 14\%$, and correlation 0.65 between them. With $z = 2.33$, each has an individual risk budget of $2.33 \times 0.14 \times 360 \approx$ USD 117.4m. At zero correlation the pair would total $117.4\sqrt2 \approx$ USD 166m.
scenarios.ask: Is the sleeve's actual total risk budget above USD 166m, below it, or too close to call?

options.label: Below
options.why: Only a negative correlation could push the total below the ρ = 0 figure. ρ = +0.65 adds a positive cross term.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: The multiplier is √(2 + 2 × 0.65) = √3.3 = 1.82, against √2 = 1.41. The total is about 213, well above 166.

scenarios.takeaway: For two equal budgets, total = B × √(2 + 2ρ): between B√2 at ρ = 0 and 2B at ρ = 1.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe the risk budgeting process and calculate risk budgets across asset classes and active managers.

scenarios.setup: USD 800m is split between two independent active managers to maximise IR, subject to 5% total tracking error. A: IR 0.75, TEV 8%. B: IR 0.50, TEV 8%. The optimum gives $IR_p = \sqrt{0.75^2 + 0.50^2} = 0.901$ and $x_i = IR_i\,(\omega_p/IR_p)/\omega_i$, so $x_A = 0.75 \times (0.05/0.901)/0.08 = 52.0\%$.
scenarios.ask: The weight left in the benchmark, $1 - x_A - x_B$: positive, negative, or roughly zero?

options.label: Negative
options.why: x_B = (0.50/0.75) × 52.0% = 34.7%, so the two managers total 86.7%, under 100%.

options.label: Roughly zero
options.why: The manager weights aren't forced to sum to one. 13.3% sits in the benchmark, which uses up no tracking-error budget.

scenarios.takeaway: Risk budgets are proportional to IRs. Any leftover capital goes to the zero-TEV benchmark, so manager weights need not sum to 100%.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe the risk budgeting process and calculate risk budgets across asset classes and active managers.

scenarios.setup: Convertible arbitrage: you are long one convertible with delta 53% and a conversion ratio of 21.2037 shares, and you delta-hedge by shorting the stock.
scenarios.ask: How many shares do you short?

options.label: ≈ 3.4 shares
options.why: Scale slip: about 0.3× the true figure.

options.label: ≈ 40 shares
options.why: Divided the conversion ratio by delta instead of multiplying.

options.label: ≈ 110 shares
options.why: Scale slip: 10× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: Shares to short = delta × conversion ratio: the bond's share-equivalents scaled by its current sensitivity.
scenarios.lo_text: Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies.

scenarios.setup: Convertible arbitrage: long one convertible at USD 1,013.75 (delta 53%, conversion ratio 21.2037), short $0.53 \times 21.2037 \approx 11.24$ shares at USD 41.54. The stock falls 5% (USD 2.08 a share), and the model marks the convertible down to USD 991.78, a loss of USD 21.97 on that leg.
scenarios.ask: Net P&L on the hedged position (ignoring coupons, borrow fees and dividends): positive, negative, or too close to call?

options.label: Negative
options.why: The short leg gains 11.24 × 2.08 ≈ 23.34, which more than covers the 21.97 lost on the convertible.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: The net is +1.37: small, but the sign is reliable. The convex long leg loses less than the linear short leg gains.

scenarios.takeaway: A delta-hedged convertible is long convexity: small gains whichever way the stock moves.
scenarios.lo_text: Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies.

scenarios.setup: Same hedge: long one convertible at USD 1,013.75, short 11.24 shares at USD 41.54. This time the stock **rises** 5%, and the model marks the convertible up to USD 1,038.07.
scenarios.ask: Hedged P&L (ignoring coupons, borrow fees and dividends): gain, loss, or exactly zero?

options.label: Loss
options.why: The short leg loses 11.24 × 2.08 = 23.34, but the convertible gains 24.32, for a net of +0.98.

options.label: Exactly zero
options.why: Delta neutralises only the first-order move. The convertible's convexity leaves a small gain of +0.98.

scenarios.takeaway: Delta-hedged convertible = long volatility. It gains on both a 5% rise and a 5% fall.
scenarios.lo_text: Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies.

scenarios.setup: $r_f = 3\%$. The market returned 11% with $\sigma = 20\%$. Donald's portfolio returned 15% with $\sigma = 40\%$ and correlation 0.80 with the market. So far: $\beta_p = 0.80 \times 40/20 = 1.60$.
scenarios.ask: Jensen's alpha: positive, negative, or too close to call?

options.label: Positive
options.why: 15% beats the market's 11%, but the CAPM required return at β = 1.60 is 3 + 1.60 × 8 = 15.8%, so alpha is −0.8%.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: −0.8% is small, but its sign is clear, and Sharpe (0.30 vs 0.40) and Treynor (7.5 vs 8.0) both agree the portfolio lagged.

scenarios.takeaway: Beating the market on raw return isn't alpha. Charge for β first: β > 1 raises the hurdle.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe risk-adjusted performance measures, such as Sharpe’s measure, Treynor’s measure, Jensen’s measure (Jensen’s alpha), and the information ratio, and identify the circumstances under which the use of each measure is most relevant.

scenarios.setup: An illiquid-fund database reports a mean return of 12% and volatility of 8%. With $r_f = 2\%$, the reported Sharpe ratio is 1.25. Two corrections are pending: survivorship cuts the return by 4 points (to 8%), and unsmoothing lifts volatility to 11%.
scenarios.ask: Applied on its own, which correction pulls the Sharpe ratio down further, or is it too close to call?

options.label: The volatility (unsmoothing) fix
options.why: Volatility alone gives 10/11 = 0.91. The return fix gives 6/8 = 0.75, a bigger cut, because it removes 40% of the excess return.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: The two single-fix ratios are 0.75 and 0.91, which are 0.16 apart.

scenarios.takeaway: Reported illiquid Sharpe ratios are inflated twice: the return is overstated and the volatility understated.
scenarios.lo_text: Assess the impact of biases on reported returns for illiquid assets.

scenarios.setup: A pension fund has USD 100,000 of assets and USD 90,000 of liabilities. Expected surplus growth is 5% of assets a year, and the 99% one-year surplus VaR is 22% of assets. Expected surplus in a year: $10{,}000 + 5{,}000 =$ USD 15,000.
scenarios.ask: At the 1% tail, is the surplus positive (still a surplus), negative (a deficit), or too close to call?

options.label: Positive
options.why: VaR is 22% × 100,000 = USD 22,000, bigger than the 15,000 expected cushion: 15,000 − 22,000 = −7,000.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: A USD 7,000 deficit against a USD 22,000 VaR is not borderline.

scenarios.takeaway: Tail surplus = expected surplus − surplus VaR. A VaR bigger than the cushion means a deficit in the tail.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe and compare the following types of risk: absolute risk, relative risk, policy-mix risk, active management risk, funding risk, and sponsor risk.

scenarios.setup: A private fund called USD 100m at $t = 0$ and USD 50m at $t = 1$, then distributed USD 220m at $t = 2$. A reference index went 1.00 → 1.10 → 1.21. Raw multiple (MOIC) $= 220/150 = 1.47\times$.
scenarios.ask: Will the public market equivalent (PME) come out higher than 1.47, lower, or the same?

options.label: Higher
options.why: PME discounts each cash flow by index growth. The distribution is furthest out (÷1.21) while the calls are discounted less, so the ratio shrinks: 181.8/145.5 = 1.25.

options.label: The same
options.why: That would happen only if the index were flat. It grew 21%, and PME strips that out.

scenarios.takeaway: PME = MOIC with the market's return taken out. In a rising market it's below the raw multiple, and above 1 means the fund beat the index.
scenarios.lo_text: Apply and compare different methods to measure the performance of private equity investments and describe their advantages and disadvantages.

scenarios.setup: Capital-structure trade: buy one USD 1,000-face bond (6% annual coupon) at USD 350 and short 120 shares at USD 2.50. In two years the firm liquidates: both coupons are paid, the bond recovers USD 400, and the stock goes to zero.
scenarios.ask: Total gain on the combined position is closest to…

options.label: ≈ USD 1,400
options.why: Scale slip: about 3× the true figure.

options.label: ≈ USD 4,700
options.why: Scale slip: 10× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 14,100
options.why: Scale slip: 30× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: Long senior / short junior pays twice in liquidation: the recovery gain on the bond, plus the full short proceeds when the equity is wiped out.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain the mechanics of a distressed securities strategy, and describe challenges, risks and considerations that may arise when implementing this strategy.

scenarios.setup: An endowment holds USD 700m of public equity and USD 300m of private equity, against a 30% private-equity target. Public equities fall 30% in a quarter. The private-equity book still carries last quarter's valuation, and no capital is called or distributed.
scenarios.ask: The reported private-equity weight: above target, below target, or on target?

options.label: Below target
options.why: The denominator shrank (1,000 → 790) while the stale 300 numerator didn't move: 300/790 = 38%.

options.label: On target
options.why: That would require private equity to be marked down 30% as well. It hasn't been repriced.

scenarios.takeaway: Denominator effect: a public-market drop mechanically overweights stale-marked private assets.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain how different risks can arise for investors in private markets and assess how these risks can be measured.

scenarios.setup: An active position has alpha 0.80% and beta 1.50. The benchmark's alpha is 0.060%.
scenarios.ask: After neutralising for benchmark exposure, the position's alpha is higher than 0.80%, lower, or unchanged?

options.label: Higher
options.why: The part of alpha that comes from benchmark exposure, 0.060 × 1.50 = 0.09, is subtracted, which gives 0.71%.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: It would be unchanged only if the benchmark alpha were zero. Here 0.09 comes off.

scenarios.takeaway: Benchmark-neutral alpha = α − β × α_benchmark. With a positive benchmark alpha, neutralising only takes alpha away.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe neutralization and the different approaches used for refining alphas to be neutral.

scenarios.setup: A hedge fund holds USD 100 of stock financed with a USD 75 margin loan, so equity is USD 25 and debt-to-equity is 3.0×. The stock falls 10%.
scenarios.ask: Debt-to-equity leverage: rises, falls, or unchanged?

options.label: Falls
options.why: The loan stays at 75 while equity takes the whole 10 loss, dropping to 15: 75/15 = 5.0×.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: It would stay the same only if the loan shrank with the asset. It doesn't, so equity takes the full loss.

scenarios.takeaway: Price falls raise leverage mechanically. Getting back to target forces sales, and that selling feeds the spiral.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain how the activities of hedge funds and exposure to hedge funds can increase systemic risk.

scenarios.setup: A stock's no-trade band: buy only if alpha exceeds $PC + 2\lambda_A\psi\,MCAR$, and sell only if alpha drops below $2\lambda_A\psi\,MCAR - SC$. The purchase cost is 0.40% and the sales cost 0.60%. Active risk aversion $\lambda_A$ doubles from 0.10 to 0.20.
scenarios.ask: The band's width: widens, narrows, unchanged, or can't tell without the stock's alpha?

options.label: Widens
options.why: The centring term 2λψMCAR appears in both bounds and cancels. Width = PC + SC = 1.00% whatever λ is; higher λ only shifts the band up.

options.label: Narrows
options.why: Risk aversion moves where the band sits, not its width. The width is round-trip cost, PC + SC = 1.00%.

options.label: Can't tell without the stock's alpha
options.why: Alpha is what gets compared with the band; it doesn't set the band's width. The width is PC + SC.

scenarios.takeaway: The no-trade band is PC + SC wide. Risk aversion shifts it without resizing it.
scenarios.lo_text: Determine the optimal no-trade region for rebalancing with transaction costs.

scenarios.setup: A manager goes from 10 to 20 stocks, spreading the additions across several industries. Assume the portfolio's excess return and beta are unchanged.
scenarios.ask: The portfolio's Sharpe ratio: rises, falls, or roughly unchanged?

options.label: Falls
options.why: Diversification cuts idiosyncratic variance σ²(e), so total σ falls. With the excess return fixed, Sharpe goes up.

options.label: Roughly unchanged
options.why: That describes Treynor, whose denominator β doesn't move. Sharpe divides by total σ, which does fall.

working.label: Result
working.display: $\sigma_p \downarrow$ with the numerator fixed $\Rightarrow$ Sharpe $\uparrow$; Treynor (÷β) unchanged

scenarios.takeaway: Sharpe rewards diversification because it divides by total σ. Treynor ignores it because it divides by β.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe risk-adjusted performance measures, such as Sharpe’s measure, Treynor’s measure, Jensen’s measure (Jensen’s alpha), and the information ratio, and identify the circumstances under which the use of each measure is most relevant.

scenarios.setup: A low-volatility fund beat the Russell 1000 by 0.28% a year. The risk-matched benchmark is 65% Russell 1000 + 35% risk-free asset, and $r_f$ is well below the Russell's return.
scenarios.ask: Measured against the risk-matched benchmark, the fund's alpha: rises, falls, or unchanged?

options.label: Falls
options.why: The blend returns less than the Russell because 35% of it earns $r_f$. With the fund's return fixed, fund − benchmark gets bigger.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: Alpha is a residual against the benchmark, so it moves whenever the benchmark's return does. Here the benchmark's return falls.

working.label: Alpha
working.display: $\alpha = r_{fund} - r_B$: benchmark down $\Rightarrow \alpha$ up (and tracking error falls, so IR rises too)

scenarios.takeaway: A benchmark riskier than the fund understates alpha. Matching the fund's risk lowers the hurdle and raises alpha.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain the difficulties in measuring the performance of actively managed portfolios.

scenarios.setup: Pricing-kernel model: $E(r_i) - R_f = \beta(i,m)\,\lambda(m)$ with $\lambda(m) = -0.09$. An asset's $\beta(i,m)$ moves from −0.95 to −0.33.
scenarios.ask: Its risk premium: rises, falls, or unchanged?

options.label: Rises
options.why: β goes up (toward zero), but λ is negative: (−0.33)(−0.09) = 2.97%, down from 8.55%.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: The premium is proportional to β(i,m). A smaller magnitude of negative β means a smaller premium.

scenarios.takeaway: Against the kernel, a higher (less negative) β means a lower premium. The asset pays off more in bad times, so it needs less compensation.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe factors that impact asset prices and explain the theory of factor risk premiums.

scenarios.setup: A USD 30m portfolio holds a Consumer ETF (USD 20m, $\sigma = 12\%$) and a Materials ETF (USD 10m, $\sigma = 38\%$), with correlation +0.15. The 95% individual VaRs are 3.95m and 6.25m, portfolio VaR is 7.88m, and Consumer's component VaR is about 2.45m. The correlation doubles to +0.30.
scenarios.ask: Consumer's component VaR: rises, falls, or unchanged?

options.label: Falls
options.why: Higher ρ raises Consumer's covariance with the portfolio and lifts portfolio VaR itself. Both push component VaR up, from 2.45 to 2.76.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: Component VaR = individual VaR × ρ(i,p), and ρ(i,p) rises when the pairwise correlation rises.

scenarios.takeaway: In a long two-asset book, higher correlation means less diversification, so each position's component VaR goes up.
scenarios.lo_text: Define, calculate, and compare the following portfolio VaR measures: diversified and undiversified portfolio VaR, individual VaR, incremental VaR, marginal VaR, and component VaR.

scenarios.setup: An illiquid asset is appraised only quarterly, so its reported return series misses the price moves between observations.
scenarios.ask: Reported beta relative to the true beta: overstated, understated, or unbiased?

options.label: Overstated
options.why: Infrequent trading smooths the series. Betas, volatilities and correlations all come out too low. (Overstated *returns* come from survivorship and selection bias, a different effect.)

options.label: Unbiased
options.why: Missing the variation between observations is not the same as there being none. Sampled risk measures are biased down.

working.label: Mechanism
working.display: Sparse sampling $\Rightarrow$ smoothed returns $\Rightarrow$ $\hat\beta,\ \hat\sigma,\ \hat\rho$ all biased down
