options.why: Assumed the drift cancels out over one year. It sits inside the exponent and moves the 5% worst-case value up by 14 points of log return.

scenarios.takeaway: In lognormal VaR a positive expected return lowers the loss quantile; ignore it only when the horizon is short.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).

scenarios.setup: A stock trades at a midpoint of INR 200 with an average bid-ask spread of INR 0.80, held constant. Position: 10,000 shares. Daily return volatility is 2% and returns are normal with zero mean. Use $z = 2.33$ (99%).
scenarios.ask: The one-day 99% liquidity-adjusted VaR (VaR plus half-spread cost) is closest to:

options.label: INR 970
options.why: Scale slip: 1/100 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: INR 4,000
options.why: Kept only the half-spread cost ($\tfrac12 \times 0.004 \times 2{,}000{,}000$) and left the market VaR out.

options.label: INR 32,333
options.why: Scale slip: 1/3 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: Market VaR dominates a liquid-ish name: the half-spread cost is small, but it is added on top, not instead.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).

scenarios.setup: Normal market. A bank holds 25m shares quoted 90.8 / 92.4 (USD) and 35m ounces of a commodity quoted 24.0 / 26.2 (USD). Liquidation cost of a leg is half the dollar spread times the quantity.
scenarios.ask: Which leg is more expensive to liquidate?

options.label: The shares, because that position is far larger in dollar value
options.why: Ranked legs by position value. Cost depends on the spread relative to price: shares 1.7%, commodity 8.8%.

options.label: They cost about the same
options.why: Treated both as 'a spread of about USD 2 on tens of millions of units' without comparing the two spreads: 1.6 versus 2.2, on different quantities.

scenarios.takeaway: A thin position in a wide-spread asset can cost more to unwind than a big position in a tight one.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).

scenarios.setup: Stressed-market unwind, 95% ($z = 1.645$). Two long positions with perfectly correlated, normal proportional spreads: \$25,000 with mean = sd = 0.050, and \$40,000 with mean = sd = 0.030. Cost $= \tfrac12 \sum \alpha_i(\mu_i + z\sigma_i)$.
scenarios.ask: Compared with the normal-market unwind cost (spread means only), the stressed cost is:

options.label: Exactly double
options.why: Used $\mu + \sigma$ and left out the z-score. With $\sigma = \mu$ that would double the cost, but $z = 1.645$ makes the factor $1 + 1.645$.

options.label: Less than double
options.why: Treated the volatility term as a small cushion on top of the mean. Here $\sigma$ equals $\mu$, so $z\sigma$ alone is 1.645 times the mean.

scenarios.takeaway: When the spread's sd equals its mean, the stressed cost is $(1+z)$ times the normal cost.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).

scenarios.setup: 50,000 shares, bid 39.00 / offer 41.00, position \$2.0m. Daily price volatility 2.00%. The proportional spread has mean $0.05$ and sd $0.02$. Use $z = 1.65$ for both price and spread; liquidity cost uses the worst-case spread $\tfrac12(\mu + z\sigma)$.
scenarios.ask: In the one-day 95% LVaR, which part is larger?

options.label: The market VaR
options.why: Used the normal-market cost $\tfrac12 \times 5\% = 2.5\%$ of the position, which sits below the 3.3% VaR. The worst-case spread adds $1.65 \times 2\%$.

options.label: They are equal
options.why: Saw 2% volatility and a 2% spread sd and assumed both parts match. The cost also carries the 5% mean spread.

scenarios.takeaway: Under a worst-case spread the cost leg can outweigh the market-risk leg even for a liquid-looking stock.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).

scenarios.setup: 50,000 shares quoted bid 22.20 / offer 23.10. The dollar bid-offer spread is normal with mean equal to the quoted spread and standard deviation \$1.70. Use the one-tail $z = 1.645$ (95%).
scenarios.ask: The worst-case (95%) spread per share is closest to:

options.why: Used the quoted spread only, which is the normal-market figure.
Added one standard deviation ($0.90 + 1.70$) and dropped the z-score.
Used the two-tail $z = 1.96$. A wider spread is the only adverse case, so the one-tail value applies.

scenarios.takeaway: In a stressed spread the volatility term can be three times the mean: do not stop at the quote.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).

scenarios.setup: Stressed cost, 99% ($z = 2.326$). A bank holds 1m shares of X (mid \$72) and 1m units of Y (mid \$47). Dollar spread per unit: X mean \$1.30, sd \$1.03; Y mean \$1.32, sd \$0.88. Spreads are normal and perfectly correlated.
scenarios.ask: The cost of liquidating both positions in a stressed market is closest to:

options.label: \$10m
options.why: Scale slip: 3× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: \$35m
options.why: Slipped one decimal place on the $z\sigma$ products when adding them to the means (scale slip, 10 times).

options.label: \$210m
options.why: Applied the dollar spreads as if they were proportional, multiplying by the \$72m and \$47m position values instead of by the unit counts.

scenarios.takeaway: Per-unit dollar spreads multiply units, not position value. Stressed cost = half the stressed spread times units.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).

scenarios.setup: An illiquid asset is quoted bid \$89.00, offer \$96.00. The proportional bid-offer spread is the dollar spread divided by the midpoint price.
scenarios.ask: The proportional spread is closest to:

options.why: Divided by 925 instead of 92.5 (a decimal slip in the midpoint).
Divided by 9.25 instead of 92.5 (a decimal slip in the midpoint).
Quoted the dollar spread $96 - 89$ and never divided by price.

scenarios.takeaway: A proportional spread is a small fraction: a few percent for an illiquid name, never above 1.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).

scenarios.setup: A stock has bid \$331 and ask \$335. The sample sd of the proportional spread is $0.00019$. Expected per-share cost $= P \cdot s/2 = \$2.00$. The 95% upper bound adds $P \cdot \tfrac12 \cdot z\sigma_s$ with $z = 1.65$ and $P$ the midprice.
scenarios.ask: The extra amount the 95% upper bound adds to the \$2.00 expected cost is:

options.label: About \$0.50
options.why: Read $\sigma_s = 0.00019$ as 0.19% ($0.0019$), ten times too large.

options.label: About \$2.00
options.why: Added a second full expected cost instead of the small risk term, doubling it to \$4.00.

scenarios.takeaway: The spread's sd is tiny next to its level, so the upper bound is only a few cents above the expected cost.
scenarios.lo_text: Calculate the expected transactions cost and the spread risk factor for a transaction and calculate the liquidity adjustment to VaR for a position to be liquidated over a number of trading days.

scenarios.setup: One-day 99% VaR is \$5m. The position is sold in 10 equal parts, one at the end of each day. The liquidity adjustment multiplies VaR by $\sqrt{(1+T)(1+2T)/(6T)}$, with $T = 10$.
scenarios.ask: Compared with simply scaling VaR to ten days, $5\text{m} \times \sqrt{10} \approx \$15.8\text{m}$, the liquidity-adjusted VaR is:

options.label: Higher
options.why: Assumed the liquidity adjustment adds risk on top of the ten-day figure. The position shrinks each day, so average exposure is smaller than holding it all ten days.

options.label: The same
options.why: Treated the factor as $\sqrt{T}$, which would hold the whole position for all ten days.

scenarios.takeaway: Selling down over T days gives a factor of about 2 for T = 10: bigger than 1 day, smaller than the whole position held for $\sqrt{T}$.
scenarios.lo_text: Calculate the expected transactions cost and the spread risk factor for a transaction and calculate the liquidity adjustment to VaR for a position to be liquidated over a number of trading days.

scenarios.setup: Bell Aviation: bid \$32.45, ask \$32.90, sd of the proportional spread $0.004$, $z = 2.33$ (99%). Midprice $32.675$. The spread factor is $\tfrac12(s + z\sigma_s)$, and per-share cost is midprice times the factor.
scenarios.ask: The 99% spread factor is closest to:

options.why: Dropped the volatility term and kept only $\tfrac12 s$, the expected-cost factor.
Forgot the one-half in $\tfrac12(s + z\sigma_s)$.
Kept only the volatility term, $\tfrac12 \times 2.33 \times 0.004$, and left out the spread itself.

scenarios.takeaway: Half the spread plus half a z-sd of it: the factor lands near 1.2% for a name with a 1.4% spread.
scenarios.lo_text: Calculate the expected transactions cost and the spread risk factor for a transaction and calculate the liquidity adjustment to VaR for a position to be liquidated over a number of trading days.

scenarios.setup: A position is sold off in equal parts over $T = 8$ trading days. Liquidity-adjusted VaR is the 1-day VaR times $\sqrt{(1+T)(1+2T)/(6T)}$.
scenarios.ask: The percentage by which LVaR exceeds the 1-day VaR is closest to:

options.why: Took the factor minus one, 0.785, and read it as 0.785% instead of 78.5%.
Scale slip: 1/10 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Scale slip: 1/3 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: The liquidation factor is a square root, so 8 days adds under 80%, nowhere near 8 times.
scenarios.lo_text: Calculate the expected transactions cost and the spread risk factor for a transaction and calculate the liquidity adjustment to VaR for a position to be liquidated over a number of trading days.

scenarios.setup: Equity position of USD 1,000,000 with annual volatility 34.0%. Assume 250 trading days a year, i.i.d. normal returns and a 99% quantile of 2.33. The first step of the LVaR chain is the plain 1-day 99% VaR.
scenarios.ask: The 1-day 99% VaR is closest to:

options.label: About USD 790,000
options.why: Used the annual volatility directly, with no scaling down to one day: $1{,}000{,}000\times0.34\times2.33$.

options.label: About USD 3,200
options.why: Divided the annual volatility by 250 instead of by $\sqrt{250}$.

scenarios.takeaway: Annual to daily volatility divides by $\sqrt{250}\approx 15.8$, not by 250.
scenarios.lo_text: Calculate the expected transactions cost and the spread risk factor for a transaction and calculate the liquidity adjustment to VaR for a position to be liquidated over a number of trading days.

scenarios.setup: A share trades at a midprice of USD 50.00 with a bid-ask spread of USD 0.35. The relative spread has a standard deviation of 0.20% (0.0020). The 99% transactions cost per share is the half-spread plus its spread risk: $P\times\tfrac12(s + 2.33\,\sigma_s)$.
scenarios.ask: Which part of the 99% cost per share is larger?

options.label: The spread-risk add-on
options.why: Dropped the $\tfrac12$ on the risk term: $2.33\times0.0020\times50 = 0.233$ would beat 0.175, but with the $\tfrac12$ it is only 0.1165.

options.label: They are equal
options.why: The two pieces sit in the same range but not at the same value: 0.175 against 0.1165.

scenarios.takeaway: In the transactions-cost formula the half-spread is the bulk, with the 99% spread risk adding a smaller top-up.
scenarios.lo_text: Calculate the expected transactions cost and the spread risk factor for a transaction and calculate the liquidity adjustment to VaR for a position to be liquidated over a number of trading days.

scenarios.setup: A position with a 1-day VaR of USD 62 million is liquidated in equal parts over $T = 4$ trading days. LVaR $=$ VaR$_{1\text{-day}}\times\sqrt{(1+T)(1+2T)/(6T)}$. Plain square-root-of-time scaling over 4 days would give $62\times\sqrt{4} = $ USD 124 million.
scenarios.ask: Compared with USD 124 million, the LVaR is:

options.label: Equal
options.why: Treated the liquidation factor as $\sqrt{T} = 2$. The actual factor is $\sqrt{45/24} = 1.37$.

options.label: Higher
options.why: Assumed the sell-down adds risk on top of $\sqrt{T}$ scaling. The position shrinks as it is sold, so average exposure is smaller.

scenarios.takeaway: The sell-down ramp makes LVaR grow more slowly than $\sqrt{T}$ scaling: the position shrinks while it is sold.
scenarios.lo_text: Calculate the expected transactions cost and the spread risk factor for a transaction and calculate the liquidity adjustment to VaR for a position to be liquidated over a number of trading days.

scenarios.setup: A share is priced at USD 50.00 with a bid-ask spread of USD 0.350. The relative spread $s$ has a volatility of 20 basis points (0.20%). The 99% transactions cost per share is $P\times\tfrac12(s + 2.33\,\sigma_s)$.
scenarios.ask: The 99% transactions cost per share is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.006
options.why: Stopped at the relative cost $0.00583$ and never multiplied by the USD 50 price.

options.label: ≈ USD 0.03
options.why: Scale slip (1/10): lost a decimal place in the final multiplication.

options.label: ≈ USD 0.097
options.why: Scale slip: 1/3 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: Convert basis points to decimals before plugging in, and remember the cost is per share: multiply by the price.
scenarios.lo_text: Calculate the expected transactions cost and the spread risk factor for a transaction and calculate the liquidity adjustment to VaR for a position to be liquidated over a number of trading days.

scenarios.setup: A Treasury bill with face value USD 100 is bought for USD 88 and matures in 120 days. Bank discount rate: $\frac{F-P}{F}\times\frac{360}{t}$. Bond-equivalent yield: $\frac{F-P}{P}\times\frac{365}{t}$.
scenarios.ask: For this bill, the bond-equivalent yield is:

options.label: Lower than the discount rate
options.why: Thought the discount rate, quoted on the bigger-looking face value, must be the larger. It divides by the larger base (100, not 88) and uses the shorter 360-day year, so it understates the yield.

options.label: Equal to the discount rate
options.why: Treated both as the same annualised return. They use different bases (face against price) and different year lengths (360 against 365).

scenarios.takeaway: Discount rate divides by face and uses 360 days; both choices make it lower than the yield on price.
scenarios.lo_text: Compare various money market and capital market instruments and discuss their advantages and disadvantages.

scenarios.setup: A Treasury bill is priced at USD 89.84 per USD 100 face and matures in 124 days. The bank discount rate uses face value as the base and a 360-day year.
scenarios.ask: The bank discount rate is closest to:

options.why: Stopped at the 124-day discount of 10.16 per 100 and never annualised it.
Scale slip: 3× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Scale slip (10×): misplaced the decimal after annualising.

scenarios.takeaway: Annualise by scaling up: $360/t$ is a number above 1 for any bill under a year.
scenarios.lo_text: Compare various money market and capital market instruments and discuss their advantages and disadvantages.

scenarios.setup: A money-market security is priced at USD 95 per USD 100 face, with 85 days to maturity (360-day year). The same data sheet lists a required rate of return of 12% and a yield to maturity of 8%.
scenarios.ask: The bank discount rate is closest to:

options.label: About 12%
options.why: Lifted the required rate of return off the data sheet. It is not an input to a discount rate.

options.label: About 8%
options.why: Lifted the stated yield to maturity. The discount rate is computed from price, face and days.

options.label: About 5%
options.why: Stopped at the USD 5 raw discount and never annualised it by 360/85.

scenarios.takeaway: A discount rate comes from price, face value and days. Other rates quoted alongside are distractors.
scenarios.lo_text: Compare various money market and capital market instruments and discuss their advantages and disadvantages.

scenarios.setup: A bond with par USD 1,500 pays a 10% annual coupon (USD 150) and matures in 4 years. It trades at USD 1,200. Its current yield is $150/1{,}200 = 12.5\%$.
scenarios.ask: The yield to maturity is:

options.label: Equal to 12.5%
options.why: Treated the coupon over price as the whole return. The bond also gains USD 300 as it pulls up to par.

options.label: Below 12.5%
options.why: Anchored on the 10% coupon rate and pulled the figure down. A bond below par earns its coupon plus the pull to par.

scenarios.takeaway: A bond bought below par has YTM above its current yield, which is above its coupon rate.
scenarios.lo_text: Identify and discuss various factors that affect the choice of investment securities by a bank.

scenarios.setup: A bond with par USD 2,000 pays an 8% annual coupon (USD 160), matures in 5 years and trades at USD 1,600. A quick estimate of yield is (annual coupon + annual pull to par) divided by the average of price and par.
scenarios.ask: That estimate is closest to:

options.label: About 10%
options.why: Used the current yield $160/1{,}600$ only, ignoring the USD 400 pull to par.

options.label: About 8%
options.why: Used the coupon rate, which ignores both the discount price and the pull to par.

scenarios.takeaway: For a discount bond: coupon rate < current yield < YTM.
scenarios.lo_text: Identify and discuss various factors that affect the choice of investment securities by a bank.

scenarios.setup: A taxed financial firm in the 35% federal bracket holds an Aaa municipal bond with a 5% gross yield to maturity, which is tax-exempt. The tax-equivalent yield is the tax-exempt yield divided by $(1 - t)$.
scenarios.ask: The taxable bond that gives the same after-tax return must yield:

options.label: Less than 5%
options.why: Multiplied by $(1-t) = 0.65$, getting 3.25%, as if the municipal bond were the taxed one.

options.label: Exactly 5%
options.why: Ignored the 35% tax on the taxable bond. A 5% taxable bond would leave only 3.25% after tax.

scenarios.takeaway: Tax-equivalent yield is always above the muni yield: divide by $(1-t)$, never multiply.
scenarios.lo_text: Identify and discuss various factors that affect the choice of investment securities by a bank.

scenarios.setup: A bank holds a municipal bond with a 5% tax-exempt return, funded at a pretax cost of 3.7%. The tax rate is 40%, and only 75% of the interest expense is deductible. Net after-tax return is the 1.30% gross spread plus the tax shield on deductible interest.
scenarios.ask: Compared with the 1.30% gross spread, the net after-tax return is:

options.label: Equal to 1.30%
options.why: Left out the tax shield. The deductible part of the funding cost reduces the bank's taxes and adds to the return.

options.label: Below 1.30%
options.why: Taxed the spread at 40% ($1.30\times0.60 = 0.78\%$). The municipal interest itself is exempt.

scenarios.takeaway: On a bank-qualified muni the funding cost partly shields tax, so the net return is above the pretax spread.
scenarios.lo_text: Identify and discuss various factors that affect the choice of investment securities by a bank.

scenarios.setup: A bank buys a bank-qualified municipal bond with a 5.5% tax-exempt return, funded at 4.7%. The marginal tax rate is 34%, and 80% of the interest expense is deductible. Net after-tax return is the gross spread plus the tax shield on the deductible interest.
scenarios.ask: The net after-tax return is closest to:

options.why: Taxed the 0.80% spread at 34% and called the tax the return.
Stopped at the gross spread and left out the tax shield on the deductible interest.
Quoted the bond's own return and ignored the funding cost.

scenarios.takeaway: The deductible funding cost is worth more than the spread itself here: shield 1.28% against spread 0.80%.
scenarios.lo_text: Identify and discuss various factors that affect the choice of investment securities by a bank.

scenarios.setup: Mountain Top Savings projects a net liquidity deficit of USD 10m next week. Supplies (USD m): deposit inflows 26, nondeposit revenue 18, customer loan repayments 23, asset sales 10, money market borrowings 15. Demands other than deposit withdrawals: quality loans 32, repayment of borrowings 15, dividends 10, operating expenses 15.
scenarios.ask: The deposit withdrawals needed to produce the −10 position are:

options.label: USD 20m
options.why: Stopped at supply minus the other demands (92 − 72 = 20), which would give a balanced position, not a deficit.

options.label: USD 10m
options.why: Read the −10 deficit as the withdrawal figure itself.

scenarios.takeaway: Net position $=$ supply $-$ demand: withdrawals must exceed the pre-withdrawal surplus by the size of the deficit.
scenarios.lo_text: Calculate a bank’s net liquidity position and explain factors that affect the supply and demand of liquidity at a bank.

scenarios.setup: ABC Bank forecasts next-day cash flows (USD m). Inflows: deposit inflows 119, money market borrowings 110, asset sales 61, nondeposit-services revenue 118, scheduled loan repayments 122. Outflows: deposit withdrawals 129, acceptable loan requests 90, stockholder dividends 172, repayment of bank borrowings 84, operating expenses 70.
scenarios.ask: The projected net liquidity position is a:

options.label: Surplus
options.why: Left the USD 172m dividend out of the demands, giving $530 - 373 = +157$.

options.label: Exact balance
options.why: Treated 530 against 545 as close enough to net out. The gap is USD 15m of outflows with no source.

scenarios.takeaway: Add every inflow and every outflow, dividends included. A small gap can still be a deficit.
scenarios.lo_text: Calculate a bank’s net liquidity position and explain factors that affect the supply and demand of liquidity at a bank.

scenarios.setup: Greenlux State Bank, next 24 hours (USD m): incoming deposits 90, customer loan repayments 25, asset sales 20, nondeposit fee income 15; deposit withdrawals 60, acceptable loan requests 45, repayment of the bank's own borrowings 5.
scenarios.ask: The projected net liquidity position is a:

options.label: Deficit
options.why: Counted both 'repayment' items as outflows. Customer loan repayments are a source of liquidity; only repaying the bank's own borrowings is a use: $125 - 135 = -10$.

scenarios.takeaway: Repayments of loans owed to the bank are a source; repayments of borrowings the bank owes are a use.
scenarios.lo_text: Calculate a bank’s net liquidity position and explain factors that affect the supply and demand of liquidity at a bank.

scenarios.setup: Grand Bank's liquidity manager sees four scenarios for next month's liquidity position (USD m), with probabilities: 45% at −500, 20% at −575, 25% at +350, 10% at +100.
scenarios.ask: Compared with the simple average of the four outcomes (−156.25), the expected (probability-weighted) position is:

options.label: A smaller deficit
options.why: Weighted the surplus scenarios too heavily. They carry only 35% of the probability, against 65% for the two deficit scenarios.

options.label: The same
options.why: Used equal weights of 25%, which is what the simple average does.

scenarios.takeaway: Expected value uses the probabilities: here the likelier deficit cases pull it below the plain average.
scenarios.lo_text: Estimate a bank’s liquidity needs through three methods (sources and uses of funds, structure of funds, and liquidity indicators).

scenarios.setup: Daylight Bank (USD m): federal funds sold and reverse repos 396; federal funds purchased and repurchase agreements 488; total assets 3,431. Other balance-sheet items are not needed. Net fed funds and repo position $=$ (sold − purchased) / total assets.
scenarios.ask: The net position is:

options.label: Positive, a net lender
options.why: Subtracted in the wrong order (purchased minus sold), giving +2.68%.

options.label: Zero
options.why: Treated the two lines as offsetting. They differ by USD 92m.

scenarios.takeaway: Sold minus purchased: a negative net position means the bank is a net borrower in the fed funds and repo market.
scenarios.lo_text: Estimate a bank’s liquidity needs through three methods (sources and uses of funds, structure of funds, and liquidity indicators).

scenarios.setup: Daylight Bank (USD m): cash and due from depository institutions 546; US Treasuries 382; other securities 550; pledged securities 503; fed funds sold and reverse repos 396; net loans 2,374; total assets 3,431; total deposits 2,686; core deposits 1,111. The cash position indicator is cash and due from depository institutions divided by total assets.
scenarios.ask: The indicator is closest to:

options.why: Divided by core deposits (1,111) instead of total assets.
Scale slip (10×): misplaced the decimal when converting to a percent.
Scale slip: 30× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: Check the denominator: the cash position indicator is measured against total assets, and a cash ratio above 100% should always ring an alarm.
scenarios.lo_text: Estimate a bank’s liquidity needs through three methods (sources and uses of funds, structure of funds, and liquidity indicators).

scenarios.setup: Kingstreet Savings, vulnerable funds (USD m): checkable deposits 20, savings deposits 40, nonpersonal time deposits 70. The legal reserve is 10% on checkable and savings deposits and 0% on nonpersonal time deposits. The 50% desired reserve is applied to funds net of legal reserves.
scenarios.ask: The legal reserves held against the vulnerable funds are:

options.label: USD 13.0m
options.why: Applied the 10% to all 130 including time deposits, which carry a 0% requirement.

options.label: USD 2.0m
options.why: Applied 10% to checkable deposits only and left out savings deposits.

scenarios.takeaway: Legal reserves apply only to the categories that carry a requirement, and are deducted before the desired percentage.
scenarios.lo_text: Estimate a bank’s liquidity needs through three methods (sources and uses of funds, structure of funds, and liquidity indicators).

scenarios.setup: A bank's liabilities (USD m, desired reserve): hot money 50 at 80%, vulnerable funds 55 at 30%, core funds 100 at 20%. Legal reserves are 3% of each category, and the desired percentages apply after deducting them. Loans are 165 and could reach 225, a 60 loan requirement that is not part of the liability reserve.
scenarios.ask: The liability liquidity reserve is:

options.label: Equal to USD 76.5m
options.why: Applied the desired percentages to the gross balances ($40+16.5+20 = 76.5$) and skipped the 3% legal-reserve deduction.

options.label: Above USD 130m
options.why: Added the USD 60m loan requirement, which belongs to the total liquidity requirement, not the liability reserve.

scenarios.takeaway: Net the legal reserves first: the liability reserve is slightly below the gross figure, and loans are added only for the total requirement.
scenarios.lo_text: Estimate a bank’s liquidity needs through three methods (sources and uses of funds, structure of funds, and liquidity indicators).

scenarios.setup: Liquidity gap table for institution XYZ, cash flows by expiry. Year 1: notional in $+20$, interest in $+6$, interest out $-4$. Year 2: interest in $+5$, notional out $-10$, interest out $-4$. The TSECCF is the running total of the net flows, starting at year 1.
scenarios.ask: After the year-2 expiry, the TSECCF is:

options.label: Negative (about $-9$)
options.why: Reported the year-2 net flow alone. TSECCF is cumulative, so the year-1 surplus of $+22$ carries into year 2.

options.label: Above the year-1 figure
options.why: Added the year-2 outflow instead of subtracting it ($22 + 9 = 31$). A net outflow lowers the running total.

options.label: Positive, but below the year-1 figure

scenarios.takeaway: TSECCF is a running total: last period's balance plus this period's net flow, not this period's flow alone.
scenarios.lo_text: Interpret the term structure of expected cash flows and cumulative cash flows.

scenarios.setup: A 10-year-plus liquidity gap table. Over the whole life of the book, notional inflows total $100$ ($25 + 60 + 15$) and notional outflows total $-100$ ($-20 - 35 - 20 - 25$, the last one beyond year 10). Interest received totals $40$ and interest paid totals $-26$. The TSECCF in the final (over 10 years) bucket is the cumulative total of every flow.
scenarios.ask: The TSECCF in the final bucket is:

options.label: Zero
options.why: Assumed everything cancels because the notional flows do. Interest does not net to zero here: $40 - 26 = +14$ remains.

options.label: Negative
options.why: Focused on the last bucket's $-25$ notional outflow. The cumulative figure carries all the earlier inflows too.

scenarios.takeaway: Once all principal has repaid, the final cumulative gap is just the net interest left over.
scenarios.lo_text: Interpret the term structure of expected cash flows and cumulative cash flows.

scenarios.setup: A bank holds a bond of notional $1{,}000{,}000$ bought on a coupon date. It pays a $10\%$ annual coupon, semiannually. After 10 months the bank sells notional $300{,}000$ at a clean price of $99.95$ (per 100). The liquidity-generation table records the cash actually received, which is the dirty price.
scenarios.ask: The inflow recorded for this sale is closest to:

options.why: Counted only the accrued interest on the 300,000 and left out the clean price.
Scale slip (0.1×). The sale is 30% of a 1,000,000 position at about par, so the inflow is in the hundreds of thousands.
Applied the dirty price to the whole 1,000,000 notional instead of the 300,000 sold.

scenarios.takeaway: Sales generate the dirty price, clean price plus interest accrued since the last coupon (here 4 months, not 10).
scenarios.lo_text: Discuss the impact of available asset transactions on cash flows and liquidity generation capacity.

scenarios.setup: A bank buys a bond on a coupon date and enters a repo on it exactly 3 months later. The bond pays a $3.5\%$ annual coupon, semiannually, and is quoted at a clean price of $97$ (per 100). The cash lent against it depends on the dirty price.
scenarios.ask: Accrued interest at the repo start, per 100 of notional, is closest to:

options.why: Took a full semiannual coupon ($3.5/2$). Only 3 months of the 6-month period have elapsed.
Took a full year of coupon. The coupon accrues only since the last payment date.

working.label: Fraction of a year since last coupon

scenarios.takeaway: Accrued interest runs from the last coupon date: annual coupon × time since that date, not a whole coupon.
scenarios.lo_text: Discuss the impact of available asset transactions on cash flows and liquidity generation capacity.

scenarios.setup: Promise Bank issues a 50-day negotiable CD with face value USD 10 million at a $5\%$ annual rate. Interest accrues on a 360-day year and is paid with the principal at maturity.
scenarios.ask: The interest Promise Bank pays at maturity is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 500,000
options.why: Left out the $50/360$ fraction and charged a full year of interest.

options.label: ≈ USD 2,070,000
options.why: Scale slip: 30× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 6,900,000
options.why: Scale slip: 100× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: Money-market interest is principal × rate × days/360. A 50-day CD earns about 14% of a year's interest.
scenarios.lo_text: Distinguish between the various sources of non-deposit liabilities at a bank.

scenarios.setup: A credit union borrows USD 200 million overnight through a repurchase agreement at a $5\%$ annual RP rate, on a 360-day year. One year of interest on this amount would be USD 10 million.
scenarios.ask: Interest for the one night is:

options.label: Above USD 50,000
options.why: Charged two nights, about USD 55,556 (a weekend), or forgot to divide by 360. The loan is overnight, so one day.

scenarios.takeaway: Overnight cost is the annual rate divided by 360: roughly 0.014% of the amount borrowed.
scenarios.lo_text: Distinguish between the various sources of non-deposit liabilities at a bank.

scenarios.setup: A bank raises USD 775m of short-term funds, of which USD 700m is net investable. Negotiable CDs cost $2.40\%$ in interest plus $0.25\%$ noninterest cost; commercial paper costs $2.35\%$ plus $0.50\%$. Noninterest costs are a percentage of the full USD 775m. Effective cost is total cost divided by the net investable funds.
scenarios.ask: Which has the higher effective cost rate?

options.label: Negotiable CDs
options.why: Ranked by the market rate alone ($2.40\% > 2.35\%$). The extra $0.25\%$ of noninterest cost on commercial paper outweighs its $0.05\%$ rate advantage.

options.label: They are equal
options.why: The common $775/700$ gross-up scales both rates by the same factor; it does not remove the $0.20\%$ gap in total cost.

scenarios.takeaway: Effective cost = (interest + noninterest) over net investable funds. Noninterest costs can reverse a ranking by market rate.
scenarios.lo_text: Discuss factors affecting the choice of non-deposit funding sources.

scenarios.setup: Niche Bank raises USD 1,000m, of which only USD 900m is net investable. Federal funds cost $2.10\%$ in interest plus a $0.42\%$ noninterest cost, both stated on the USD 1,000m raised. The dollar cost is already done: $0.0252 \times 1{,}000 = $ USD 25.2m.
scenarios.ask: The effective cost rate of the federal funds is closest to:

options.why: Divided the cost by the USD 1,000m raised. Effective cost uses the USD 900m that can actually be invested.
Multiplied by $0.9$ instead of dividing by it. Less investable money pushes the effective rate up, not down.

scenarios.takeaway: Costs are on funds raised, but the rate is measured on funds net investable, so the effective cost exceeds the market rate plus noninterest cost.
scenarios.lo_text: Discuss factors affecting the choice of non-deposit funding sources.

scenarios.setup: ABC Bank funds earning assets of USD 1,240m. The break-even cost rate covers borrowed funds only. Total costs: money market USD 275m at $3.51\%$, time and savings deposits USD 580m at $3.10\%$, checkable deposits USD 385m at $3.28\%$. Stockholders' equity of USD 290m has a $12.75\%$ required return, which enters the overall cost later, not the break-even.
scenarios.ask: Which source adds the most dollar cost to the break-even numerator?

options.label: Money market borrowings
options.why: Picked the highest rate ($3.51\%$). Cost in dollars is rate times amount, and money market is the smallest block at USD 275m.

options.label: Stockholders' equity
options.why: Its $12.75\%$ on USD 290m is the largest dollar figure (about USD 37m), but equity is excluded from the break-even on borrowed funds.

scenarios.takeaway: Break-even counts borrowed-funds cost only. Rank sources by rate times amount, not by rate.
scenarios.lo_text: Calculate overall cost of funds using both the historical average cost approach and the pooled-funds approach.

scenarios.setup: Pathway Bank's stockholders require a $12\%$ after-tax return and the tax rate is $15\%$. To find the weighted average overall cost of capital, the equity return must first be restated as a pre-tax figure.
scenarios.ask: The pre-tax equity cost is:

options.label: Below 12% (about 10.2%)
options.why: Multiplied by $(1 - 0.15)$. That converts a pre-tax figure into after-tax; here it must go the other way, dividing by $(1 - t)$.

options.label: Exactly 12%
options.why: Skipped the tax gross-up. The bank must earn $12\%$ after paying tax, so the pre-tax need is higher.

scenarios.takeaway: Pre-tax cost of equity = after-tax return / (1 − t). Taxes raise the hurdle, never lower it.
scenarios.lo_text: Calculate overall cost of funds using both the historical average cost approach and the pooled-funds approach.

scenarios.setup: KBC Bank must raise USD 800m to fund USD 600m of new loans. It raises USD 550m of time deposits at $5\%$ interest with a $2\%$ noninterest cost, and USD 250m of transaction deposits with no interest and a $3\%$ noninterest cost. All percentages are of the amount raised.
scenarios.ask: Total expense (interest plus noninterest) to be covered is closest to:

options.label: USD 27.5m
options.why: Counted interest only ($550 \times 5\%$). Noninterest costs on both sources are real expenses of raising the funds.

options.label: USD 18.5m
options.why: Counted noninterest costs only ($11.0 + 7.5$) and left out the interest paid on the time deposits.

scenarios.takeaway: Pooled cost (46/800 = 5.75%) divides total expense by all funds raised; the hurdle rate (46/600 = 7.67%) divides it by funds placed in assets.
scenarios.lo_text: Calculate overall cost of funds using both the historical average cost approach and the pooled-funds approach.

scenarios.setup: Blue Star Bank expects to raise USD 300m, of which USD 250m will be invested in earning assets. Total expected interest and overhead costs on the new funds are USD 22m. The pooled-funds cost divides these costs by all funds raised; the hurdle rate divides them by the funds invested in earning assets.
scenarios.ask: Compare the two rates:

options.label: The pooled-funds cost is higher
options.why: Reversed the denominators. Pooled cost is spread over all USD 300m raised, the larger base, so it is the smaller rate.

options.label: They are equal
options.why: Same USD 22m numerator, but the denominators differ (300 against 250), so the rates differ.

scenarios.takeaway: Same cost, smaller base: the hurdle rate (funds actually invested) always exceeds the pooled cost when some funds sit idle.
scenarios.lo_text: Calculate overall cost of funds using both the historical average cost approach and the pooled-funds approach.

scenarios.setup: A six-year loan amortizes linearly, repaying one sixth of principal at each year-end, so it is six loans maturing in years 1 to 6. Term liquidity premiums (bps) for 1 to 6 years: $6, 14, 18, 24, 27, 32$. Matched-maturity funding charges each tranche its own term's premium, weighted by how long it is outstanding. The plain average of the six premiums is $20.2$ bps; a bullet loan would pay the 6-year premium, $32$ bps.
scenarios.ask: The charge on the amortizing loan is:

options.label: Below 20.2 bps
options.why: Took the plain average as a floor and then lowered it for amortization. Weighting by term gives the longer, higher-premium tranches more weight, so the charge sits above the plain average.

options.label: 32 bps
options.why: That is the bullet-loan charge. Here most of the principal is repaid early, so the single 6-year premium overstates the cost.

scenarios.takeaway: Linear amortization weights each year's premium by its term: the charge lands between the average premium and the bullet premium.
scenarios.lo_text: Compare the various approaches to liquidity transfer pricing (zero cost, average cost, and matchedmaturity marginal cost).

scenarios.setup: A four-year loan repays equal principal each year, so it is four tranches maturing in years 1 to 4. The term liquidity premiums are $12, 17, 24, 30$ bps for 1 to 4 years. Under matched-maturity marginal cost of funds, each tranche's premium is weighted by its term.
scenarios.ask: The charge for funding liquidity risk is closest to:

options.label: ≈ 83 bps
options.why: Added the four premiums ($12+17+24+30$) with no weights and no division.

options.label: ≈ 240 bps
options.why: Built the weighted sum ($238$) but never divided by the sum of weights.

options.label: ≈ 720 bps
options.why: Scale slip: 30× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: The charge is a term-weighted average of the premiums, so it must land between the shortest and longest premium (12 to 30).
scenarios.lo_text: Compare the various approaches to liquidity transfer pricing (zero cost, average cost, and matchedmaturity marginal cost).

scenarios.setup: A credit union has earning assets of USD 575m and a net interest margin of $2.50\%$. The margin then rises by $10\%$ in relative terms (to $2.75\%$) and earning assets grow by $20\%$.
scenarios.ask: The increase in net interest income is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 1.4m
options.why: Applied the higher margin to the old asset base only, ignoring the $20\%$ asset growth.

options.label: ≈ USD 19m
options.why: Reported the new level of net interest income (USD 18.98m) rather than the change from the old level.

options.label: ≈ USD 138m
options.why: Scale slip: 30× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: NII = margin × earning assets, so a 10% rise in margin and a 20% rise in assets compound to about +32%.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe interest-sensitive gap management and apply this strategy to maximize a bank’s net interest margin.

scenarios.setup: A savings bank has a cumulative interest-sensitive gap of USD 25m, which then rises by $60\%$. Market rates rise by $25\%$ from $3.00\%$ to $3.75\%$, and every rate-sensitive item reprices by the same amount.
scenarios.ask: The change in net interest income at the new gap is closest to:

options.label: ≈ +USD 0.03m
options.why: Scale slip: read the rate move as $0.075$ percentage points instead of $0.75$.

options.label: ≈ +USD 0.10m
options.why: Scale slip: 1/3 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ +USD 1.2m
options.why: Used the $3\%$ rate level instead of the $0.75$ percentage-point move.

scenarios.takeaway: ΔNII = gap × Δrate. Use the change in the rate (0.75 points), not its level or its percentage rise.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe interest-sensitive gap management and apply this strategy to maximize a bank’s net interest margin.

scenarios.setup: New Comers State Bank (USD m). Two years ago: interest revenues 78, interest expenses 68, loans 400, investments 200. Currently: interest revenues 82, interest expenses 64, loans 450, investments 200. Earning assets are loans plus investments; net interest margin is net interest income over earning assets.
scenarios.ask: From two years ago to now, the net interest margin has:

options.label: Fallen
options.why: Compared revenue to assets instead of net interest income: $78/600 = 13.0\%$ against $82/650 = 12.6\%$. NIM uses revenue minus expense.

options.label: Stayed about the same
options.why: Net interest income rose from 10 to 18 (up 80%) while earning assets grew only 8%, so the margin moves a lot.

scenarios.takeaway: NIM is built on net interest income. A small change in revenue and expense moves the margin a lot.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe interest-sensitive gap management and apply this strategy to maximize a bank’s net interest margin.

scenarios.setup: Bright Bank reports (USD m): interest revenues 83, interest costs 72, total earning assets 942.
scenarios.ask: The net interest margin is closest to:

options.why: Divided interest costs ($72$) by earning assets instead of net interest income.
Scale slip: 30× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: NIM = (interest revenue − interest cost) / earning assets. A bank's margin is a thin slice, usually a few percent at most.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe interest-sensitive gap management and apply this strategy to maximize a bank’s net interest margin.

scenarios.setup: A bank has a cumulative one-year gap (rate-sensitive assets minus rate-sensitive liabilities) of +USD 128m. Rates are expected to fall by 1.5 percentage points over the year.
scenarios.ask: Net interest income is expected to:

options.label: Rise, by about USD 1.9m
options.why: Sign slip. A positive gap gains when rates rise; a fall in rates squeezes asset income more than funding cost, so NII drops.

options.label: Stay unchanged
options.why: Treated a positive gap as a hedged book. Only a gap near zero leaves NII unaffected by a parallel rate move.

scenarios.takeaway: Change in NII is about the rate change times the cumulative gap, so a positive gap loses when rates fall.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe interest-sensitive gap management and apply this strategy to maximize a bank’s net interest margin.

scenarios.setup: A bank has interest-sensitive assets of USD 470m, interest-sensitive liabilities of USD 876m and total assets of USD 1,000m. The dollar gap is already worked out as ISA minus ISL = -USD 406m.
scenarios.ask: The relative interest-sensitive gap (dollar gap divided by total assets) is closest to:

options.label: About -86%
options.why: Divided the gap by interest-sensitive assets (470) instead of total assets.

options.label: About +41%
options.why: Sign slip: took ISL minus ISA, which flips a liability-sensitive bank into an asset-sensitive one.

options.label: About -0.41%
options.why: Left the ratio $-0.406$ as a decimal and read it as a percent figure.

scenarios.takeaway: The relative gap scales the dollar gap by total assets, not by either sensitive side; the sign says which side is bigger.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe interest-sensitive gap management and apply this strategy to maximize a bank’s net interest margin.

scenarios.setup: A bank reports a net interest margin of 2.45%. Interest revenue is USD 100m and interest expense is USD 64m.
scenarios.ask: Earning assets are closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.88m
options.why: Multiplied net interest income by the margin instead of dividing.

options.label: ≈ USD 14.7m
options.why: Entered the margin as 2.45 instead of 0.0245, a percent-as-decimal slip.

options.label: ≈ USD 490m
options.why: Scale slip: 1/3 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: NIM is net interest income over earning assets; invert it with NII, not revenue, and keep the margin as a decimal.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe interest-sensitive gap management and apply this strategy to maximize a bank’s net interest margin.

scenarios.setup: A bank has total assets of USD 1,212m and zero equity, so liabilities are also USD 1,212m. Rate-sensitive liabilities are USD 156m and cost 4%. All other liabilities are not rate-sensitive and cost 6%.
scenarios.ask: Which part of the interest expense bill is larger?

options.label: The non-rate-sensitive liabilities: USD 1,056m at 6%, about USD 63m
The rate-sensitive liabilities: USD 156m at 4%, about USD 6m
options.why: Treated the USD 156m as the whole liability side. With zero equity the other 1,056 is also funded, at 6%.

options.label: About equal
options.why: The 6% rate is only 1.5 times the 4% rate, but the base is nearly seven times larger, so the non-rate-sensitive leg dominates.

scenarios.takeaway: With zero equity every asset is funded by a liability; the big non-rate-sensitive block drives the interest bill.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe interest-sensitive gap management and apply this strategy to maximize a bank’s net interest margin.

scenarios.setup: A bank has interest-sensitive assets of USD 500m and interest-sensitive liabilities of USD 300m.
scenarios.ask: The interest-sensitivity ratio, ISA / ISL, is:

options.label: Below 1, so the bank is liability sensitive
options.why: Inverted the ratio: ISL / ISA = 0.60 is the reciprocal, not the interest-sensitivity ratio.

options.label: Above 1, so the bank is asset sensitive
Exactly 1
options.why: The ratio is 1 only when ISA equals ISL; here assets exceed liabilities by USD 200m.

scenarios.takeaway: ISA over ISL above 1 means more assets than liabilities reprice: asset sensitive, positive gap.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe interest-sensitive gap management and apply this strategy to maximize a bank’s net interest margin.

scenarios.setup: ABC Bank reports: interest income USD 143m, interest expense USD 128m, total earning assets USD 950m, shareholders equity USD 300m, cash USD 93m.
scenarios.ask: Net interest margin (net interest income over earning assets) falls in which range?

options.label: Between 2% and 10%
options.why: Divided net interest income by equity (15 / 300 = 5.0%) instead of earning assets.

options.label: Above 10%
options.why: Used gross interest income, not net: 143 / 950 = 15.1%. The margin is on the spread over funding cost.

scenarios.takeaway: NIM is a thin number: net interest income is a small residual of two large flows, divided by earning assets.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe interest-sensitive gap management and apply this strategy to maximize a bank’s net interest margin.

scenarios.setup: A bank has assets of USD 180m with duration 4 years and liabilities of USD 150m with duration 3 years. Market yields jump from 9% to 13%.
scenarios.ask: Using duration, the bank's net worth:

options.label: Rises
options.why: Looked only at the liability side: liabilities lose about USD 16.5m, which looks like a gain. Assets lose more, about USD 26.4m.

options.label: Is unchanged
options.why: Assumed both sides moving cancels out. Dollar durations are 720 (assets) against 450 (liabilities), so they do not offset.

scenarios.takeaway: Net worth moves by the change in assets minus the change in liabilities; the longer, larger asset side loses more when yields rise.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe duration gap management and apply this strategy to protect a bank’s net worth.

scenarios.setup: Liquidity-adjusted VaR = regular VaR + cost of unwinding in a normal market. One-day 99% VaR is GBP 9.4m. Equity block: mid value GBP 200m, quote bid 49.80 / offer 50.20. Corporate bond: mid value GBP 150m, quote bid 98.70 / offer 99.30.
scenarios.ask: The cost of unwinding (the add-on to VaR) is closest to:

options.label: GBP 2.5m
options.why: Charged the full bid-offer spread on each position instead of half. Selling crosses only half the spread, from mid to bid.

options.label: GBP 10.65m
options.why: That is the full liquidity-adjusted VaR (9.4 + 1.25), not the add-on itself.

scenarios.takeaway: Unwinding costs half the proportional spread times mid value; the add-on is small next to the VaR itself.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).

scenarios.setup: Stressed liquidity-adjusted VaR, spreads normal, 99% spread confidence ($\lambda = 2.326$). Provincial bonds: mid value CAD 120m, proportional spread mean 1.0%, sd 1.2%. A stock position of 2m shares quoted bid CAD 39.60 / offer CAD 40.40, with dollar spread mean CAD 0.16 and sd CAD 0.20. Regular VaR is CAD 7.5m.
scenarios.ask: The stressed cost of liquidation (the add-on to the VaR) is closest to:

options.label: ≈ CAD 0.76m
options.why: Used mean spreads only and dropped the $\lambda\sigma$ term, which gives the normal-market cost.

options.label: ≈ CAD 8.7m
options.why: Scale slip: 3× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ CAD 27m
options.why: Fed the stock's dollar spread (0.16, 0.20) in as proportions instead of dividing by the CAD 40 mid.

scenarios.takeaway: Stressed cost uses mean plus lambda times sd per position, with dollar spreads converted to proportions first.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).

scenarios.setup: A fund holds 2m shares quoted bid SGD 25.10 / ask SGD 25.30. Daily changes in the relative spread are normal with zero mean and volatility 0.45%. The 99% transaction cost uses the spread risk factor $\tfrac12(\bar s + 2.33\sigma_s)$ times position value.
scenarios.ask: The 99% spread risk factor is closest to:

options.why: Dropped the $2.33\sigma_s$ term, leaving only the expected half-spread $\tfrac12\bar s$.
Dropped the current spread $\bar s$ and kept only $\tfrac12(2.33\sigma_s)$.
Forgot the factor $\tfrac12$ in front of the bracket.

scenarios.takeaway: The 99% spread factor adds 2.33 volatilities to the current relative spread, then takes half because selling crosses half the spread.
scenarios.lo_text: Calculate the expected transactions cost and the spread risk factor for a transaction and calculate the liquidity adjustment to VaR for a position to be liquidated over a number of trading days.

scenarios.setup: A fund holds 2.4m shares of a stock that trades about 1.2m shares a day. Its policy caps its own selling at 25% of daily volume, and it liquidates in equal parts at each day end.
scenarios.ask: The time to escape the position is closest to:

options.label: 2 trading days
options.why: Ignored the 25% cap and assumed the fund can sell the whole 1.2m shares of daily volume.

options.label: 0.5 trading days
options.why: Multiplied by the 25% cap instead of letting it limit the daily sale: 2.4 / 1.2 × 0.25.

scenarios.takeaway: Time to escape is the position over the shares the fund will actually trade each day, not over total market volume.
scenarios.lo_text: Calculate the expected transactions cost and the spread risk factor for a transaction and calculate the liquidity adjustment to VaR for a position to be liquidated over a number of trading days.

scenarios.setup: A thrift uses the structure-of-funds approach and wants to meet all good loan demand at 100%. Loans are USD 117m today but recently peaked at USD 132m, and loans are expected to grow 8% a year. Loan potential is the recent peak grown at the trend rate.
scenarios.ask: The extra loan liquidity requirement above today's loans is closest to:

options.label: USD 15m
options.why: Used the recent peak without growing it: 132 - 117.

options.label: USD 9.4m
options.why: Grew today's 117 by 8% instead of the recent peak: 117 × 1.08 - 117.

options.label: USD 143m
options.why: Stopped at potential loans (132 × 1.08) and did not subtract the loans already on the books.

scenarios.takeaway: The loan requirement is potential loans minus current loans; potential loans start from the recent peak.
scenarios.lo_text: Estimate a bank’s liquidity needs through three methods (sources and uses of funds, structure of funds, and liquidity indicators).

scenarios.setup: A bank builds its term structure of expected cash flows (CAD m). Assets earn 5% and liabilities cost 3%, paid each year end on balances outstanding that year; an item pays interest in its maturity year. Items: bonds held 60 (mature year 1), loans 140 (year 4), deposits 50 (year 2), bonds issued 110 (year 5), equity 40 (repaid only at end of business). No initial cash.
scenarios.ask: After year 2, the cumulated expected cash flow is:

options.label: Negative, about CAD -48m
options.why: Took the year-2 flow alone (7.0 - 50 - 4.8 = -47.8) and forgot to cumulate year 1's inflow of 65.2.

options.label: Zero
options.why: Assumed the 60 bond redemption just pays for the 50 deposits. Year-1 net interest and the surplus of 10 still leave a positive balance.

scenarios.takeaway: Cumulate the flows: a big year-2 outflow does not turn the cumulated position negative if year 1 left a larger inflow.
scenarios.lo_text: Interpret the term structure of expected cash flows and cumulative cash flows.

scenarios.setup: A French bank has initial cash of EUR 1.5m and expected cash flows for years 1 to 6 of +15.0, -6.0, +2.0, -16.5, +1.2, -0.9 (EUR m).
scenarios.ask: The lowest point of the cumulated position (including initial cash) is:

options.label: -5.5, at year 4
options.why: Left out the initial cash of 1.5 when cumulating.

options.label: -16.5, at year 4
options.why: Read the year-4 single-year flow as the position, without cumulating the earlier surplus.

options.label: -3.7, at year 6
options.why: Assumed the last date is the worst. Years 5 and 6 recover and then slip back, but stay above year 4.

scenarios.takeaway: The binding date is the minimum of the running total, which starts from initial cash.
scenarios.lo_text: Interpret the term structure of expected cash flows and cumulative cash flows.

scenarios.setup: A bank repos EUR 800,000 notional of an 8% annual-coupon bond (semiannual) three months after a coupon date. The expected clean price is 99.60, accrued interest is 2% of notional, the haircut is 12%. The clean value of the repoed notional is EUR 796,800.
scenarios.ask: The cash raised at the start of the repo is:

options.label: Higher than EUR 796,800: accrued interest is added on top
options.why: Added the accrued interest (dirty value EUR 812,800) and stopped before applying the haircut.

options.label: About equal to EUR 796,800
options.why: Assumed the haircut and the accrued interest cancel. The haircut cuts 12% of value; accrued adds only 2%.

options.label: Lower than EUR 796,800: the 12% haircut outweighs the 2% accrued interest

scenarios.takeaway: A repo lends the dirty value less the haircut, so a large haircut can leave the cash below even the clean value.
scenarios.lo_text: Discuss the impact of available asset transactions on cash flows and liquidity generation capacity.

scenarios.setup: A bank holds AUD 2m notional of a 6% annual-coupon bond paying semiannually. Three months after a coupon date it enters a six-month sell/buyback on AUD 800,000 notional. Coupons paid before the buyback belong to the buyer. The full holding would pay a coupon of AUD 60,000 on the next coupon date.
scenarios.ask: The coupon the bank records in its expected cash flows on that date is:

options.label: Lower than AUD 60,000: AUD 36,000 on the AUD 1.2m still owned
AUD 60,000, unchanged
options.why: That is the repo treatment, where the bank keeps ownership and every coupon. In a sell/buyback the buyer owns the bond.

options.label: Zero
options.why: Only the 800,000 sold passes to the buyer; the bank still owns and is paid on the remaining 1.2m.

scenarios.takeaway: In a sell/buyback ownership passes, so the coupon on the sold notional leaves the seller's cash flows; in a repo it does not.
scenarios.lo_text: Discuss the impact of available asset transactions on cash flows and liquidity generation capacity.

scenarios.setup: A bank has initial cash of SGD 2.0m and expected cash flows (SGD m) for years 1 to 6 of +3.0, -4.5, -6.0, +1.0, -1.5, +45.0, including 5% year-end coupons on 40 notional of a bond. It sells part of the bond at the end of year 3, just after the coupon, at 98.00. The lowest cumulated position before any sale is -6.0, at year 5. The naive sale to cover it is 6.0 / 0.98 = 6.12.
scenarios.ask: The true minimum notional to sell is:

options.label: Lower than 6.12
options.why: Counted the cash from the sale but not the 5% coupons given up in years 4 and 5, then thought a smaller sale is enough.

options.label: Higher than 6.12: the coupons given up deepen the deficit in years 4 and 5
Exactly 6.12
options.why: Covered the year-5 deficit at the sale price but ignored that each unit sold also removes a 5% coupon in years 4 and 5.

scenarios.takeaway: Selling a coupon bond early costs its later coupons, so the amount needed is more than deficit divided by price.
scenarios.lo_text: Discuss the impact of available asset transactions on cash flows and liquidity generation capacity.

scenarios.setup: A bank raises GBP 500m of new funds (deposits, interbank borrowing and equity). The expected interest and operating costs on all of them total GBP 38.0m, which is 7.60% of the money raised. Only part of each source can be placed in earning assets, between 50% and 95%, GBP 387m in total.
scenarios.ask: The minimum before-tax return the bank must earn on new earning assets to cover these costs is:

options.label: Below 7.60%
options.why: Divided the costs by a larger base. The base is the money placed in earning assets, which is smaller than the money raised.

options.label: Exactly 7.60%
options.why: Assumed every pound raised is invested. Reserves and other non-earning uses take about a quarter of the funds.

scenarios.takeaway: The hurdle rate spreads the cost of all new funds over only the part that earns, so it exceeds the cost per pound raised.
scenarios.lo_text: Calculate overall cost of funds using both the historical average cost approach and the pooled-funds approach.

scenarios.setup: Repricing schedule over one year, USD m, assets / liabilities that are interest sensitive: next 7 days 60 / 45; 8 to 30 days 140 / 190; 31 to 90 days 95 / 120; 91 to 360 days 210 / 225.
scenarios.ask: The one-year cumulative gap (ISA minus ISL, all buckets) is closest to:

options.label: +USD 15m
options.why: Took only the first bucket, which is asset sensitive, and stopped there.

options.label: +USD 75m
options.why: Sign slip: subtracted assets from liabilities.

options.label: -USD 50m
options.why: Took the largest single bucket (8 to 30 days) instead of the sum of all four.

scenarios.takeaway: Cumulate every bucket inside the horizon; the early asset-sensitive bucket is outweighed by the liability-sensitive ones.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe interest-sensitive gap management and apply this strategy to maximize a bank’s net interest margin.

scenarios.setup: A bank has assets of JPY 600bn with average duration 2.8 years and liabilities of JPY 540bn. It wants net worth immune to small parallel rate changes.
scenarios.ask: Compared with the asset duration of 2.8 years, the liability duration it needs is:

options.label: The same, 2.8 years
options.why: Matched durations ignoring leverage. The smaller liability base must have a longer duration to offset the same yen change in value.

options.label: Shorter, about 2.5 years
options.why: Scaled by liabilities over assets instead of assets over liabilities: 2.8 × 540/600 = 2.52.

scenarios.takeaway: Immunisation matches dollar durations, so when liabilities are smaller than assets their duration must be longer.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe duration gap management and apply this strategy to protect a bank’s net worth.

scenarios.setup: A bond has a USD 1,000 face value, a 6% annual coupon, 10 years to maturity and a yield to maturity of 5%.
scenarios.ask: Its Macaulay duration is:

options.label: Equal to 10 years
options.why: Duration equals maturity only for a zero-coupon bond; coupons return part of the value early.

options.label: Above 10 years
options.why: Duration is a weighted average of payment times, none later than year 10, so it cannot exceed maturity.

scenarios.takeaway: Coupons pull the average payment time forward, so duration of a coupon bond is shorter than its maturity.
scenarios.lo_text: Apply investment maturity strategies and maturity management tools based on the yield curve and duration.

scenarios.setup: A 20-year bond pays a 7% annual coupon on USD 1,000 face value. The yield to maturity is 10%.
scenarios.ask: As a step in finding its duration, the bond's price is closest to:

options.label: About USD 1,000, at par
options.why: A bond prices at par only when the coupon equals the yield; here 7% is below 10%.

options.label: About USD 1,255, above par
options.why: Reversed the price-yield relation: a coupon below the yield means a discount, not a premium.

scenarios.takeaway: Coupon below yield means price below par; sanity-check the price before computing the weighted times.
scenarios.lo_text: Apply investment maturity strategies and maturity management tools based on the yield curve and duration.

scenarios.setup: A bond has a duration of 8.89 years. Yields on comparable bonds fall from 7.50% to 7.25%.
scenarios.ask: The approximate percentage change in the bond's price is closest to:

options.why: Left out the duration and used only $\Delta y/(1+y)$.
Read the 0.25-point fall as 2.5 points, a factor-of-ten slip.
Used the new yield level 7.25% instead of the 0.25-point change in yield.

scenarios.takeaway: Use the change in yield, not its level, scale by duration and by 1 + y, and the sign is opposite to the yield move.
scenarios.lo_text: Apply investment maturity strategies and maturity management tools based on the yield curve and duration.

scenarios.setup: Base case: deposit withdrawals of USD 25m a month and 30% drawdown on USD 120m of committed credit lines over the year. Stress case: withdrawals USD 35m a month and drawdown of 55%.
scenarios.ask: Which change adds more outflow over the 12 months?

options.label: The extra credit-line drawdown, +USD 30m
options.why: Compared a 25-point jump with a USD 10m monthly step without annualising or applying it to the USD 120m base: 0.25 × 120 = 30 against 10 × 12 = 120.

options.label: About equal
options.why: Both look like moderate increases, but one is a monthly amount repeated 12 times.

scenarios.takeaway: Annualise monthly flows before comparing; percentage drawdowns apply to the committed amount, not to a monthly figure.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process.

scenarios.setup: A bank has a normal liquidity asset buffer of USD 60.0m. Under stress, outflows are USD 28.0m and inflows are USD 15.0m. It also holds USD 16.0m of operational liquidity, which runs day-to-day payments and cannot meet general liabilities.
scenarios.ask: The net stressed drain on the buffer is closest to:

options.label: USD 43m
options.why: Added inflows to outflows (28 + 15) instead of netting them.

options.label: USD 28m
options.why: Used outflows alone and ignored the inflows that offset them.

options.label: USD -3m
options.why: Also deducted the USD 16m operational liquidity. It is neither added nor subtracted.

scenarios.takeaway: The stressed buffer is the normal buffer less outflows plus inflows; operational liquidity stays out of it.
scenarios.lo_text: Estimate contingent liquidity via the liquid asset buffer.

scenarios.setup: Firm A holds a USD 1,000m buffer of highly liquid assets, plus USD 120m of operational liquidity kept outside the buffer. In a stress, customers withdraw USD 150m of deposits, borrowers repay USD 80m of loans, and USD 60m of margin and collateral calls hit the derivatives book.
scenarios.ask: The stressed liquidity buffer is:

options.label: Above USD 900m
options.why: Added the USD 120m of operational liquidity back to the buffer: $870 + 120 = 990$. Operational liquidity is outside the buffer and is not counted.

scenarios.takeaway: Stressed buffer = normal buffer minus stressed outflows plus stressed inflows. Liquidity held outside the buffer does not count.
scenarios.lo_text: Estimate contingent liquidity via the liquid asset buffer.

scenarios.setup: A bank has a USD 240m liquid asset buffer. Stress outflows total USD 220m (deposits 90, unsecured wholesale 70, secured runoff 35, facility drawdowns 25). Contractual inflows are USD 30m of loan repayments and USD 20m of secured funding maturities, but the scenario says only 60% of these inflows are realised.
scenarios.ask: How much inflow should be counted in the stressed buffer?

options.label: USD 50m
options.why: Counted the full contractual inflows and ignored the 60% realisation limit.

options.label: USD 20m
options.why: Applied 40% instead of 60%: the scenario says 60% of inflows are realised, not that 60% is lost.

scenarios.takeaway: Haircut the inflows first, then net: inflows only help the buffer to the extent the scenario lets them materialise.
scenarios.lo_text: Estimate contingent liquidity via the liquid asset buffer.

scenarios.setup: Bright Bank at 31 December 2018: total customer loans are 547,478 and total customer deposits are 612,152 (same units).
scenarios.ask: Is the loan-to-deposit ratio above or below 0.95?

options.label: Above 0.95
options.why: Divided deposits by loans: $612{,}152 / 547{,}478 = 1.12$. The ratio is loans over deposits, and loans are the smaller number here.

scenarios.takeaway: Loan-to-deposit is loans divided by deposits. Loans are the smaller figure, so the ratio is under 1.
scenarios.lo_text: Compare and interpret different types of liquidity risk reports.

scenarios.setup: Bright Bank forecasts, for 30 June 2019, customer deposits of 599,774 and customer loans of 480,122 (same units). Management targets a loan-to-deposit ratio of 85% and holds deposits constant.
scenarios.ask: By how much must loans rise? Closest to:

options.why: Scale slip: one decimal place out, 1/10 of the right size.
Lifted loans to 100% of deposits ($599{,}774 - 480{,}122$) instead of 85%.
Reported the target loan level $0.85 \times 599{,}774$, not the increase over the current 480,122.

scenarios.takeaway: A target ratio gives a target level; the question asks for the change, so subtract today's figure.
scenarios.lo_text: Compare and interpret different types of liquidity risk reports.

scenarios.setup: In a bank's daily liquidity report the one-month bucket shows a cumulative cash gap of -640m (inflows less outflows) and counterbalancing capacity of 800m of liquid securities that can be sold or pledged.
scenarios.ask: The liquidity gap for that bucket, after counterbalancing capacity, is:

options.label: Negative: a shortfall remains
options.why: Either left the capacity out ($-640$) or subtracted it ($-640 - 800 = -1{,}440$). Capacity is a positive cushion against the cash gap.

options.label: Positive: the capacity covers the shortfall

scenarios.takeaway: Counterbalancing capacity is added to the cumulative cash gap; a positive result means the bucket is covered.
scenarios.lo_text: Compare and interpret different types of liquidity risk reports.

scenarios.setup: Prime Limited expects next month (USD m): new deposits 400, withdrawals 600, new loan demand 500, credit-line drawings 200, securities sales 375 and securities purchases 100.
scenarios.ask: The available funds gap (uses of funds less sources of funds) is:

options.label: Positive: the bank must raise funding
Negative: the bank has a surplus
options.why: Counted the USD 600m of withdrawals as a source of funds: sources become $400 + 600 + 375 = 1{,}375$ against uses of 800. Withdrawals are a use.

scenarios.takeaway: Withdrawals drain funding, so they sit with the uses. A positive gap means money-market funding is needed.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe and calculate the available funds gap.

scenarios.setup: A commercial bank sees a new quality loan request of USD 660m, plans to buy USD 330m of new Treasuries on Friday, and expects USD 358m of drawings on credit lines. Deposits and customer funds received today are USD 456m, with USD 265m more expected in the coming week. Current funding gap is zero.
scenarios.ask: Total loans and investments (uses of funds) are:

options.label: USD 990m
options.why: Left out the USD 358m of credit-line drawings: $660 + 330 = 990$.

options.label: USD 1,018m
options.why: Left out the USD 330m Treasury purchase: $660 + 358 = 1{,}018$.

scenarios.takeaway: In the available funds gap, uses include loans, securities purchases and committed credit-line drawings.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe and calculate the available funds gap.

scenarios.setup: A bank has new quality loan requests of USD 250m, plans to buy USD 100m of Treasuries this week and expects USD 140m of credit-line drawings. It received USD 110m of deposits today and expects USD 230m more over the coming week.
scenarios.ask: The available funds gap (USD m) is closest to:

options.why: Scale slip: one decimal place out, 1/10 of the right size.
Stopped at total uses ($250 + 100 + 140$) and never netted off the USD 340m of deposit inflows.
Scale slip: one decimal place out, 10 times the right size.

scenarios.takeaway: AFG is a net figure: total uses minus total sources, not either side alone.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe and calculate the available funds gap.

scenarios.setup: Bluemont Bank borrows USD 85m in a repo against government bonds for 12 days. The repo rate is 4% annualised, actual/360.
scenarios.ask: Total interest cost is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 9,400
options.why: Charged one day only: $85\text{m} \times 4\% / 360$. The 12 days were never multiplied in.

options.label: ≈ USD 37,667
options.why: Scale slip: 1/3 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 1,130,000
options.why: Percent-as-decimal slip: used $0.4$ instead of $0.04$, ten times too large.

scenarios.takeaway: Repo interest is amount times rate times days over 360. Twelve days is a small slice of the year, so a figure near the annual interest must be wrong.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe the mechanics of repurchase agreements (repos) and calculate the settlement for a repo transaction.

scenarios.setup: Promise Bank borrows USD 30m overnight in a repo at 4%. Money-market repos use actual/360; bonds often use actual/365.
scenarios.ask: Compared with an actual/365 count, the actual/360 interest for one night is:

options.label: Lower
options.why: Read the bigger year (365) as producing more interest. The year is the divisor: the shorter 360-day year makes each day worth more.

options.label: The same
options.why: The day count basis changes the divisor: $30\text{m} \times 4\% / 360 = 3{,}333.33$ against $/365 = 3{,}287.67$.

scenarios.takeaway: A shorter year basis divides by less, so each day of interest is larger: actual/360 charges more than actual/365.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe the mechanics of repurchase agreements (repos) and calculate the settlement for a repo transaction.

scenarios.setup: A bank buys a bond (face USD 100,000, 5% semi-annual coupon) on a coupon date and, three months later, repos it. Clean price is 98 per 100, the repo haircut is 5%, the repo rate is 3% and the term is 6 months. Use 30/360-style simple accrual.
scenarios.ask: The cash the bank receives at the start of the repo is:

options.label: Below the clean value of USD 98,000
Above the clean value of USD 98,000
options.why: Stopped at the dirty value (clean plus USD 1,250 accrued = 99,250) and skipped the 5% haircut.

scenarios.takeaway: Dirty value first, haircut second, then repo interest on the cash actually received. The haircut outweighs the accrued interest.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe the mechanics of repurchase agreements (repos) and calculate the settlement for a repo transaction.

scenarios.setup: A bank buys a bond (face USD 100,000) with a 6% semi-annual coupon on a coupon date, and repos it three months later. Use 30/360-style simple accrual.
scenarios.ask: The accrued interest at the repo date is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 6,000
options.why: A full year of coupon, ignoring that only three months have passed.

options.label: ≈ USD 15,000
options.why: Scale slip: 10× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 60,000
options.why: Percent-as-decimal slip on the annual coupon: used $0.60$ instead of $0.06$.

scenarios.takeaway: Accrued interest is the coupon times the fraction of the period elapsed: three months of a six-month period is half a coupon.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe the mechanics of repurchase agreements (repos) and calculate the settlement for a repo transaction.

scenarios.setup: Ludska Bank sells government bonds (face USD 1,000,000) at an invoice price of USD 1,100,000 and agrees to repurchase them 90 days later at the invoice price plus interest at 4% p.a., actual/360.
scenarios.ask: The repo interest, as a share of the cash lent, is:

options.why: Used the annual rate and forgot the $90/360$ day fraction.
Inverted the day fraction: $4\% \times 360/90$ instead of $4\% \times 90/360$.

scenarios.takeaway: 90 days is a quarter of a 360-day year, so the term interest is a quarter of the annual rate.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe the mechanics of repurchase agreements (repos) and calculate the settlement for a repo transaction.

scenarios.setup: HJK Bank sells bonds (face USD 120m) at an invoice price of USD 159m and agrees to repurchase them 122 days later at the invoice price plus interest at a repo rate of 0.26% p.a., actual/360.
scenarios.ask: The repo interest paid is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 14,000
options.why: Decimal-place slip: read 0.26% as 0.026%, one tenth of the right size.

options.label: ≈ USD 46,667
options.why: Scale slip: 1/3 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 410,000
options.why: A full year of interest at 0.26%: forgot the $122/360$ day fraction.

working.label: Annual interest on the cash lent

scenarios.takeaway: Interest runs on the cash lent (the invoice price) for days over 360. A sub-1% rate over four months is a tiny fraction of the cash.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe the mechanics of repurchase agreements (repos) and calculate the settlement for a repo transaction.

scenarios.setup: Counterparty K sells EUR 300m face of bonds at an invoice price of EUR 350.25m on 1 January 2015 and agrees to repurchase them on 1 July 2015 at the invoice price plus interest at a 0.26% repo rate, actual/360.
scenarios.ask: How many days of interest accrue between 1 January and 1 July 2015?

options.label: 180 days
options.why: Used 30-day months (30/360). The convention here is actual days, and February 2015 has 28.

options.label: 183 days
options.why: Took half of a 365-day year (182.5) and rounded up instead of counting the actual calendar days.

scenarios.takeaway: Under actual/360, count the actual calendar days (181 here). It is not simply half of 360 or 365.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe the mechanics of repurchase agreements (repos) and calculate the settlement for a repo transaction.

scenarios.setup: Prime Bank sells bonds with USD 200m face value at an invoice price of USD 250m and repurchases them 183 days later at the invoice price plus interest at a 0.34% repo rate, actual/360.
scenarios.ask: Interest charged on the invoice price, compared with interest on the face value, is:

options.label: Smaller
options.why: Assumed face value is the bigger base. Here the bonds trade above par, so the invoice price (250) exceeds face (200).

options.label: The same
options.why: Rate and days match, but the bases differ ($250$ vs $200$), so the dollar interest differs.

scenarios.takeaway: Repo interest is charged on the cash lent, which is the invoice price, not the face value of the collateral.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe the mechanics of repurchase agreements (repos) and calculate the settlement for a repo transaction.

scenarios.setup: Counterparty A sells a security for USD 180.0m on 1 June 2015 and repurchases it on 1 September 2015 at the invoice price plus interest at 0.90%, actual/360. June has 30 days, July and August 31 each.
scenarios.ask: Compared with a flat 90-day accrual (three months at 30 days each), the actual/360 interest is:

options.label: Lower
options.why: Treated the 31-day months as 30-day months, so assumed the count is 90 or fewer. The actual count is $30 + 31 + 31 = 92$.

options.label: Equal
options.why: Three months equals 90 days only under a 30/360 convention. Actual/360 counts 92 days here.

scenarios.takeaway: Actual/360 counts the real calendar days; three months containing two 31-day months run to 92 days, not 90.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe the mechanics of repurchase agreements (repos) and calculate the settlement for a repo transaction.
