scenarios.lo_text: Summarize the December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework in the following areas: - The standardized approach to credit risk - The internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches for credit risk - The CVA risk framework - The operational risk framework - The leverage ratio framework

scenarios.setup: Basel III output floor, fully phased in at 72.5% of standardised-approach RWA. A bank's RWA from its approved internal models is USD 600bn; the same exposures under standardised approaches give USD 900bn.
scenarios.ask: Is the output floor binding, so that regulatory RWA is above USD 600bn?

options.label: No: model RWA of USD 600bn stands
options.why: Applied 72.5% to the bank's own model RWA ($0.725 \times 600 = 435$), which looks harmless. The floor is a share of the standardised figure: $0.725 \times 900 = 652.5$.

options.label: Yes: the floor, about USD 650bn, sets RWA

scenarios.takeaway: Output floor: RWA = max(model RWA, 72.5% of standardised RWA). It binds when models give more than 27.5% less than the standardised approach.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe the revised output floor introduced as part of the Basel III reforms and approaches to be used when calculating the output floor.

scenarios.setup: A structured-lending unit's year, JPY bn: revenues 14.0, direct costs 2.5, funding transfer charge 8.0, expected credit loss 1.2. Its economic capital of 12.0 earns the 1.0% JGB risk-free rate. Tax rate 30%. The pack also lists regulatory capital (16.0) and a 0.9 trading VaR, which are not part of this numerator.
scenarios.ask: After-tax risk-adjusted income (the RAROC numerator) is:

options.label: JPY 2.42bn
options.why: Stopped before the tax step: $14.0 - 2.5 - 8.0 - 1.2 + 0.12 = 2.42$ is pre-tax, and the numerator is after tax.

options.label: JPY 1.61bn
options.why: Left out the return on economic capital: $(14.0 - 2.5 - 8.0 - 1.2) \times 0.7 = 1.61$. The capital buffer earns $r_f \times EC = 0.12$, which is added back.

options.label: JPY 7.29bn
options.why: Forgot the 8.0 funding transfer charge, so the income is overstated by $8.0 \times 0.7 = 5.6$.

scenarios.takeaway: RAROC numerator: revenue less costs, funding and expected loss, plus the return on economic capital, then taxed. Divide by economic capital (12.0) for 14.1%.
scenarios.lo_text: Calculate and interpret the RAROC for a project, loan, or loan portfolio and use RAROC to compare business unit performance.

scenarios.setup: A SGD 800m corporate loan portfolio yields 8.5%, with direct costs of SGD 7m a year. It is funded by deposits transfer-priced at 5.5%. Expected loss is 0.8% of the portfolio a year. Economic capital is 6% of the portfolio, held in government bonds yielding 4%. Tax rate 25%; after-tax hurdle rate 12%.
scenarios.ask: Compared with zero, the portfolio's NIACC (after-tax income less the hurdle charge on economic capital) is:

options.label: Negative
options.why: Divided after-tax income by the SGD 800m portfolio instead of the SGD 48m of economic capital, getting about 1.2% against a 12% hurdle. The hurdle is a return on capital.

scenarios.takeaway: Hurdle comparisons are on economic capital: RAROC is 9.39/48 = 19.6%, well above 12%, so NIACC is positive (about SGD 3.6m).
scenarios.lo_text: Calculate and interpret the RAROC for a project, loan, or loan portfolio and use RAROC to compare business unit performance.

scenarios.setup: A bank sets one firm-wide hurdle rate as the weighted average of its cost of common equity (CAPM, beta 1.2, risk-free 4%, market return 10%) and its cost of preferred equity (7.0% yield). Common equity: market value CAD 6.0bn, book value CAD 3.0bn. Preferred: market value CAD 1.5bn. Tax rate 25%.
scenarios.ask: The weight on common equity in the blend is closest to:

options.why: Used the book value of common (3.0) against the preferred (1.5): $3.0/4.5 = 67\%$. Weights come from market values, $6.0/7.5$.
Put the book value of common over the market total: $3.0/7.5 = 40\%$. Numerator and denominator must both be market values.

scenarios.takeaway: Capital-structure weights are market values. With 80% common at 11.2% and 20% preferred at 7.0%, the hurdle is 10.36%, between the two costs.
scenarios.lo_text: Calculate the hurdle rate and apply this rate in making business decisions using RAROC.

scenarios.setup: To find the break-even revenue on a CAD 500m loan book we work backwards. Economic capital is CAD 40m, the hurdle rate is 12% after tax, and the tax rate is 28%. Direct costs are CAD 4m a year, funding is at 4.5%, expected loss 0.6% a year, and the capital earns 3.5% in government bonds.
scenarios.ask: The pre-tax risk-adjusted income the book needs so that the after-tax return just equals the hurdle is closest to:

options.label: CAD 4.80m
options.why: Treated the after-tax hurdle charge $12\% \times 40$ as if it were pre-tax. It must be grossed up for the 28% tax.

options.label: CAD 3.46m
options.why: Multiplied by $(1 - 0.28)$ instead of dividing: tax makes the required pre-tax figure larger than 4.80, not smaller.

scenarios.takeaway: Working back from a required after-tax figure, divide by $(1 - t)$. Pre-tax income must exceed the after-tax hurdle charge.
scenarios.lo_text: Calculate the hurdle rate and apply this rate in making business decisions using RAROC.

scenarios.setup: An equipment-leasing activity has an expected after-tax RAROC of 12.4%. The bank's traditional hurdle is 10.5%, the risk-free rate 3.0% and the expected market return 8.0%. The activity passes the adjusted-RAROC test while $\text{RAROC} - \beta_E (R_M - r_f) > r_f$.
scenarios.ask: The highest equity beta at which it still passes is closest to:

options.why: Scale slip: 1/100 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Scale slip: 1/30 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Compared RAROC with the traditional 10.5% hurdle instead of $r_f$: $(12.4 - 10.5)/5.0 = 0.38$. The adjusted test is against the risk-free rate.

scenarios.takeaway: Adjusted RAROC charges shareholders $\beta (R_M - r_f)$ and demands what is left exceed $r_f$. Break-even beta is (RAROC - r_f) over the market premium.
scenarios.lo_text: Calculate the adjusted RAROC for a project to determine its viability.

scenarios.setup: A Basel II Foundation IRB bank computes capital for a JPY 50bn senior unsecured loan to a highly rated Japanese corporate. Its own estimates are PD 0.01% and LGD 30%. Under Foundation IRB the supervisor sets a floor on corporate PDs and fixes LGD for senior unsecured claims.
scenarios.ask: The PD and LGD that go into the capital formula are:

options.label: PD 0.01%, LGD 30%
options.why: Used the bank's own estimates for both. That is Advanced IRB; under Foundation the bank supplies only PD, and even that is floored.

options.label: PD 0.03%, LGD 30%
options.why: Applied the PD floor but kept the internal LGD. Foundation IRB uses the supervisory 45% for senior unsecured claims.

options.label: PD 0.01%, LGD 45%
options.why: Took the supervisory LGD but forgot the 0.03% floor on corporate PDs, so the 0.01% estimate is raised.

scenarios.takeaway: Foundation IRB: own PD (floored at 0.03% for corporates), supervisory LGD 45% for senior unsecured, supervisory maturity of 2.5 years.
scenarios.lo_text: Compare the standardized internal ratings-based (IRB) approach, the foundation IRB approach, and the advanced IRB approach for the calculation of credit risk capital under Basel II.

scenarios.setup: Basel 2.5 market-risk capital, one-day 99% figures in CAD m. VaR: yesterday 6.5, 60-day average 1.6. Stressed VaR: yesterday 7.4, 60-day average 6.9. Four backtesting exceptions in 250 days give a multiplier of 3 on both. Each term is the larger of yesterday's figure and 3 times its average. The two are added and scaled to ten days by the square root of time.
scenarios.ask: The market-risk capital charge is closest to:

options.label: CAD 27.2m
options.why: Left out the ten-day scaling: $6.5 + 20.7 = 27.2$ is still a one-day figure.

options.label: CAD 272m
options.why: Scaled by 10 days instead of $\sqrt{10}$: $27.2 \times 10 = 272$.

options.label: CAD 860m
options.why: Scale slip (10x): applied the ten-day scaling twice, as $27.2 \times 10 \times \sqrt{10}$.

scenarios.takeaway: Scale one-day figures to ten days with the square root of time (about 3.16), not by 10. The larger-of rule can bind on either the latest figure or the multiplied average.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe and calculate the stressed VaR introduced in Basel 2.5 and calculate the market risk capital charge.

scenarios.setup: NSFR build for a bank, funding in CAD m with ASF factors: stable retail deposits 620 (95%), 3-month wholesale CDs 240 (0%), 10-year senior bonds 180 (100%), common equity 110 (100%).
scenarios.ask: Available stable funding (ASF) is:

options.label: CAD 1,150m
options.why: Added the amounts without the ASF factors. Short-term CDs count for nothing and retail deposits only 95%.

options.label: CAD 910m
options.why: Left the retail deposits at 100% instead of 95%: $620 + 180 + 110 = 910$.

scenarios.takeaway: ASF = sum of funding x its factor. Against required stable funding of 725, NSFR is 879/725, about 121%.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe and calculate ratios intended to improve the management of liquidity risk, including the required leverage ratio, the liquidity coverage ratio, and the net stable funding ratio.

scenarios.setup: A bank's available stable funding is SGD 630m against required stable funding of SGD 675m (NSFR 93%), a gap of SGD 45m. It will raise new stable retail deposits (ASF factor 95%) and invest all the proceeds in own-sovereign debt (RSF factor 5%) until NSFR is exactly 100%.
scenarios.ask: The new deposits needed, compared with the SGD 45m gap, are:

options.label: Less than SGD 45m
options.why: That needs each SGD raised to add more than SGD 1 of net stable funding. It adds 0.95 of ASF and also creates 0.05 of required funding, so it adds only 0.90.

options.label: Exactly SGD 45m
options.why: Treated each SGD raised as closing SGD 1 of the gap, ignoring both the 95% ASF factor and the 5% RSF on the new sovereign debt.

scenarios.takeaway: New funding closes an NSFR gap net of what it adds to required funding. Each SGD of deposits closes only about 0.90, so the need exceeds the gap.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe and calculate ratios intended to improve the management of liquidity risk, including the required leverage ratio, the liquidity coverage ratio, and the net stable funding ratio.

scenarios.setup: Output floor, EUR bn. Modelled RWA: credit 480, counterparty 60, CVA 30, market 62, operational 70 (total 702). Standardised-only RWA: credit 760, counterparty 90, CVA 30, market 80, operational 70 (total 1,030). The fully phased-in floor is 72.5% of the standardised total, applied to total RWA.
scenarios.ask: After the floor, total RWA is:

options.label: Unchanged at EUR 702bn
options.why: Applied the floor to one line only: $72.5\% \times 760 = 551$ looks slack against 480-702. The floor is on the total, $72.5\% \times 1{,}030 = 747$.

scenarios.takeaway: The output floor is on total RWA: modelled RWA at 68% of the standardised total sit below 72.5%, so the floor binds and adds about EUR 45bn.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe the revised output floor introduced as part of the Basel III reforms and approaches to be used when calculating the output floor.

scenarios.setup: Output floor phase-in for 2026: the floor is 70% of standardised-only RWA. The supervisor caps the increase in RWA caused by the floor at 25% of RWA before the floor. A bank has RWA of EUR 80bn on its approved approaches and EUR 150bn on standardised approaches only.
scenarios.ask: Its RWA for 2026 is:

options.label: EUR 80bn
options.why: Ignored the floor altogether. At 70% of 150 the floor is 105, above 80.

options.label: EUR 105bn
options.why: Applied the floor but not the cap. The increase 25 exceeds the allowed 25% of 80, which is 20.

options.label: EUR 108.75bn
options.why: Used the fully phased-in 72.5% instead of the 70% for 2026, and skipped the cap.

scenarios.takeaway: With a cap, RWA = min(floored RWA, 1.25 x pre-floor RWA). Check the floor first, then the cap.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe the revised output floor introduced as part of the Basel III reforms and approaches to be used when calculating the output floor.

scenarios.setup: A bank wants its economic capital to cover unexpected losses at a confidence level matched to a target credit rating. That rating has a one-year default probability of 0.07%. The next rating up has 0.03%.
scenarios.ask: The confidence level to use is:

options.why: Used the default probability of the next rating up (0.03%). The target rating's own 0.07% sets the level.
Percent slip: subtracted 0.07 from 1 as if it were 7%, giving 93%.

scenarios.takeaway: Confidence level = 1 minus the default probability of the target rating. A better rating means a higher confidence level and more capital.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain and differentiate between regulatory capital and economic capital requirements as prescribed in Basel regulations.

scenarios.setup: A leveraged fund holds economic capital equal to the worst-case loss at 99.5% confidence minus expected loss. Expected loss is USD 50m and unchanged. The worst-case loss rises from USD 500m to USD 1bn.
scenarios.ask: The increase in economic capital is:

options.label: Smaller than USD 500m
options.why: Deducted the USD 50m expected loss from the change, getting 450. Expected loss is deducted from both levels and cancels in the difference.

options.label: Larger than USD 500m
options.why: Reported the new capital level of USD 950m rather than the increase.

scenarios.takeaway: A constant deduction cancels in a change: the move in economic capital equals the move in worst-case loss.
scenarios.lo_text: Define, compare, and contrast risk capital, economic capital, and regulatory capital and explain methods and motivations for using economic capital approaches to allocate risk capital.

scenarios.setup: A credit portfolio has a loan-equivalent exposure of USD 480m. Expected loss is 1.0% of exposure and is already covered by pricing and loan-loss reserves. The worst-case loss at the bank's confidence level is 3.0% of exposure.
scenarios.ask: Economic capital to attribute, as a percentage of exposure, is:

options.why: Took the whole worst-case loss as capital. The 1.0% expected loss is covered by pricing and reserves, so it is deducted.
Took the expected loss itself as the capital. Capital covers the unexpected part, not the expected loss.
Added the expected loss to the worst-case loss instead of subtracting it.

scenarios.takeaway: Economic capital = worst-case loss minus expected loss, here 2.0% of USD 480m = USD 9.6m.
scenarios.lo_text: Define, compare, and contrast risk capital, economic capital, and regulatory capital and explain methods and motivations for using economic capital approaches to allocate risk capital.

scenarios.setup: Basel I. Bank A has capital of USD 10m (Tier 1 6 plus Tier 2 4). Assets: USD 50m claim on an OECD bank (20% weight), USD 100m corporate loans (100%), USD 40m uninsured residential mortgages (50%).
scenarios.ask: Risk-weighted assets are:

options.label: USD 190m
options.why: Added the assets at face value with no weights.

options.label: USD 150m
options.why: Gave the mortgages 100% instead of 50%: $10 + 100 + 40 = 150$.

scenarios.takeaway: RWA is the weighted sum, 130. The capital ratio is then 10/130 = 7.7%, below the 8% minimum.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain the calculation of risk-weighted assets and the capital requirement per the original Basel I guidelines.

scenarios.setup: Basel I. A bank holds USD 1.5bn of loans to corporations, of which USD 600m is commercial real estate, plus USD 300m of OECD government claims and USD 500m of cash. Weights: 0% for cash and OECD government, 50% for uninsured residential mortgages, 100% for all other claims.
scenarios.ask: Risk-weighted assets, compared with the USD 1.5bn of corporate loans, are:

options.label: Lower
options.why: Gave the USD 600m of commercial real estate the 50% weight, which applies to residential mortgages only: $900 + 300 = 1{,}200$.

options.label: Higher
options.why: Weighted the OECD government claims and cash above 0%. They carry 0%, so they add nothing.

scenarios.takeaway: Basel I relief for property applies to residential mortgages only. Commercial real estate is an 'other claim' at 100%.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain the calculation of risk-weighted assets and the capital requirement per the original Basel I guidelines.

scenarios.setup: Basel I current exposure method. A EUR 1bn interest-rate swap has more than five years left (add-on 1.5% of notional) and is currently worth -EUR 2m to the bank. The counterparty is a corporate, weighted at 50%.
scenarios.ask: The swap's credit equivalent amount, compared with the EUR 15m add-on, is:

options.label: Less than the add-on
options.why: Netted the negative value against the add-on: $15 - 2 = 13$. Current exposure is $\max(V, 0)$, so a loss to the bank counts as zero.

options.label: More than the add-on
options.why: Added the size of the negative value, $2 + 15 = 17$. The bank loses nothing today if the counterparty defaults.

scenarios.takeaway: Credit equivalent amount = max(V, 0) + add-on. A negative mark adds nothing and also does not reduce the add-on.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain the calculation of risk-weighted assets and the capital requirement per the original Basel I guidelines.

scenarios.setup: Basel I current exposure method. A USD 200m interest-rate swap has six years left and is worth +USD 3.5m to the bank. The add-on for interest-rate contracts over five years is 1.5% of notional. The counterparty is an OECD bank at a 20% risk weight.
scenarios.ask: The swap's risk-weighted asset amount is closest to:

options.label: USD 0.043m
options.why: Scale slip: 1/30 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: USD 0.13m
options.why: Scale slip (1/10): the correct 1.3 divided by 10.

options.label: USD 0.43m
options.why: Scale slip: 1/3 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: Derivative RWA = (max(V, 0) + add-on) x counterparty weight: the credit equivalent amount is not yet the RWA.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain the calculation of risk-weighted assets and the capital requirement per the original Basel I guidelines.

scenarios.setup: Basel I capital, EUR: ordinary equity 150m, subordinated debt with original maturity over 5 years 50m, and perpetual cumulative preferred stock 20m. No noncumulative preferred is held.
scenarios.ask: Tier 2 capital is:

options.label: EUR 50m
options.why: Put the cumulative preferred into Tier 1 (giving Tier 1 = 170m) and left only the subordinated debt in Tier 2.

options.label: EUR 20m
options.why: Counted only the preferred and dropped the subordinated debt, which is also Tier 2.

working.label: Limit check
working.display: Tier 2 of 70 is below half of total capital (110 of 220), so all of it counts

scenarios.takeaway: Basel I: only equity and noncumulative perpetual preferred are Tier 1. Cumulative preferred sits in Tier 2 with qualifying subordinated debt.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain the calculation of risk-weighted assets and the capital requirement per the original Basel I guidelines.

scenarios.setup: Basel II capital adequacy. A bank has Tier 1 capital of USD 200m, Tier 2 capital of USD 100m and risk-weighted assets of USD 2 billion.
scenarios.ask: The capital adequacy ratio is closest to:

options.why: Left the ratio as the decimal 0.15 and then wrote a percent sign.
Read RWA as USD 200m (dropped a zero from 2 billion), so 300 / 200.
Inverted the ratio: RWA / capital = 2,000 / 300.

scenarios.takeaway: CAR uses total capital (Tier 1 + Tier 2) over RWA. Keep millions and billions on the same scale before dividing.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe changes to the Basel regulations made as part of Basel II, including the three pillars.

scenarios.setup: Basel 2.5 standardized charges for a correlation book. Positions: a USD 60m AA securitization tranche (1.6%), a USD 25m BBB re-securitization tranche (18% on the re-securitization schedule) and an USD 8m unrated securitization tranche (100%).
scenarios.ask: Which position carries the largest capital charge?

options.label: The USD 60m AA tranche
options.why: Followed the largest notional. At 1.6% it charges only USD 0.96m.

options.label: The USD 25m BBB re-securitization
options.why: Looked at the middle size and rating: 25 × 18% = USD 4.50m, still short of the unrated tranche.

scenarios.takeaway: Unrated and below-BB positions are charged dollar for dollar, so the smallest position can dominate the capital charge.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe the comprehensive risk (CR) capital charge for portfolios of positions that are sensitive to correlations between default risks.

scenarios.setup: Basel III bank, USD m: common stock 730, unrealized gain on long-term marketable equity securities 33, five-year subordinated debt 28, goodwill 92. Tier 1 is common stock plus the unrealized gain, less goodwill.
scenarios.ask: Tier 1 capital compared with the USD 730m of common stock is:

options.label: Above USD 730m
options.why: Added the gain and forgot that goodwill is deducted, or even added it: 730 + 33 = 763.

options.label: Equal to USD 730m
options.why: Treated the gain and the goodwill as offsetting. They are 33 up against 92 down.

scenarios.takeaway: Goodwill is deducted from Tier 1, and here it outweighs the unrealized gain, so Tier 1 sits below common stock.
scenarios.lo_text: Define in the context of Basel III and calculate where appropriate: - Tier 1 capital and its components - Tier 2 capital and its components - Required Tier 1 equity capital, total Tier 1 capital, and total capital

scenarios.setup: Basel III balance sheet, EUR m: common equity 2,010; non-callable preferred equity 500; subordinated debt 1,500; retained earnings 3,210; goodwill 850. RWA are EUR 49,700m.
scenarios.ask: The Core Tier 1 (CET1) capital in the numerator is:

options.label: EUR 4,870m
options.why: Counted the preferred equity, which is Additional Tier 1, not CET1.

options.label: EUR 5,220m
options.why: Forgot to deduct goodwill: 2,010 + 3,210.

options.label: EUR 6,370m
options.why: Counted the preferred equity and the subordinated debt (Tier 2) as well.

scenarios.takeaway: CET1 is common equity plus retained earnings, less goodwill and intangibles. Preferred shares and subordinated debt belong to other tiers.
scenarios.lo_text: Define in the context of Basel III and calculate where appropriate: - Tier 1 capital and its components - Tier 2 capital and its components - Required Tier 1 equity capital, total Tier 1 capital, and total capital

scenarios.setup: Prime Bank has RWA of USD 200m. Under fully phased-in Basel III it must meet the CET1 minimum plus the capital conservation buffer (ignore any G-SIB or countercyclical buffer).
scenarios.ask: The CET1 ratio it must hold is:

options.why: Used the CET1 minimum alone and left the conservation buffer out.
Built on the 6% Tier 1 minimum instead of the 4.5% CET1 minimum: 6.0% + 2.5%.
Built on the 8% total capital minimum: 8.0% + 2.5%.

scenarios.takeaway: The conservation buffer is stacked on the CET1 minimum and must itself be CET1, so the requirement is 7.0%, not a total-capital figure.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe the motivations for and calculate the capital conservation buffer and the countercyclical buffer, including special rules for globally systemically important banks (G-SIBs).

scenarios.setup: Basel III CET1 buffer zone: with a 2.5% conservation buffer it runs from 4.5% to 7.0%, split into four equal quartiles. Minimum earnings retained, lowest to highest quartile: 100%, 80%, 60%, 40% (0% above the zone). A bank has CET1 of 6.0%. A 2.5% countercyclical buffer is then switched on, widening the zone to 4.5%–9.5%.
scenarios.ask: Its maximum dividend, as a percent of earnings, compared with before the switch-on:

options.label: Higher
options.why: Assumed a larger buffer means more room. The same 6.0% now sits in a lower quartile of a wider zone.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: Kept the old quartile width of 0.625%. With the wider zone each quartile is 1.25%.

working.label: Before: zone 4.5%–7.0%
working.display: Quartiles of 0.625%; 6.0% is in the 3rd, so retain 60% and pay up to 40%

working.label: After: zone 4.5%–9.5%
working.display: Quartiles of 1.25%; 6.0% is in the 2nd, so retain 80% and pay up to 20%

scenarios.takeaway: A bigger buffer stretches the zone, so the same CET1 ratio falls into a lower quartile and the payout allowed shrinks.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe the motivations for and calculate the capital conservation buffer and the countercyclical buffer, including special rules for globally systemically important banks (G-SIBs).

scenarios.setup: Basel operational loss event. Gross loss USD 5,000,000. Forgone revenue (opportunity cost) USD 3,000,000. An estimated recovery of USD 1,500,000, 50% likely, none received yet. Insurance premiums of USD 12,500 paid while the event ran.
scenarios.ask: The operational loss recorded for the event compared with the USD 5.0m gross loss is:

options.label: Above the gross loss
options.why: Added the forgone revenue. Opportunity cost is not a P&L charge, expense or provision, so it is not in the loss.

options.label: Below the gross loss
options.why: Netted the recovery, even probability-weighted (5.00 − 0.75 = 4.25). A recovery only reduces the loss once it is received.

scenarios.takeaway: Gross loss counts direct charges only: no opportunity cost, no premiums, and no recovery until the cash is in.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe general and specific criteria recommended by the Basel Committee for the identification, collection, and treatment of operational loss data.

scenarios.setup: Fault tree for a rogue trader. Five independent conditions must ALL occur: 20%, 1%, 30%, 30% and 50%. A rogue event costs USD 100m. The firm has 1,000 traders, each with the same probabilities.
scenarios.ask: Expected annual loss for the firm is closest to:

options.label: USD 50,000,000
options.why: Used only the last condition: 50% × USD 100m. All five conditions must hold together, so the probabilities multiply.

options.label: USD 270,000,000
options.why: Scale slip: 30× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: USD 900,000,000
options.why: Read the joint probability 0.009% as 0.9%, a factor of 100 too large.

scenarios.takeaway: In an AND gate the probabilities multiply, so five conditions shrink the odds fast; then scale by the number of traders.
scenarios.lo_text: Estimate operational risk exposures based on the fault tree model given probability assumptions.

scenarios.setup: Fault tree for a phishing-driven data leak, all events independent. The phishing email arrives: 99%. The firewall works as intended: 95%. The leak path needs the email to arrive AND to get past the firewall, before the later nodes (employee, detective controls, leak) are applied.
scenarios.ask: After those first two nodes the running probability is closest to:

options.why: Used the firewall's success probability (0.95) instead of its failure probability (0.05): 0.99 × 0.95.
Ignored the firewall node altogether.

scenarios.takeaway: A control node enters a fault tree through its failure probability, because the loss path needs the control to fail.
scenarios.lo_text: Estimate operational risk exposures based on the fault tree model given probability assumptions.

scenarios.setup: Basel II standardized approach, Year 1 gross income (USD m): corporate finance 11.9 at a 17.99% multiplier, retail banking −26.2 at a 12.11% multiplier. The year's figure is the multiplier-weighted sum across the two lines.
scenarios.ask: The Year 1 weighted sum is:

options.label: Positive
options.why: Dropped the sign on the retail loss and added it: 2.14 + 3.17 = +5.31.

options.label: Zero
options.why: Applied a floor at zero to the sum. The arithmetic itself gives a nonzero number: the loss line outweighs the profit line.

scenarios.takeaway: A negative business-line income offsets the other lines inside the year, and here it tips the year's total below zero.
scenarios.lo_text: Compare the basic indicator approach, the standardized approach, and the advanced measurement approach for the calculation of operational risk capital under Basel II.

scenarios.setup: Basel II basic indicator approach (alpha 15%). Total annual gross income across all business lines, USD m: Year 1 65, Year 2 71, Year 3 74, all positive.
scenarios.ask: Operational risk capital is closest to (USD m):

options.why: Scale slip: 1/10 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Averaged and then divided by 3 a second time.
Applied 15% to the three-year sum without averaging.

scenarios.takeaway: The basic indicator approach is 15% of average positive gross income. Business-line multipliers belong to the standardized approach.
scenarios.lo_text: Compare the basic indicator approach, the standardized approach, and the advanced measurement approach for the calculation of operational risk capital under Basel II.

scenarios.setup: EU securitization risk retention. A loan pool is tranched into a USD 320m senior, a USD 50m mezzanine and a USD 30m equity tranche. The originator must retain at least 5% of each tranche.
scenarios.ask: The minimum total retained is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 60m
options.why: Scale slip: 3× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 200m
options.why: Read 5% as 50% of the USD 400m pool.

options.label: ≈ USD 600m
options.why: Scale slip: 30× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: Retention of 5% of each tranche equals 5% of the whole pool, and the senior tranche is where most of it sits.
scenarios.lo_text: Provide examples of legislative and regulatory reforms that were introduced after the 2007-2009 financial crisis.

scenarios.setup: Basel III standardized approach, business indicator, annual averages in EUR m: interest income 1,100; interest expense 380; interest-earning assets 40,000; dividend income 20. In the interest, leases and dividend component, absolute net interest income is capped at 2.25% of interest-earning assets, then dividend income is added.
scenarios.ask: The interest, leases and dividend component is:

options.label: EUR 920m
options.why: Took the cap (2.25% × 40,000 = 900) instead of the smaller net interest income of 720, then added 20.

options.label: EUR 1,120m
options.why: Used gross interest income of 1,100 (no expense netting, no cap), then added 20.

scenarios.takeaway: The cap only bites when net interest income exceeds 2.25% of assets. Here 720 is below 900, so it passes through unchanged.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain the elements of the new standardized approach to measure operational risk capital, including the business indicator, internal loss multiplier, and loss component, and calculate the operational risk capital requirement for a bank using this approach.

scenarios.setup: Basel III standardized operational risk. Ten-year average annual operating loss is EUR 80m (high-quality data) and the business indicator component BIC is EUR 900m. Loss component LC = 15 × average loss. ILM = ln[e − 1 + (LC/BIC)^0.8] and capital = BIC × ILM, with no supervisory override.
scenarios.ask: Capital compared with the BIC of EUR 900m is:

options.label: Below EUR 900m
options.why: Forgot the 15× and compared the raw EUR 80m loss with BIC: that would give ILM about 0.62 and capital about EUR 559m.

options.label: Equal to EUR 900m
options.why: ILM equals 1 only when LC = BIC. Here LC is 1,200, above BIC.

scenarios.takeaway: ILM is exactly 1 when LC equals BIC. A loss history that puts LC above BIC pushes capital above the BIC.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain the elements of the new standardized approach to measure operational risk capital, including the business indicator, internal loss multiplier, and loss component, and calculate the operational risk capital requirement for a bank using this approach.

scenarios.setup: Basel III business indicator for a European bank, EUR bn, years 20X6 to 20X9. ILDC: 0.95, 1.3, 1.8, 1.6. Services SC: 1.6, 2.2, 2.6, 1.8. Financial FC (absolute): 0.5, 1.1, 1.3, 1.5. BI is the sum of the three components, each averaged over the latest three years (ending 20X9).
scenarios.ask: The BI at 31 December 20X9 is closest to:

options.label: ≈ EUR 0.17bn
options.why: Scale slip: 1/30 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ EUR 0.51bn
options.why: Scale slip: 1/10 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ EUR 1.7bn
options.why: Averaged the three components and then divided by 3 again.

scenarios.takeaway: BI averages each component over the latest three years, so 20X6 drops out and the total is the sum of three averages.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain the elements of the new standardized approach to measure operational risk capital, including the business indicator, internal loss multiplier, and loss component, and calculate the operational risk capital requirement for a bank using this approach.

scenarios.setup: Basel I off-balance-sheet items, EUR m: transaction-related standby letters of credit 80, counterparty an OECD bank (CCF 50%); undrawn two-year commitment to corporates 200 (CCF 20%); undrawn six-month commitment to corporates 150 (CCF 0%). Risk weights: OECD bank 20%, corporate 100%.
scenarios.ask: The off-balance-sheet RWA (EUR m) is closest to:

options.why: Counted only the standby letters of credit (40 × 20%) and dropped the two-year commitment.
Put the standby letters of credit at the corporate 100% weight instead of the OECD-bank 20%: 40 + 40.
Counted the six-month commitments at 100% of face value. A 0% CCF removes them entirely.

scenarios.takeaway: Convert with the CCF first, then apply the counterparty's risk weight. Short commitments at 0% CCF add nothing.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain the calculation of risk-weighted assets and the capital requirement per the original Basel I guidelines.

scenarios.setup: A G-SIB's private-sector credit exposures and the countercyclical buffer (CCyB) rate of each country: home country X 50% of exposures at 1.0%; country Y 30% at 2.5%; country Z 20% at 0.0%.
scenarios.ask: The bank's CCyB add-on is:

options.why: Used the home-country rate alone. The buffer follows where the exposures are, not where the bank is based.
Took the simple average of the three national rates instead of weighting by exposure.
Used the highest national rate.

scenarios.takeaway: A bank's CCyB is the exposure-weighted average of the national buffers where its credit exposures sit.
scenarios.lo_text: Describe the motivations for and calculate the capital conservation buffer and the countercyclical buffer, including special rules for globally systemically important banks (G-SIBs).

scenarios.setup: Basel III standardized approach for operational risk. Marginal coefficients on the Business Indicator (BI): 12% on the first EUR 1bn, 15% on the slice from EUR 1bn to EUR 30bn, 18% on everything above EUR 30bn. The bank's BI is EUR 40bn and the internal loss multiplier is set to 1.
scenarios.ask: Operational risk capital is closest to:

options.label: ≈ EUR 1,800m
options.why: Charged only the top slice, 18% × EUR 10bn, and dropped the two lower slices (120 and 4,350).

options.label: ≈ EUR 40,000m
options.why: Took the BI itself as the charge and never applied the marginal coefficients.

options.label: ≈ EUR 189,000m
options.why: Scale slip: 30× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: Marginal coefficients apply slice by slice: the 15% middle slice does most of the work even for a very large bank.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain the elements of the new standardized approach to measure operational risk capital, including the business indicator, internal loss multiplier, and loss component, and calculate the operational risk capital requirement for a bank using this approach.

scenarios.setup: Standardized approach, internal loss multiplier $ILM = \ln[e - 1 + (LC/BIC)^{0.8}]$, where $LC = 15 \times$ average annual loss. Ten years of verified losses (EUR bn): 3.8, 2.9, 2.8, 2.8, 0.6, 0.4, 0.1, 0.2, 0.1, 0.2. The Business Indicator Component is $BIC$ = EUR 18bn.
scenarios.ask: Is the ILM above 1, below 1, or exactly 1?

options.label: Below 1
options.why: Used the average loss of 1.39 as $LC$ and left out the factor of 15. Then $LC/BIC = 0.077$ and ILM $\approx 0.61$.

options.label: Exactly 1
options.why: ILM equals 1 only when $LC = BIC$ (the bracket is then $e$). Here $LC = 20.85$ against $BIC = 18$.

scenarios.takeaway: ILM crosses 1 exactly where $LC = BIC$: a loss component above the BIC pushes capital above the BIC.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain the elements of the new standardized approach to measure operational risk capital, including the business indicator, internal loss multiplier, and loss component, and calculate the operational risk capital requirement for a bank using this approach.

scenarios.setup: Default Basel rules, no national discretion. A bank has a Business Indicator of EUR 960m and ten years of annual losses averaging EUR 352m (peak EUR 0.9bn). Coefficients: 12% up to EUR 1bn. In the lowest BI bucket the internal loss multiplier is not driven by the loss history. The loss component is $15 \times$ average loss.
scenarios.ask: Operational risk capital is closest to:

options.label: ≈ EUR 3.8m
options.why: Scale slip: 1/30 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ EUR 12m
options.why: Coefficient slip: applied 1.2% instead of 12%, ten times too small.

options.label: ≈ EUR 38m
options.why: Scale slip: 1/3 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: Below EUR 1bn of BI, capital is just 12% of BI. Loss history only matters from bucket 2 up.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain the elements of the new standardized approach to measure operational risk capital, including the business indicator, internal loss multiplier, and loss component, and calculate the operational risk capital requirement for a bank using this approach.

scenarios.setup: A bank has a Business Indicator of EUR 34.5bn. The marginal coefficients are 12% on the first EUR 1bn, 15% on the slice from EUR 1bn to EUR 30bn and 18% on the part above EUR 30bn. The Business Indicator Component is the sum of the three slices.
scenarios.ask: Which of the three slices contributes most to the BIC?

options.label: The 12% slice (first EUR 1bn)
options.why: It has the smallest rate and the narrowest band: $12\% \times 1 = 0.12$bn.

options.label: The 18% slice (above EUR 30bn)
options.why: The 18% rate is the highest, but it only applies to EUR 4.5bn of BI: $18\% \times 4.5 = 0.81$bn.

scenarios.takeaway: A slice's contribution is rate times width. The middle slice is 29 times wider than the first, so it dominates.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain the elements of the new standardized approach to measure operational risk capital, including the business indicator, internal loss multiplier, and loss component, and calculate the operational risk capital requirement for a bank using this approach.

scenarios.setup: Standardized approach. Marginal coefficients: 12% on the first EUR 1bn of BI, 15% on the slice from EUR 1bn to EUR 30bn, 18% above. A bank has a Business Indicator of EUR 13bn, so $12\% \times 13 = 1.56$ and $15\% \times 13 = 1.95$ (EUR bn).
scenarios.ask: Where does the BIC fall?

options.label: Above 15% of BI (above EUR 1.95bn)
options.why: No slice is charged above 15%, and part of BI is charged at only 12%, so the blended rate cannot exceed 15%.

options.label: Below 12% of BI (under EUR 1.56bn)
options.why: The lowest coefficient is 12% and it applies to just EUR 1bn. The other EUR 12bn is charged at 15%, so the blended rate is well above 12%.

options.label: Between 12% and 15% of BI, just under the 15% end

scenarios.takeaway: The blended rate is a weighted average of the marginal rates. It sits between them and moves toward the top rate as BI grows.
scenarios.lo_text: Explain the elements of the new standardized approach to measure operational risk capital, including the business indicator, internal loss multiplier, and loss component, and calculate the operational risk capital requirement for a bank using this approach.

scenarios.setup: Altman Z-score, $Z = 1.2X_1 + 1.4X_2 + 3.3X_3 + 0.6X_4 + 0.999X_5$. A firm has total assets 670,000, working capital 170,000, retained earnings 300,000, EBIT 60,000, market equity 380,000, total liabilities 240,000 and sales 2,200,000.
scenarios.ask: Which is bigger: the $0.999X_5$ (sales/assets) term alone, or the other four terms combined?

options.label: The other four combined
options.why: The four together come to only about 2.18. Sales are 3.3× total assets, so $X_5 \approx 3.28$ on its own outweighs them.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: 3.28 versus 2.18 is a 50% gap. Asset turnover (3.28) is by far the largest ratio, and its weight of 0.999 barely shrinks it.

scenarios.takeaway: For a high-turnover firm, X5 (sales/assets) can carry most of the Z-score. Check it first.

scenarios.setup: S&P cumulative default rates for a **B**-rated issuer: 3.34% by year 1, 7.80% by year 2, 11.75% by year 3. The cumulative figure keeps climbing.
scenarios.ask: Is the marginal (unconditional) PD in year 3 larger or smaller than in year 2?

options.label: Larger in year 3
options.why: A rising cumulative PD tells you nothing about whether the yearly increments are rising. Year 2 adds 4.46 points and year 3 adds only 3.95.

options.label: Equal
options.why: The increments are 4.46 and 3.95. They differ by about half a point, so they are not equal.

working.label: Comparison
working.display: $3.95\% < 4.46\%$: the B-rated marginal profile peaks in year 2 and then falls

scenarios.takeaway: Speculative-grade marginal PDs peak early and then decline once the issuer survives. Investment-grade marginal PDs tend to rise over time.

scenarios.setup: Constant hazard rate $\lambda = 2\%$. Cumulative PD is $1 - e^{-0.02 \times 4} = 7.69\%$ by year 4 and $1 - e^{-0.02 \times 5} = 9.52\%$ by year 5. So the unconditional PD during year 5 is $1.83\%$.
scenarios.ask: The PD in year 5 *conditional on surviving to year 4*: higher than, lower than, or equal to 1.83%?

options.label: Lower than 1.83%
options.why: Conditioning divides by the survival probability $1 - 0.0769 < 1$, which can only make the number larger.

options.label: Equal to 1.83%
options.why: The two coincide only in year 1, when survival to the start of the year is 100%. By year 5 the survival factor is 92.3%.

scenarios.takeaway: Conditional PD = marginal / survival, so it is always at least as large as the unconditional PD. Under a constant hazard it stays flat at 1 − e^(−λ).

scenarios.setup: CDS spreads: 5-year 90 bp, 10-year 110 bp. Expected recovery is 65%. Average hazard rates are bootstrapped with $\bar\lambda = s/(1-RR)$.
scenarios.ask: The average hazard rate between year 5 and year 10 is closest to?

options.why: Scale slip: 1/30 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Scale slip (0.1×), e.g. a decimal slip when converting bp to percent.
You bootstrapped the raw spreads, $(10 \times 1.10\% - 5 \times 0.90\%)/5$, without dividing by $LGD = 0.35$.

scenarios.takeaway: Forward hazard = time-weighted difference of cumulative averages, divided by the gap in years. Gross spreads up by LGD first.

scenarios.setup: 5-year iTraxx Europe is quoted bid 150 bp / ask 152 bp. The index has 125 names. An investor buys EUR 500,000 of protection on *each* name.
scenarios.ask: The annual premium paid is closest to?

options.label: ≈ EUR 2,850,000
options.why: Scale slip: 3× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ EUR 9,500,000
options.why: Scale slip: 10× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ EUR 28,500,000
options.why: Scale slip: 30× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

working.label: Rate
working.display: Buyer of protection pays the ask: $152 \text{ bp} = 0.0152$

scenarios.takeaway: Index premium = ask spread × notional per name × number of names. A protection buyer pays the ask.

scenarios.setup: Merton model. Equity $E_0 = 3$, equity volatility $\sigma_E = 80\%$, solved firm value $V_0 = 12.40$, and equity delta $N(d_1) = 0.912$. Use $\sigma_E E_0 = N(d_1)\,\sigma_V V_0$.
scenarios.ask: Asset volatility $\sigma_V$ is closest to?

options.why: Scale slip (0.3×).
That is the equity volatility. Equity is a levered claim, so $\sigma_V$ must be much lower than $\sigma_E$.
You inverted the leverage ratio: $\sigma_E \times V_0/E_0 = 0.8 \times 12.4/3$. Asset vol cannot exceed equity vol here.

scenarios.takeaway: Asset vol = equity vol × (E/V) ÷ delta. With leverage it comes out far below equity vol.

scenarios.setup: The CDS-bond basis is defined as $\text{CDS spread} - \text{bond yield spread}$. A CDS contract lets the protection buyer deliver the *cheapest-to-deliver* bond on default.
scenarios.ask: This feature pushes the basis: positive, negative, or no effect?

options.label: Negative
options.why: Negative-basis drivers make CDS protection worth less than it looks: counterparty risk, accrued interest excluded from the payoff, bonds above par. The CTD option works the other way.

options.label: No effect
options.why: The CTD option has value to the protection buyer, and the seller charges for it in the spread.

working.label: Who holds the option
working.display: The protection buyer chooses what to deliver, which is an extra option

working.label: Effect
working.display: Protection is worth more → CDS spread rises relative to the bond spread → basis > 0

scenarios.takeaway: Anything that hands the protection buyer an extra option (CTD, restructuring clause) pushes the basis positive.

scenarios.setup: A counterparty's credit spread is 2%. The implied hazard rate is $\lambda = s/(1-RR)$. The desk revises its recovery assumption from 40% to 60%, with the spread unchanged.
scenarios.ask: The implied hazard rate: rises, falls, or unchanged?

options.label: Falls
options.why: Intuition says 'better recovery, safer name', but the spread is fixed. A smaller LGD means a larger default probability is needed to explain the same spread.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: The spread is unchanged, but it is divided by LGD. LGD moves from 0.60 to 0.40, so the ratio moves too.

working.label: CVA side
working.display: LGD falls from 60% to 40%. Per the reading, the LGD effect dominates, so CVA falls even though the implied PD rises

scenarios.takeaway: Holding the spread fixed, higher recovery → higher implied PD but lower CVA.

scenarios.setup: $EPE = 100$, $ENE = -80$, both LGDs 60%, counterparty $PD_C = 2\%$, own $PD_I = 1.5\%$. You have computed $CVA = -0.6(100)(0.02) = -1.20$. Next comes $DVA = -LGD_I \times ENE \times PD_I$, and then $BCVA = CVA + DVA$.
scenarios.ask: Compared with CVA alone (−1.20), is BCVA more negative, less negative, or the same?

options.label: More negative
options.why: You treated DVA as another cost. With $ENE < 0$ the product $-LGD \times ENE \times PD$ is **positive**, so DVA is a benefit. Taking it as negative gives −1.92.

options.label: The same
options.why: That is unilateral CVA, which ignores your own default. BCVA admits both defaults, so the DVA term is switched on.

scenarios.takeaway: ENE is negative, so DVA comes out positive. BCVA is less negative than UCVA.

scenarios.setup: A swap with notional USD 100m and risky duration 3.75 carries a CVA of $-90{,}000$. The desk wants it as a running spread.
scenarios.ask: The running spread is closest to?

options.label: ≈ −9.0 bp
options.why: You divided by notional only ($-90{,}000/100\text{m}$). The upfront CVA must also be spread over the risky duration.

options.label: ≈ −34 bp
options.why: You multiplied by the risky duration instead of dividing.

options.label: ≈ 240 bp
options.why: Scale slip: 100× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: Running spread = CVA ÷ (risky duration × notional). A negative CVA gives a negative spread, charged to the counterparty.

scenarios.setup: You have a bilateral trade. Your exposure to the counterparty tends to *increase* as its credit quality *worsens* (wrong-way risk).
scenarios.ask: Relative to the independence case, your DVA: increases, decreases, or unaffected?

options.label: Increases
options.why: That is the CVA effect: wrong-way risk increases CVA. DVA moves the opposite way. The same correlation reduces DVA.

options.label: Unaffected
options.why: CVA and DVA are driven by the same exposure paths. A dependence between exposure and default changes both.

working.label: Wrong-way risk
working.display: Positive correlation between your exposure and the counterparty's default probability

working.label: Directions
working.display: CVA ↑ (cost grows), DVA ↓ (benefit shrinks). Right-way risk flips both

scenarios.takeaway: Wrong-way risk: CVA up, DVA down. Right-way risk: CVA down, DVA up.

scenarios.setup: A securitization has equity, mezzanine and senior tranches. Default probabilities are held fixed while the default correlation across the loan pool increases.
scenarios.ask: The value of the **equity** tranche: rises, falls, or depends on the default rate?

options.label: Falls
options.why: That is the senior tranche. Higher correlation makes the extreme pool-wide losses that reach a senior note more likely.

options.label: Depends on the default rate
options.why: That describes the mezzanine tranche, which flips: down at low default rates, up at high ones.

working.label: Low correlation
working.display: Defaults cluster near their expected value, so the equity writedown is near-certain

working.label: High correlation
working.display: Outcomes spread out, including more scenarios with zero or very few defaults. That upside goes to equity

scenarios.takeaway: Correlation is a bet on dispersion: equity is long it, senior is short it, and mezzanine flips.

scenarios.setup: A CLO has 100 loans of USD 1m at 8.5%. Bond coupons due are USD 5,675,000 a year. Up to USD 1,750,000 of excess spread a year goes to the OC account and the rest goes to equity. 5% of surviving loans default each year, paying no interest, and are not replaced. 95 loans survived year 1.
scenarios.ask: Cash paid to equity in year 2 is closest to?

options.label: ≈ USD 0.0083m
options.why: Scale slip: 1/30 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 0.025m
options.why: Scale slip: 1/10 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 0.074m
options.why: Scale slip (0.3×).

scenarios.takeaway: Equity gets only what excess spread leaves above the OC cap, and each year's defaults shrink the base.

scenarios.setup: Same CLO. Year 1: 95 loans paid 8.5% on USD 1m each, excess spread was USD 2,400,000, and equity got USD 650,000 after the USD 1,750,000 OC diversion. Year 2: 4.75 more loans default. Bond coupons due stay at USD 5,675,000.
scenarios.ask: In year 2, how does the excess spread compare with the USD 1.75m cap?

options.label: Above the cap: equity still gets a small residual
Below the cap: all of it goes to the OC account
options.why: Excess spread falls but is still about USD 2.0m: $90.25 \times 85{,}000 - 5{,}675{,}000$. It is USD 246k above the cap.

options.label: Negative: the OC account pays the shortfall
options.why: Excess spread turns negative only once fewer than $5{,}675{,}000/85{,}000 = 66.8$ loans survive. There are 90.25 here.

scenarios.takeaway: Two custodian tests each year: is excess spread > 0, and is it > the cap K? Equity is paid only if both are yes.

scenarios.setup: Same CLO, same 5% annual default rate on surviving loans. At the start of year 5, $100 \times 0.95^4 = 81.45$ loans survive, each USD 1m at 8.5%; loans that default during year 5 pay no interest that year. Bond coupons due are USD 5,675,000 and the OC cap is USD 1,750,000.
scenarios.ask: Year-5 excess spread is:

options.label: Above the cap: equity gets the residual
options.why: About 77.4 loans pay interest, giving USD 6.58m. That leaves only about USD 0.90m of excess spread, well short of the USD 1.75m cap.

options.label: Positive but below the cap: all of it goes to OC, equity gets nothing
Negative: the OC account pays the shortfall
options.why: Negative only below $5{,}675{,}000/85{,}000 = 66.8$ surviving loans. At 77.4 the structure still covers its coupons.

working.label: vs cap
working.display: $902{,}150 < 1{,}750{,}000$ → all diverted to OC, equity gets 0

scenarios.takeaway: Excess spread shrinks with the pool. Equity cash dries up well before the structure fails to cover coupons.

scenarios.setup: Next week a bank expects USD 150m of new qualifying loan requests and a USD 75m Treasury purchase. It also expects USD 135m of drawings on existing credit lines. You've already totalled sources: USD 185m received today plus USD 100m expected = USD 285m.
scenarios.ask: The available funds gap: a shortfall (positive), a surplus (negative), or about zero?

options.label: A surplus
options.why: You dropped the credit-line drawings: $150 + 75 - 285 = -60$. Drawings on committed lines are a use of funds.

options.label: About zero
options.why: You dropped the securities purchase: $150 + 135 - 285 = 0$. Planned investments are a use too.

scenarios.takeaway: AFG = (loans + investments + expected line drawings) − (current + expected inflows). Positive means a shortfall.

scenarios.setup: Historical average cost approach. Total funds raised USD 1,000m, total interest paid USD 65m, other operating costs USD 10m, earning assets USD 750m.
scenarios.ask: Which is bigger: the weighted average interest expense (step 1) or the break-even cost rate on earning assets (step 2)?

options.label: The weighted interest expense
options.why: Step 2 adds USD 10m of operating costs to the numerator and divides by the smaller earning-asset base. Both push it up.

options.label: About equal
options.why: Even with the wrong USD 1,000m denominator, step 2 would be 7.5%. With the correct USD 750m it is 10%, well above 6.5%.

scenarios.takeaway: The denominator switches from total funds (step 1) to earning assets (steps 2–3). 6.5%, 10% and 12.46% are all correct answers to different questions.

scenarios.setup: Pooled-funds approach. New funds: USD 100m transaction deposits (50% placeable), USD 100m time deposits (60% placeable) and USD 100m new equity (90% placeable). Total operating cost is USD 30m. Suppose the time-deposit placeable share drops to 40%, with costs unchanged.
scenarios.ask: The hurdle rate on earning assets: rises, falls, or unchanged?

options.label: Falls
options.why: A smaller placeable base cannot lower the hurdle. The same USD 30m must be recovered from fewer earning dollars.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: The pooled funds *expense* (30/300 = 10%) is unchanged. The hurdle, though, divides by dollars placeable, which fall from 200 to 180.

scenarios.takeaway: Pooled-funds hurdle = operating costs ÷ dollars placeable in earning assets. Less placeable money means a higher hurdle.

scenarios.setup: A repo: bonds with face USD 10m and market value USD 11m are sold for USD 11m and repurchased after 31 days. The repo rate is 0.3% (actual/360), with no haircut or accrued interest.
scenarios.ask: The repo interest (settlement minus USD 11m) is closest to?

options.label: ≈ USD 280
options.why: You read 0.3% as 0.03%, a slip by a factor of 10.

options.label: ≈ USD 33,000
options.why: You applied the annual rate for a full year ($0.003 \times 11\text{m}$) and forgot the $31/360$ day fraction.

options.label: ≈ USD 280,000
options.why: You used 0.3 (30%) instead of 0.003, a percent-to-decimal slip.

working.label: Contract price
working.display: USD 11m market value (not the USD 10m face)

scenarios.takeaway: Repo settlement = contract price × (1 + rate × days/360), on market value. At 0.3% a month's interest is tiny.

scenarios.setup: The OTR 10-year trades special: the special spread is 0.22% for 125 days (actual/360). Price is 101.90 and DV01 is 0.085 per 100 face.
scenarios.ask: The financing advantage, in yield terms, is closest to?

options.label: ≈ 0.0066 bp
options.why: You multiplied the dollar value by DV01 instead of dividing. Dollar value ÷ DV01 gives basis points.

options.label: ≈ 9 bp
options.why: Scale slip (10×).

options.label: ≈ 92 bp
options.why: You used 0.22 as the decimal spread instead of 0.0022.

scenarios.takeaway: Financing value: spread × days/360 → scale by price/100 → divide by DV01. It comes out at under a basis point.

scenarios.setup: The OTR 10-year trades about 2.00 per 100 face rich to the C-STRIPS curve. You've valued its financing advantage (lending it at the special rate for 125 days) at 7.7 cents per 100 face.
scenarios.ask: The rest of the premium (richness minus financing), attributed to liquidity: bigger or smaller than the financing value?

options.label: Smaller: richness is mostly financing
options.why: 7.7 cents out of about 2 dollars is under 4%. Specialness explains only a sliver of OTR richness.

options.label: Much bigger: richness is mostly liquidity
About the same
options.why: About 1.92 of liquidity against 0.077 of financing is a ratio of roughly 25 to 1.

scenarios.takeaway: OTR premium = liquidity advantage + financing advantage, and the liquidity part is usually by far the larger.

scenarios.setup: Since 2009 a failed delivery of a Treasury incurs a penalty rate of $\max(3\% - \text{FFR},\, 0)$. The fed funds rate rises from 1% to 2%.
scenarios.ask: The penalty rate, and so the cap on the special spread: rises, falls, or unchanged?

options.label: Rises
options.why: The penalty moves inversely with the fed funds rate. It is largest (3%) when rates are zero.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: The 0 floor binds only once FFR ≥ 3%. At 1–2% the penalty is still falling one-for-one with FFR.

scenarios.takeaway: Fails penalty = max(3% − FFR, 0): high rates mean a low penalty, and zero rates mean the full 3%.

scenarios.setup: Special spread = GC repo rate − special repo rate for the on-the-run Treasury. Compare the days just before the next auction with the days just after it.
scenarios.ask: Just before the auction, the OTR special spread is: wider, narrower, or the same?

options.label: Narrower
options.why: Right after an auction the new OTR issue is in surplus supply, which narrows specialness. Before the auction, demand for the scarce issue pushes it wider.

options.label: The same
options.why: Special spreads follow a systematic auction-cycle pattern; they are not flat.

working.label: After auction
working.display: New supply of the OTR issue → less scarce as collateral → special rate nearer GC → narrower

working.label: Before auction
working.display: Rising demand for the issue to borrow → special rate falls further below GC → wider

scenarios.takeaway: OTR special spreads: wide before an auction, narrow just after (new supply).

scenarios.setup: A portfolio holds five positions of USD 2 million each. Every position has return volatility $\sigma = 30\%$ and every pair is correlated at $\rho = 0.2$. Use $z = 2.33$ and $\sigma_P = \sigma\sqrt{1/N + (1 - 1/N)\rho}$.
scenarios.ask: Portfolio VaR is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.84m
options.why: Used one USD 2m position as the portfolio value. Five positions of USD 2m is a USD 10m portfolio.

options.label: ≈ USD 13m
options.why: Scale slip (3×). Even with no diversification at all ($\sigma_P = 30\%$) VaR is only $2.33 \times 0.30 \times 10 = \text{USD } 7.0\text{m}$, so the answer must sit below that.

options.label: ≈ USD 42m
options.why: Scale slip (10×). The undiversified ceiling is USD 7.0m; nothing with $\rho < 1$ can exceed it.

scenarios.takeaway: Equal-weight VaR sits between the large-$N$ floor $z\sigma\sqrt{\rho}\,P$ and the undiversified ceiling $z\sigma P$, and $P$ is the whole portfolio, not one position.

scenarios.setup: Portfolio X has a VaR of EUR 400,000 and holds four equally weighted assets of EUR 1,000,000 each. Asset A has a beta of 1.2 against the portfolio.
scenarios.ask: Asset A's marginal VaR (change in portfolio VaR per extra euro in A) is closest to:

options.why: Scale slip: 1/10 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Also multiplied by A's 25% weight. $\text{MVaR}_A \times w_A$ is A's component VaR per euro of portfolio, not the per-euro marginal VaR.
Divided by one asset's EUR 1m instead of the EUR 4m portfolio.

scenarios.takeaway: Marginal VaR is a per-dollar number, $(\text{VaR}_P / P) \times \beta_i$. It sits near 0.1, not in the thousands.

scenarios.setup: Assets A and B are uncorrelated: volatilities 6% and 14%, positions USD 4m and USD 2m. Per-dollar covariances with the portfolio are $\text{cov}(R_A, R_P) = 0.0144$ and $\text{cov}(R_B, R_P) = 0.0392$, and the portfolio's dollar variance is $0.136$ (in USD m$^2$). Use $z = 1.65$.
scenarios.ask: The rise in VaR from adding USD 10,000 to asset A is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 21
options.why: Scale slip: 1/30 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 64
options.why: Scale slip: 1/10 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 190
options.why: Scale slip (0.3×). $\text{MVaR}_A \approx 0.064$ per dollar, so a USD 10,000 add moves VaR by several hundred dollars.

scenarios.takeaway: For a small trade, incremental VaR ≈ marginal VaR × trade size. On a USD 10k add that is hundreds of dollars, not the whole position.

scenarios.setup: Assets A and B are uncorrelated: A (6% vol, USD 4m) and B (14% vol, USD 2m). You have the per-dollar covariances with the portfolio, $\text{cov}(R_A, R_P) = 0.0144$ and $\text{cov}(R_B, R_P) = 0.0392$. Both marginal VaRs share the same factor $z / \sigma_P$.
scenarios.ask: Which asset has the larger marginal VaR, and so is the one to trim to cut VaR fastest?

options.label: A, because its position is twice as large
options.why: Position size does not decide it. MVaR is proportional to $\text{cov}(R_i, R_P)$, and B's 0.0392 is 2.7× A's 0.0144 despite the smaller position.

options.label: Neither: uncorrelated assets have equal marginal VaRs
options.why: Zero correlation between A and B does not equalise their covariance with the portfolio. Each still covaries with the portfolio through its own $\sigma_i^2 x_i$.

scenarios.takeaway: To cut VaR fastest, trim the position with the highest marginal VaR. Here that is the smaller but more volatile B.

scenarios.setup: A CAD 248m portfolio (volatility 16%) holds CAD 15m of stock T (volatility 13%). The correlation between T and the portfolio is 0.45. Use a 1-year 95% VaR with $z = 1.645$.
scenarios.ask: The component VaR of stock T is closest to:

options.label: ≈ CAD 0.096m
options.why: Dropped the position size. $1.645 \times 0.13 \times 0.45$ is per CAD 1 of T, not for the CAD 15m holding.

options.label: ≈ CAD 3.9m
options.why: Two slips: T's individual VaR computed with the portfolio's 16% volatility instead of T's 13%, and never multiplied by the correlation.

options.label: ≈ CAD 29m
options.why: Applied the correlation to the whole portfolio's VaR, $1.645 \times 0.16 \times 248 \times 0.45$. The CAD 248m is a red herring.

scenarios.takeaway: Component VaR = individual VaR × correlation with the portfolio. The portfolio's size never enters.

scenarios.setup: Stock T is a CAD 15m holding (volatility 13%) in a larger portfolio. You've computed its 95% individual VaR: $\text{VaR}_T = 15 \times 0.13 \times 1.645 = \text{CAD } 3.21\text{m}$. T's correlation with the portfolio is 0.45.
scenarios.ask: T's component VaR is above CAD 3.21m, below it, or equal to it?

options.label: Above CAD 3.21m
options.why: Component VaR is $\text{VaR}_T \times \rho$ and $\rho \le 1$, so it can never exceed the stand-alone figure.

options.label: Equal to CAD 3.21m
options.why: This is the classic intermediate-result slip: stopping at the individual VaR. The two are equal only at ρ = 1.

scenarios.takeaway: Component VaR ≤ individual VaR. With ρ = 0.45 it is under half.

scenarios.setup: A portfolio holds USD 8m in asset A and USD 4m in asset B. Daily volatilities are 1.5% and 2.0%, and the correlation is 0.6. Use $z = 2.33$ (99%) and a 10-day horizon.
scenarios.ask: The 10-day 99% VaR is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.043m
options.why: Scale slip: 1/30 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 0.13m
options.why: Scale slip: 1/10 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 0.42m
options.why: Forgot the $\sqrt{10}$. That is the 1-day VaR.

scenarios.takeaway: Scale VaR by $\sqrt{t}$. A σ built from dollar positions is already in dollars, so don't multiply by portfolio value again.

scenarios.setup: A portfolio holds two long positions: USD 8m in A (1.5% daily vol) and USD 4m in B (2.0% daily vol), correlated at 0.6, with a 10-day 99% VaR of USD 1.32m. The correlation rises to 0.9. Positions and volatilities are unchanged.
scenarios.ask: The 10-day VaR:

options.label: Falls
options.why: Higher correlation means less diversification. The cross term $2x_Ax_B\rho\sigma_A\sigma_B$ grows with ρ when both positions are long.

options.label: Stays roughly the same
options.why: The cross term rises from 0.0115 to 0.0173, lifting VaR from USD 1.32m to about USD 1.44m, a rise of roughly 9%.

scenarios.takeaway: With both positions long, correlation up → diversification down → VaR up.

scenarios.setup: A USD 3m portfolio holds CAD (66.67%) and EUR (33.33%) currency positions. Marginal VaRs are 0.0528 for CAD and 0.1521 for EUR. You want the lowest possible VaR with the full USD 3m still invested.
scenarios.ask: Which way should the mix shift?

options.label: Cut CAD, add EUR
options.why: Backwards. Cut the position with the highest marginal VaR (EUR, 0.1521) and add to the one with the lowest (CAD, 0.0528).

options.label: Leave it: the mix is already minimum-risk
options.why: At the global minimum all marginal VaRs are equal. 0.0528 and 0.1521 are far apart.

scenarios.takeaway: Minimum risk means all marginal VaRs are equal, so move money from the high-MVaR position to the low-MVaR one.

scenarios.setup: A USD 3m portfolio holds CAD (66.67%) and EUR (33.33%). Excess expected returns are 8% for CAD and 5% for EUR. Betas against the portfolio are 0.615 for CAD and 1.770 for EUR. The return-optimal portfolio equalises $E_i / \beta_i$ across assets.
scenarios.ask: Right now, which ratio $E_i / \beta_i$ is larger?

options.label: EUR's
options.why: EUR has the lower return and the higher beta, and both push its ratio down: 0.05 / 1.770 = 0.028 against CAD's 0.130.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: 0.130 against 0.028 is more than four times apart.

working.label: Action
working.display: Add to CAD: the optimum is at 90.21% CAD, where both ratios equal 0.0771

scenarios.takeaway: For the optimal portfolio, add to the asset with the highest excess return per unit of beta (or marginal VaR). Here that is CAD.

scenarios.setup: Two managers start from the same CAD/EUR portfolio (volatility 15.62%; excess returns 8% CAD, 5% EUR). Manager 1 rebalances to the minimum-risk mix. Manager 2 rebalances to the mix that maximises excess return per unit of VaR.
scenarios.ask: Compared with Manager 1's portfolio, Manager 2's volatility is:

options.label: Lower
options.why: Nothing can have lower volatility than the minimum-risk portfolio. That is its definition.

options.label: Identical: both equalise marginal VaRs
options.why: Only the minimum-risk portfolio equalises marginal VaRs. The optimum equalises $E_i / \text{MVaR}_i$, which tilts further into CAD (90.21% against 85.21%) and lands at 13.98% against 13.85%.

working.label: Difference
working.display: $13.98 - 13.85 = +0.13$ pts, bought with a Sharpe ratio of 0.551 against 0.546

scenarios.takeaway: Minimum-risk is not optimal. Adding return to the objective accepts a little more risk.

scenarios.setup: Two-currency portfolio: USD 2m CAD and USD 1m EUR, VaR USD 257.7k. EUR's marginal VaR is 0.1521, so its component VaR is $0.1521 \times 1{,}000{,}000 = \text{USD } 152.1\text{k}$. A full revaluation with the EUR position removed gives a VaR of USD 165.0k.
scenarios.ask: The actual VaR reduction from dropping EUR, compared with EUR's component VaR, is:

options.label: Larger
options.why: 257.7 − 165.0 = 92.7k, well under 152.1k. VaR is convex in the position, so the curve stays above its tangent and the tangent overstates the drop.

options.label: About the same, since component VaR measures exactly this
options.why: Component VaR is only a linear approximation. It works for small positions and poorly for one that is a third of the portfolio: here the gap is about USD 60k.

scenarios.takeaway: Component VaR travels down the tangent and incremental VaR down the curve. For a large position they differ a lot.

scenarios.setup: A candidate answer for the return-optimal CAD/EUR portfolio quotes weights of 90.21% CAD and 9.79% EUR, with betas against the portfolio of 1.038 (CAD) and 0.649 (EUR).
scenarios.ask: Its weighted-average beta is above 1, below 1, or equal to 1 (to rounding)?

options.label: Above 1: CAD's beta exceeds 1 and CAD dominates
Below 1: EUR's beta has dropped to 0.649
options.why: EUR's low beta carries only a 9.79% weight. The total is $0.936 + 0.064 = 1.000$.

scenarios.takeaway: Betas measured against the portfolio itself always average to exactly 1. That gives a free check on any candidate answer.

scenarios.setup: The average Dow stock correlation this month is 30%; its long-run mean is 35%. A regression of the monthly change in correlation on its level gives $Y = 0.273 - 0.78X$.
scenarios.ask: Next month's expected correlation is:

options.label: Below 30%
options.why: Took the slope's sign at face value (a = −0.78). The mean-reversion rate is minus the slope, a = +0.78, which pulls correlation up toward 35%.

options.label: Above 35%
options.why: With 0 < a < 1 the variable closes only part of the gap (78% of 5 points). It would overshoot the mean only if a > 1.

scenarios.takeaway: Regression slope = −a. With 0 < a < 1, the next value lands between today's level and the mean.

scenarios.setup: Correlation was 0.22 a year ago and is 0.35 now; its long-run mean is 0.45. The implied mean-reversion rate is $a = (S_t - S_{t-1}) / (\mu - S_{t-1})$.
scenarios.ask: Is the implied mean-reversion rate above 50%, below 50%, or too close to call?

options.label: Below 50%
options.why: Divided the move by the mean (0.13 / 0.45 = 0.29) instead of by the starting gap $\mu - S_{t-1} = 0.23$.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: Half the starting gap is 0.115 and the move is 0.13, clearly more than half (a ≈ 56.5%).

scenarios.takeaway: a is the fraction of the gap closed. Compare the move with half of $\mu - S_{t-1}$.

scenarios.setup: Dow stock correlations show a one-period mean-reversion rate of 78%. A later sample shows the mean-reversion rate rising to 90%.
scenarios.ask: The one-period-lag autocorrelation of those correlations:

options.label: Rises
options.why: The reverse property: autocorrelation = 1 − mean-reversion rate, so it goes from 0.22 to 0.10.

options.label: Is unchanged, because they measure different things
options.why: For the one-period lag they are complements that always sum to 1.

scenarios.takeaway: Mean reversion and one-lag autocorrelation sum to 1: more of one means less of the other.

scenarios.setup: In the 1972–2012 Dow study, the average equity correlation rises steadily from expansion (27%) to normal periods (33%) to recessions (37%).
scenarios.ask: Moving from a normal period into recession, correlation volatility:

options.label: Rises to its highest level
options.why: Tempting because the correlation level rises, but correlation volatility peaked in the normal period (83.06%) and dipped to 80.48% in recession.

options.label: Falls slightly, staying above its expansion level
Falls to its lowest level of the three states
options.why: The lowest volatility (71.17%) is in expansions. Recession's 80.48% is only a little below the normal period's 83.06%.

working.label: Change
working.display: $80.48 - 83.06 = -2.58$ pts; expansion is lower still at $71.17\%$

scenarios.takeaway: Correlation level peaks in recessions; correlation volatility peaks in normal times.

scenarios.setup: A 99% one-day VaR model is backtested over 252 trading days and records 6 exceptions.
scenarios.ask: Relative to its target, the model is:

options.label: Overestimating risk
options.why: The failure rate, 6/252 = 2.38%, is above the 1% target. Too many exceptions means VaR is set too low, so risk is understated.

options.label: About right
options.why: About 2.5 exceptions are expected; 6 is more than double that.

scenarios.takeaway: Too many exceptions means VaR is too low and risk is underestimated. Too few means capital is over-allocated.

scenarios.setup: A 95% daily VaR is backtested over $T = 252$ days and breached on 20 of them. Use the normal approximation $z = (x - pT)/\sqrt{p(1-p)T}$.
scenarios.ask: The test statistic z is closest to:

options.why: Scale slip: 1/10 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Divided by the variance $p(1-p)T = 11.97$ instead of its square root.
Stopped at the excess count $x - pT$ and never standardised it.

scenarios.takeaway: z is excess exceptions divided by their standard error, so it comes out in single digits. Compare it with 1.96.

scenarios.setup: A 95% daily VaR backtest shows 20 exceptions in 252 days at $p = 0.05$. You have the excess $x - pT = 7.4$ and the standard error $\sqrt{0.05 \times 0.95 \times 252} = 3.46$. The two-tailed 5% critical value is 1.96.
scenarios.ask: Is $7.4 - 1.96 \times 3.46$ positive, negative, or too close to call?

options.label: Negative, so accept the model
options.why: 1.96 × 3.46 = 6.78, which is below 7.4. Equivalently z = 2.14 > 1.96.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: The margin is about 0.6 exceptions, and z = 2.14 against 1.96 is a clear, if modest, rejection.

scenarios.takeaway: Rejection needs more than about 2 standard errors of excess exceptions. Here 7.4 > 6.8, so reject.

scenarios.setup: Basel backtest: a 99% VaR model checked over the last 250 trading days records 7 exceptions. The base capital multiplier is 3.
scenarios.ask: The capital multiplier:

options.label: Stays at 3
options.why: The green zone is 0 to 4 exceptions; 7 falls in the yellow zone.

options.label: Jumps to 4
options.why: The red zone, with multiplier 4, starts at 10 exceptions.

working.label: Zone
working.display: 7 exceptions → yellow (5 to 9): multiplier between 3 and 4

scenarios.takeaway: Basel zones: 0 to 4 green (multiplier 3), 5 to 9 yellow (3 to 4), 10 or more red (4). Expected is 2.5.

scenarios.setup: A credit line has a USD 10m limit with USD 4m drawn. Behavioural modelling puts the chance the rest is drawn at 60%. Funding the liquidity cushion costs 18 bp.
scenarios.ask: The charge for contingent liquidity risk is closest to:

options.label: ≈ 18 bp
options.why: Charged the full cushion cost, skipping both the undrawn proportion (0.60) and the drawdown likelihood (0.60).

options.label: ≈ 65 bp
options.why: Scale slip: 10× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ 650 bp
options.why: Decimal slip: treated 18 bp as 0.18 (18%) instead of 0.0018.

scenarios.takeaway: Contingent charge = undrawn share × drawdown likelihood × cushion cost, which is always a fraction of the cushion cost.

scenarios.setup: A credit line has a USD 10m limit, 60% drawdown likelihood, 18 bp cushion cost. The customer draws a further USD 2m, taking the drawn amount from USD 4m to USD 6m.
scenarios.ask: The contingent liquidity charge on the line:

options.label: Rises
options.why: Only the undrawn part is contingent. The drawn USD 6m carries its own on-balance-sheet FTP charge. The undrawn share falls from 0.60 to 0.40, so the charge goes from 6.48 to 4.32 bp.

options.label: Is unchanged, since the limit is the same
options.why: The charge scales with the undrawn proportion of the limit, not with the limit itself.

scenarios.takeaway: A drawdown moves exposure from contingent to funded: the contingent charge falls while the loan picks up its own FTP charge.

scenarios.setup: A bank prices liquidity with a single pooled average cost of funds across all funding sources and maturities. A business unit books a 10-year fixed-rate loan.
scenarios.ask: Relative to its true liquidity cost, the 10-year loan is charged:

options.label: Too much
options.why: The pooled average sits below the true cost of long-term funding, so long assets are undercharged and short assets overcharged.

options.label: About right, since averaging is unbiased
options.why: Averaging ignores maturity. It is only right for an asset whose maturity happens to match the average; a 10-year loan is at the long end.

working.label: Pooled average vs long funding
working.display: The single average cost < the marginal cost of 10-year funding

scenarios.takeaway: Pooled average cost undercharges long-term assets and overcharges short-term ones.

scenarios.setup: A 3-year CDS on a reference entity with a hazard rate of 3% per year and a recovery rate of 35%. The risk-free rate is 4% (continuous). Premiums are paid annually; defaults are assumed mid-year, with accrued premium paid on default.
scenarios.ask: The breakeven CDS spread is closest to:

options.label: ≈ 2 bp
options.why: Units slip: 0.0199 is 1.99%, which is 199 bp, not 1.99 bp.

options.label: ≈ 20 bp
options.why: Scale slip: 1/10 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ 60 bp
options.why: Scale slip (0.3×). Sanity anchor: spread ≈ hazard × (1 − R) = 3% × 0.65 ≈ 195 bp.

scenarios.takeaway: Sanity anchor for any CDS spread: $s \approx \lambda(1 - R)$, here about 195 bp.

scenarios.setup: A 3-year CDS (hazard 3%, recovery 35%, risk-free 4%). Per unit of spread, the PV of expected premium payments is $A = 2.6123$ and the PV of accrued premium on default is $B = 0.0406$. The PV of the expected payoff is $C = 0.0528$, and $s = C/(A + B)$.
scenarios.ask: If you forget $B$, the spread you compute is higher, lower, or the same to the nearest bp?

options.label: Lower
options.why: Dropping B shrinks the denominator, so s rises: 0.0528 / 2.6123 = 202 bp against 199 bp.

options.label: The same to the nearest bp
options.why: B is small but not negligible. It moves the spread by about 3 bp.

scenarios.takeaway: Forgetting the accrual leg credits the buyer with less value paid in, so the breakeven spread comes out too high.
